title: Serving HTTP

body:
The openapi/v3 package serves an API of typed operations, and its OpenAPI document. The end user’s Init declares each operation once, on a typed path, with a typed handler and the codecs of its bodies, builds the API with openapi.NewAPI, and hands it to httpserver.NewService, which serves it over TLS as Serving HTTP describes. The same declarations serve the requests and write the document, so the two can’t disagree.
The import path names the major version of OpenAPI the package follows, and the package’s name is openapi. Two packages beside it are opt-in, and openapi uses neither: jsoncodec reads and writes JSON bodies, and problem answers errors with RFC 9457 problem details. The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: OpenAPI endpoint DSL, as its revisions 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 amend it.
An API This Init serves an API of orders. It sources the server’s Settings, builds the API with NewAPI, and returns the Service that httpserver.NewService builds from both:
// Init is the end user's Init: it sources the server's Settings, builds the // orders API with NewAPI, and serves it with httpserver.NewService. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { settings, err := readSettings(ctx, s) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } api, err := openapi.NewAPI(s, openapi.Info{Title: "Orders", Version: "1.0.0"}, openapi.Unmatched{ NotFound: problem.Handler(http.StatusNotFound, jsoncodec.Problem), MethodNotAllowed: problem.Handler(http.StatusMethodNotAllowed, jsoncodec.Problem), }, openapi.RequestErrors(problem.FromRequestError, jsoncodec.Problem), openapi.CatchAll(http.StatusInternalServerError, serverError, jsoncodec.Problem), append(NewOrders().Operations(), openapi.Document(openapi.Root().Lit("openapi.json")), ), ) if err != nil { return nil, err // every mistake in the declarations, named } svc, err := httpserver.NewService(s, settings, api) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc}, nil } readSettings sources ADDR and a PEM file named by TLS_PEM_FILE, as Serving HTTP shows; the variable names are the service’s own. The service’s main is one call to httpserver.Main, which runs the App with the drain and the grace period a server behind a load balancer needs:
httpserver.Main(Init) NewAPI takes, in order:
the Setup, whose LoggerProvider the API logs through; openapi.Info, the document’s info, whose Title and Version are required. Version is the API’s, not humus’s or OpenAPI’s; openapi.Unmatched, the end user’s answers to a request no operation matches; openapi.RequestErrors, the answer to a request an operation rejects before its handler runs; openapi.CatchAll, the answer to every error nothing else answers; the operations, the document’s included; any number of openapi.APIOptions, given to every operation before its own parts. An openapi.Error is one. The answers are arguments rather than options, so an API can’t be built without them, and none has a default: openapi refers to no format, such as JSON, and writes no answer of its own. Errors describes them.
NewAPI calls each codec function, and each codec’s Schema, once, checks every declaration, and returns one error that names every mistake it found: a missing Title or Version, a nil handler, codec or answer, a path or a parameter it can’t serve, two operations at one method and path, two operations with one OperationID, two answers at one status on one operation, and the rest its doc lists. Init returns that error, and the App exits 1 with it, before it listens. NewAPI never panics over a mistake, so a path or a parameter declared as a package-level variable can’t fail its package’s initialization, and no mistake is left to fail every request.
An *openapi.API is an http.Handler. A service that also serves something the API doesn’t describe, such as a static page, mounts the API next to it on a mux of its own, with mux.Handle("/", api), and hands the mux to NewService. What is mounted next to the API isn’t in its document.
Paths A path is built from the root, one segment at a time, from literals and path parameters:
// The paths, built from the root. var ( orders = openapi.Root().Lit("orders") // /orders order = orders.Param(orderID) // /orders/{orderId} lines = order.Lit("lines") // /orders/{orderId}/lines ) Each method returns a new Path, so a prefix is a value that several paths and operations share. Root() is /, and so is the zero Path.
There are no path templates. A template is a string with a syntax: braces, wildcards such as {name...}, an anchor such as {$}, a trailing slash, a host, and a router’s own extensions. Each of them is something to parse, to reject, and to keep in step with the document, and a typo in one is found at the first request, or never. A typed path has none of them to get wrong:
The OpenAPI path and the router’s pattern are both written from the segments, such as /orders/{orderId}/lines, and the end user writes neither. A literal is made only of letters, digits, -, ., _ and ~, and isn’t empty, . or .., so it never needs escaping, in the document or on the wire. A path parameter is an openapi.PathParameter[T], a type of its own, so a query or header parameter given to Param doesn’t compile. Its name is an ASCII Go identifier, and appears once in its path. A path declares its path parameters, and an operation reads every parameter of its path, so a path and its operation can’t disagree. NewAPI checks every path, and rejects two operations at one method and path, and two paths that differ only in their parameters’ names, such as /orders/{id} and /orders/{orderId}, which OpenAPI forbids. The API redirects nothing: /orders/ and //orders are paths no operation serves. A path value is unescaped before it is decoded, so /files/a%2Fb gives the handler a/b.
Parameters A parameter is declared once, usually as a package-level value, with openapi.PathParam, openapi.QueryParam or openapi.HeaderParam, and its constraints. Each method returns a copy with one more part, so a declaration can be shared, and a variant made from it:
// orderID is the path parameter of the operations on one order. var orderID = openapi.PathParam[string]("orderId"). Description("The order's identifier."). Pattern(orderIDPattern) // byStatus and pageSize are listOrders' query parameters. var byStatus = openapi.QueryParam[OrderStatus]("status"). Description("List only the orders with this status."). Enum(Open, Cancelled). Default(Open) var pageSize = openapi.QueryParam[int]("limit"). Description("The most orders to list."). Minimum(1). Maximum(100). Default(20) // idempotencyKey is createOrder's header parameter. var idempotencyKey = openapi.HeaderParam[string]("Idempotency-Key"). Description("Sent again with the same key, the request creates no second order."). MaxLength(64) T is a string, bool, int, int64 or float64 type, such as OrderStatus, a string type of the end user’s own. A path parameter belongs to its path. A query or header parameter is read by each operation that gives it as a part, with openapi.Query or openapi.Header, and the handler reads every parameter with openapi.ParamFrom, as its own T:
func (o *Orders) listOrders(_ context.Context, req openapi.Request[openapi.EmptyBody]) ([]Order, error) { status := openapi.ParamFrom(req, byStatus) // Open when the request has no status limit := openapi.ParamFrom(req, pageSize) // 1 to 100, or 20 o.mu.Lock() defer o.mu.Unlock() listed := []Order{} for _, ord := range o.orders { if ord.Status == status && len(listed) < limit { listed = append(listed, *ord) } } return listed, nil } ParamFrom panics, naming the parameter and the operation, for a parameter the operation doesn’t read. That is a bug in the handler, and the panic is answered as Panics describes, rather than handing the handler a zero value that looks like an answer.
A path parameter is always required. A query or header parameter is optional unless it is Required(), and an absent one is its Default, or T’s zero value. A query parameter that appears more than once is rejected, and a header’s lines are read as their values joined by commas, as HTTP reads them. A header parameter’s name is matched whatever its case.
The constraints are Description, Example, Enum, Pattern, MinLength, MaxLength, Minimum and Maximum, plus Required and Default on a query or header parameter. The types check where a parameter goes and the values of its constraints, so these don’t compile:
a value of another type in Enum, Default, Example, Minimum or Maximum, which take the parameter’s own T; Required or Default on a path parameter, which has neither method; a path parameter given to Query, and a query parameter given to Path.Param; a T that isn’t one of the five. NewAPI reports the rest: Pattern, MinLength or MaxLength on a type that isn’t a string, Minimum or Maximum on one that isn’t a number, a Default or an Example that breaks the parameter’s own Enum, Pattern or bounds, a float64 value that is NaN or infinite, which the document can’t hold, a parameter given twice to one operation, and a zero parameter.
Pattern takes a compiled *regexp.Regexp, so a bad expression is a regexp.MustCompile panic where it is declared, never a 400 on every request. The document lists it as it is written, and OpenAPI reads a pattern as an ECMA-262 regular expression, so write it in the syntax RE2 and ECMA-262 share: no flags such as (?i), no \A or \z, and no POSIX classes.
A value that doesn’t parse as T or breaks a constraint, an empty path parameter, a missing required parameter and a repeated query parameter are each a *openapi.RequestError with status 400, whose Param names the parameter. The handler isn’t called, and RequestErrors answers it.
Operations openapi.Get, Post, Put, Patch and Delete each take a path, a typed handler, a decoder for the request body (Post, Put and Patch), an encoder for the response, and the operation’s parts:
// Operations returns the orders API's operations. func (o *Orders) Operations() []openapi.Operation { return []openapi.Operation{ openapi.Get(orders, o.listOrders, jsoncodec.Encoder, openapi.OperationID("listOrders"), openapi.Summary("List the orders"), openapi.Query(byStatus), openapi.Query(pageSize), ), openapi.Post(orders, o.createOrder, openapi.EmptyDecoder, jsoncodec.Encoder, openapi.OperationID("createOrder"), openapi.Summary("Create an order"), openapi.Status(http.StatusCreated), openapi.Header(idempotencyKey), ), openapi.Get(order, o.getOrder, jsoncodec.Encoder, openapi.OperationID("getOrder"), openapi.Summary("Get an order"), orderNotFound, ), openapi.Delete(order, o.cancelOrder, openapi.EmptyEncoder, openapi.OperationID("cancelOrder"), openapi.Summary("Cancel an order"), orderNotFound, ), openapi.Post(lines, o.addLine, jsoncodec.Decoder, jsoncodec.Encoder, openapi.OperationID("addLine"), openapi.Summary("Add a line to an order"), openapi.Status(http.StatusCreated), orderNotFound, invalidLine, ), } } A handler is a func(context.Context, openapi.Request[B]) (Resp, error). req.Body() is the decoded body, of type B, and openapi.EmptyBody for an operation that reads none: Get and Delete read no body, and openapi.EmptyDecoder reads none for a Post. The handler’s response is written by the encoder, and openapi.EmptyEncoder writes none. The context is the request’s.
The parts are:
the operation’s metadata in the document: openapi.Summary, Description, OperationID, Tags and Deprecated(); the query and header parameters it reads: openapi.Query and openapi.Header; its success status: openapi.Status. Without it, the status is 204 when the encoder’s media type is "", as EmptyEncoder’s is, and 200 otherwise; the answers to its errors: openapi.Error, and an openapi.CatchAll or openapi.RequestErrors of its own, which replaces NewAPI’s for this operation. A part that several operations share is a value, such as orderNotFound above. Deprecated() marks the operation in the document; the API still serves it.
A request is served in this order:
Each path parameter is decoded as its type, then each query and header parameter the operation reads. A failure is a RequestError with status 400. When the decoder’s media type isn’t "", a request whose Content-Type names another media type, parameters aside, or none at all, is a RequestError with status 415. The decoder reads the body. Its error is a RequestError with status 400, or 413 when it wraps *http.MaxBytesError, as http.MaxBytesHandler’s reader returns. The handler is called with the decoded Request. The encoder’s Encode runs, before the status is written, so a value that can’t be encoded is answered by the catch-all, never as a 200 with a broken body. The status is written, with Content-Type set to the encoder’s media type, unless that is "". The io.WriterTo that Encode returned writes the body. Codecs Every body names its codec, and nothing is assumed. humus doesn’t know what an API’s bodies are, so it doesn’t guess: an operation without its codecs doesn’t compile, and the codecs on each operation say what it reads and writes. The cost is that a JSON-only API names jsoncodec on every operation.
An openapi.Decoder[T] reads request bodies of type T in one media type, and an openapi.Encoder[T] writes them. Each has three methods:
MediaType() string, such as application/xml. A decoder’s is checked against the request’s Content-Type, and an encoder’s is the response’s. "" is no body: no Content-Type is checked or written, and the document lists no content. Schema() (openapi.Schema, error), the body’s JSON Schema, as JSON, which the document lists under the media type. NewAPI calls it once, and returns its error, so a codec that can’t handle T says so there, rather than on every request. A nil Schema lists the media type alone, as for raw bytes. Decode(r *http.Request) (T, error), or Encode(v T) (io.WriterTo, error). Decode’s error is answered with a 400, or a 413. Encode runs before the status is written, and its error is answered by the catch-all; the WriterTo it returns runs after. Decoder and Encoder are separate interfaces. With one interface for both directions, two generic codecs swapped between the body and the response compiled, and a codec that only writes, given for a request body, failed every request with a 400. With two, both are compile errors.
jsoncodec jsoncodec.Decoder and jsoncodec.Encoder are T’s codecs as application/json, and jsoncodec.Problem is T’s encoder as application/problem+json, for RFC 9457 problem details. They handle the details that are easy to get wrong:
It decodes one JSON value. An empty body, malformed JSON, a value of the wrong type and data after the value are errors, which the API answers with a 400. Unknown fields are ignored. An error from http.MaxBytesHandler’s reader stays wrapped, so the API answers it with a 413. Its Schema reflects T’s json tags with openapi.SchemaOf, and rejects a T that JSON can’t decode into or encode, such as a channel, a function or an io.Reader, so the mistake is a NewAPI error rather than every request’s. It encodes into a buffer, so a value that can’t be encoded is answered by the catch-all, and the response has a Content-Length. jsoncodec is opt-in. It uses only openapi’s exported API, as a third party’s codec would, and is named on each operation like one.
Writing a codec A codec of one’s own implements the three methods. This XML codec reads and writes T as application/xml, with a schema reflected from T’s xml tags:
// xmlCodec reads and writes T as XML, as application/xml: a second format, // whose schema SchemaOf reflects by T's xml tags. type xmlCodec[T any] struct{} // xmlDecoder is T's decoder as application/xml. func xmlDecoder[T any]() openapi.Decoder[T] { return xmlCodec[T]{} } // xmlEncoder is T's encoder as application/xml. func xmlEncoder[T any]() openapi.Encoder[T] { return xmlCodec[T]{} } func (xmlCodec[T]) MediaType() string { return "application/xml" } func (xmlCodec[T]) Schema() (openapi.Schema, error) { return openapi.SchemaOf[T]("xml") } func (xmlCodec[T]) Decode(r *http.Request) (T, error) { var v T err := xml.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&v) return v, err } func (xmlCodec[T]) Encode(v T) (io.WriterTo, error) { b, err := xml.Marshal(v) if err != nil { return nil, err } return bytes.NewReader(b), nil } It is given like any other codec, uninstantiated: openapi.Put(p, h, xmlDecoder, xmlEncoder). One operation can read one format and write another, such as jsoncodec.Decoder with xmlEncoder. An operation’s body has one codec, though, and there is no content negotiation by Content-Type or Accept: a body in a second media type is a second operation, at a path of its own.
Whether a codec buffers or streams is the codec’s to say. A decoder that buffers reads the whole body in Decode, as the XML codec does. One that streams returns a value that reads the body as the handler reads it, such as the request’s body itself. This decoder hands an upload’s handler the body unread, as an io.Reader:
// upload is the decoder of a body that is streamed: Decode hands the // handler the request's body, unread, as an io.Reader. type upload struct{} func uploadDecoder() openapi.Decoder[io.Reader] { return upload{} } func (upload) MediaType() string { return "application/octet-stream" } func (upload) Schema() (openapi.Schema, error) { return nil, nil } func (upload) Decode(r *http.Request) (io.Reader, error) { return r.Body, nil } The handler copies the body to where it is kept as the client sends it:
// putFile stores the request's body as it reads it: the decoder handed it // over unread. func (f Files) putFile(ctx context.Context, req openapi.Request[io.Reader]) (openapi.EmptyBody, error) { name := openapi.ParamFrom(req, fileName) return openapi.EmptyBody{}, f.Objects.Put(ctx, name, req.Body()) } The body is read after Decode has returned, so a body that fails partway, or runs past http.MaxBytesHandler’s limit, fails in the handler, and its error is the handler’s, answered by an Error or the catch-all, not by RequestErrors.
An encoder that buffers returns its encoded bytes, such as a *bytes.Reader. One that streams returns a WriterTo that writes as it goes. The WriterTo runs on the request’s goroutine, with the request’s context still live, so it may do more work once it has written the body. This download copies an object from a store such as S3 to the client, then records that it was downloaded:
// download is what getFile returns: what to copy, and what to do once it // has been copied. type download struct { body io.ReadCloser // the object's body done func() error // runs after the last byte is written } func (f Files) getFile(ctx context.Context, req openapi.Request[openapi.EmptyBody]) (download, error) { name := openapi.ParamFrom(req, fileName) body, err := f.Objects.Get(ctx, name) if err != nil { return download{}, err // no status yet: answered by an Error or the catch-all } return download{body: body, done: func() error { return f.Objects.MarkDownloaded(ctx, name) // ctx is still the request's }}, nil } func downloadEncoder() openapi.Encoder[download] { return downloadCodec{} } // downloadCodec writes a download as application/octet-stream. Its WriterTo, // the download itself, has no Len, so the response is chunked, and a // failure after the last byte is seen by the client. type downloadCodec struct{} func (downloadCodec) MediaType() string { return "application/octet-stream" } func (downloadCodec) Schema() (openapi.Schema, error) { return nil, nil } func (downloadCodec) Encode(d download) (io.WriterTo, error) { return d, nil } func (d download) WriteTo(w io.Writer) (int64, error) { defer func() { _ = d.body.Close() }() n, err := io.Copy(w, d.body) if err != nil { return n, err // the object failed partway: the response is cut short } return n, d.done() // a failed update: the same } The handler’s context is captured in the value it returns, and is still the request’s when WriteTo runs. The WriterTo is handed a writer that flushes each write, so each part reaches the client as it is written. Both operations are declared like any other:
openapi.Put(file, f.putFile, uploadDecoder, openapi.EmptyEncoder, openapi.OperationID("putFile"), openapi.Summary("Upload a file"), ), openapi.Get(file, f.getFile, downloadEncoder, openapi.OperationID("getFile"), openapi.Summary("Download a file"), ), An error the WriterTo returns comes after the status, so it can’t change the response; A failure after the status describes what it does instead.
Why codecs are function arguments An operation takes each codec as a function that returns it, such as jsoncodec.Encoder, rather than as a codec value. So a generic codec is passed uninstantiated, and the compiler infers its type argument from the handler: openapi.Get(order, o.getOrder, jsoncodec.Encoder) writes an Order because getOrder returns one, and the end user never writes jsoncodec.Encoder[Order]. A codec that doesn’t fit the handler’s types doesn’t compile, and the compiler’s message names both types.
Codecs are taken only as function arguments, never as a struct’s fields. Go 1.27.0’s compiler has a bug: given a generic function from another package, such as jsoncodec.Encoder, uninstantiated, as a field of a struct literal, it stops with an internal compiler error rather than inferring the type argument. The same function given as an argument compiles. An openapi.Operation is therefore built by a call, openapi.Get and the rest, rather than as a struct literal of handler and codecs, and a part that takes an encoder, such as openapi.Error, takes it as an argument too. An end user who keeps codecs in a struct of their own, to build operations from, instantiates them there, as jsoncodec.Encoder[Order].
Errors Every error has an answer the end user chose, written by an encoder the end user named:
A rejected request is a *openapi.RequestError, answered by RequestErrors, with the RequestError’s status, and the handler isn’t called. The handler’s error is answered by the first openapi.Error[E] whose E matches it, with errors.As: the operation’s own first, then the API’s. An operation’s Error for an E replaces the API’s. Anything else is answered by the catch-all, the operation’s CatchAll or NewAPI’s, with its status and the error itself if it matches E, or wrap(err) if not. A request no operation matches is answered by Unmatched. Error openapi.Error[E](status, enc) answers an error that matches E with status and E, written by enc. Given to NewAPI, it answers on every operation, and every operation’s document lists it. An error that only some operations return isn’t API-wide: it is a shared value, given to those operations, so the document lists it where it can happen:
// NotFound is the answer for an order that doesn't exist: a 404, as an RFC // 9457 problem detail. type NotFound struct{ problem.Details } // Invalid is the answer for a body that decodes, but that the API won't // accept, such as a quantity below 1: a 422. It isn't a 400, which is // RequestErrors' answer for a body that doesn't decode. type Invalid struct{ problem.Details } // Parts that several operations share. var ( // orderNotFound answers a NotFound, on the operations that address an // order. orderNotFound = openapi.Error[NotFound](http.StatusNotFound, jsoncodec.Problem) // invalidLine answers an Invalid, on the operation that reads a line. invalidLine = openapi.Error[Invalid](http.StatusUnprocessableEntity, jsoncodec.Problem) ) The handler returns a NotFound, wrapped or not, and the API answers it:
// find returns the order whose ID is id, or a NotFound naming id. func (o *Orders) find(id string) (*Order, error) { ord, ok := o.byID[id] if !ok { return nil, NotFound{problem.Details{ Type: "about:blank", Title: http.StatusText(http.StatusNotFound), Status: http.StatusNotFound, Detail: "There is no order " + id + ".", }} } return ord, nil } An answer from an Error isn’t logged: it is an answer the end user planned.
CatchAll openapi.CatchAll(status, wrap, enc) answers an error that no Error matched. NewAPI requires one, and an operation’s own replaces it. An error the catch-all answers is one the end user didn’t plan for, so the API records it, as Telemetry describes, and wrap decides what the client sees. It should not put the error’s text in the body, which may hold a database’s message or a secret; the record has it:
// serverError is the catch-all's wrap. Its answer is fixed, and never // carries err's text, which the API records instead. func serverError(err error) problem.Details { return problem.Details{ Type: "about:blank", Title: http.StatusText(http.StatusInternalServerError), Status: http.StatusInternalServerError, Detail: "The server failed to answer the request.", } } The catch-all also answers an Encode that fails, and a panic, which Panics describes. When the catch-all’s own encoder fails, its status is sent alone.
RequestErrors openapi.RequestErrors(wrap, enc) answers every *openapi.RequestError with its Status and wrap’s value. NewAPI requires one, and an operation’s own replaces it. A RequestError has:
Status: 400 for a parameter or a body that doesn’t decode, 413 for a body over http.MaxBytesHandler’s limit, and 415 for a Content-Type the operation’s decoder doesn’t read, or none; Param: the parameter that doesn’t decode, for a 400 about one, and "" otherwise; Err: why, the parameter’s error or the decoder’s. The document lists RequestErrors’ answer at 400 on an operation that reads a parameter or a body, and at 413 and 415 on one that reads a body. Its answers aren’t logged: a request the API rejects is the client’s mistake.
Unmatched openapi.Unmatched holds two http.Handlers, and NewAPI requires both:
NotFound answers a request whose path no operation serves. MethodNotAllowed answers a request whose path an operation serves, but not with the request’s method. The API sets the Allow header to the path’s methods before it calls the handler. The package writes nothing of its own for either. Unmatched is a struct, so its two handlers are named and can’t be swapped; a nil one is a NewAPI error. Their answers aren’t in the document, and aren’t logged. They are the end user’s own handlers, so a panic in one isn’t recovered by the API.
Problem details The problem package answers errors with RFC 9457 problem details, in any encoding the end user names. It is opt-in, and openapi never uses it:
problem.Details is RFC 9457’s problem detail, with json and xml tags that name its members in both serializations the RFC defines. Its Error method makes it an error, so a type that embeds it, such as NotFound above, is an error of its own that openapi.Error matches. problem.FromRequestError is a wrap for RequestErrors: type about:blank, the status’s name as the title, and the RequestError’s error as the detail. problem.Handler(status, enc) is a handler for Unmatched, which answers with status and an about:blank problem detail, keeping a 405’s Allow. Each takes any encoder of problem.Details: jsoncodec.Problem writes application/problem+json, and an XML codec of the end user’s own could write application/problem+xml.
Panics A panic of the end user’s code, on the goroutine serving an operation’s request, is answered as the document says, so the API keeps its contract even when that code has a bug. The API recovers a panic of the decoder’s Decode, of the handler, of ParamFrom, of the encoder’s Encode, and of the Len of the WriterTo it returns, which all run before the status is written. The operation’s catch-all answers it, with its status and wrap of an error that doesn’t carry the panic’s value, so the value never reaches the client, and the response is the one the document lists for the catch-all. The API records the panic, with its stack, and keeps serving every other request.
Recovering has a cost. Whatever the panicking code left half-changed, such as a map it was halfway through writing, or a lock it took without a deferred unlock, stays that way for the requests that follow. Nothing is rolled back. A recovered panic is a bug to fix, not an answer to rely on, and the operation panicked record is there so it gets fixed.
These aren’t recovered by the API:
A panic of the WriterTo’s WriteTo comes after the status, so it can’t be answered. The API records it as it records any other panic, and cuts the response short, as a WriterTo’s error does. A panic with http.ErrAbortHandler, which the end user’s code uses to abort a response on purpose, passes through to httpserver, which aborts the response without recording it. A panic while answering, in a wrap or in the encoder of an Error, a CatchAll or RequestErrors, which would panic again if it answered its own panic, and a panic in Unmatched’s handlers, pass through to httpserver, which records it and aborts the response, as Serving HTTP describes. A panic on a goroutine the end user’s code starts can’t be recovered by anything but that goroutine, and crashes the process, as it would anywhere in Go. A failure after the status The status is written before the first byte of the body, as HTTP requires, so an error from the WriterTo comes once the status, and whatever part of the body was written, have already gone out. The API can’t change the response, so it aborts it: on HTTP/2 the stream is reset, and on HTTP/1.1 the connection is closed before the final chunk. The client sees a failed response rather than one that looks complete. The error is the server’s, unless the client went away, and the API records it as response failed.
Whether a failure is seen depends on Content-Length. When the WriterTo has a Len() int method, as a *bytes.Reader does, the API sets Content-Length to it, so Len must be the number of bytes WriteTo writes: a body longer than its Len fails, and one shorter is cut short. Otherwise the response is chunked over HTTP/1.1, and has no length on HTTP/2. A response with a Content-Length that fails after its last byte has the length it was promised, and looks complete to the client. So a WriterTo that does work after the body, as the download above does, leaves Len out, so that a failure is seen.
A status that depends on that work needs the body copied elsewhere first. Encode runs before the status: it copies the object to a temporary file, say, does the work, then returns a WriterTo over the copy, and an error along the way is answered by the catch-all, with a status of its own.
There are no trailers. A failure after the status can only cut the response short.
The document openapi.Document(path) returns the operation that serves the API’s OpenAPI document, at path, with GET, as application/json. An API whose operations include no Document serves no document, and a Document whose path has a parameter, or a second Document, is a NewAPI error. NewAPI builds the document from the same declarations that serve the API’s requests, and encodes it once, so every request for it gets the same bytes.
The document is OpenAPI 3.2.0, the latest minor version of OpenAPI 3. The import path names the major version, and within it the package follows the latest minor version, since OpenAPI’s minor versions add to the one before rather than break it. When OpenAPI publishes a new 3.x, humus moves the document to it in a release of its own, whose notes say so. The end user’s code doesn’t change: the served document states the new version, and a golden file of it changes with it. The document’s info is openapi.Info’s. Each operation is listed at its path, under its method, with:
its metadata: Summary, Description, OperationID, Tags and Deprecated; its parameters, the path’s and those it gives to Query and Header, with their constraints; its request body, required, under the decoder’s media type, with the decoder’s Schema; its responses: the success status, under the encoder’s media type with its Schema; each Error, the operation’s own and the API’s, with its encoder’s; RequestErrors’ answer at 400, 413 and 415 where the operation can answer with them; and the catch-all at its status. What each body is listed as is its codec’s to say:
Codec Listed as jsoncodec.Decoder, jsoncodec.Encoder application/json, with T’s schema, reflected from its json tags jsoncodec.Problem application/problem+json, with T’s schema, reflected from its json tags a codec whose Schema is nil, such as upload and downloadCodec above its media type alone, with no schema a codec whose media type is "", such as EmptyDecoder no request body, or a response with no content a codec of one’s own, such as xmlCodec its media type, with the schema it returns, such as openapi.SchemaOf[T]("xml") Schemas are inline, since one Go type can have a different schema under each codec. openapi.SchemaOf[T](tag) reflects T’s schema from its fields, naming each property by tag, for a codec whose bodies are a Go type’s fields; it rejects a T that holds itself, which an inline schema can’t. A codec adds what its format needs, such as OpenAPI’s xml object, to the schema it returns. The document doesn’t describe itself, the requests Unmatched answers, or anything mounted next to the API.
Telemetry The API adds no spans and no metrics of its own: httpserver gives every request a server span and its metrics, as Serving HTTP describes, and the API names the span after the operation’s route, such as GET /orders/{orderId}. A 404 and a 405 have no route, so their spans are named after the method alone. The package never reads or sets OpenTelemetry’s globals. It logs through the Setup’s LoggerProvider, under the logger name github.com/z5labs/humus/openapi/v3, and emits three records, each one ERROR, in the request’s context, so each carries the request span’s trace and span IDs:
Record When Attributes request failed the catch-all answered an error http.request.method, http.route, error.type, exception.message operation panicked the API recovered a panic of the end user’s code http.request.method, http.route, exception.type, exception.message, exception.stacktrace response failed a WriterTo failed after the status was written http.request.method, http.route, error.type, exception.message Each is also an exception event on the request’s span, and operation panicked and response failed set the span’s status to Error. When the request’s context is done because the client went away, request failed and response failed go on the span only: the failure is the client’s leaving. operation panicked is emitted even then, because a panic is a bug whatever the client did. httpserver records no handler panicked for a panic the API recovered, or for a response the API aborted. Answers from an Error, from RequestErrors and from Unmatched aren’t logged.
Testing An API is tested whole, as the service that serves it, inside testing/synctest, with httpservertest, as Serving HTTP describes for any HTTP service: httpservertest.Start runs the end user’s Init on httpserver.Main’s defaults, on a humustest Host, and httpservertest.NewClient speaks HTTP/2 to it, trusting a CA that humustest.NewCA generates for the test. The requests go through the API exactly as production’s do: routing, parameters, codecs, answers and the document.
The shoppingcart’s app_test.go does it this way. Its start helper runs the service’s Init, with every variable it reads, on a new Host:
// start runs initWith on open, with every setting it needs, on a new // humustest Host, and waits for it to listen. Call it inside the bubble that // uses it. func start(t *testing.T, init func(context.Context, *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error), hostOpts ...humustest.HostOption) *service { t.Helper() ca := humustest.NewCA(t) bundle, password := ca.Issue(t, "localhost").PKCS12(t) h := humustest.NewHost(t, append(hostOpts, humustest.WithFiles(map[string][]byte{"tls.p12": bundle}))...) p, status := httpservertest.Start(t, init, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(telemetry.NoopBuilder)), humustest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "ADDR": ":8443", "TLS_PKCS12_FILE": "tls.p12", "TLS_PKCS12_PASSWORD": password, // Every field pgx uses is in the URL, so it reads nothing from // the real environment or ~/.pgpass. The password is new for // each test. "DATABASE_URL": "postgres://carts:" + rand.Text() + "@" + dbHost + "/carts?sslmode=disable", }), ) <-h.Listening("localhost:8443") return &service{h: h, client: httpservertest.NewClient(h, ca.Pool()), p: p, status: status} } Postgres can’t run on humustest’s Host, so most tests swap an in-memory store in for it: the service’s Init calls an unexported initWith with the function that opens its store, and the tests pass one that opens a map. Each test then sends requests and checks the answers, and stops the service with SIGTERM, checking that it exits 0:
func TestInit_answers_unmatched_requests_with_a_problem(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { s := start(t, func(ctx context.Context, setup *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { return initWith(ctx, setup, inMemory) }) isProblem(t, s.do(t, http.MethodGet, "/orders", "", ""), http.StatusNotFound) r := s.do(t, http.MethodPut, "/carts", "", "") isProblem(t, r, http.StatusMethodNotAllowed) require.Equal(t, http.MethodPost, r.header.Get("Allow")) s.stop(t) }) } The document is tested the same way. The test fetches it from the running service, compares it with a golden file, so a change to any declaration shows up as a change to the document in review, and validates it against the OpenAPI Initiative’s 3.2 schema, which openapi/v3 keeps in its testdata, so nothing is read from the network:
t.Run("as the golden file", func(t *testing.T) { var indented bytes.Buffer require.NoError(t, json.Indent(&indented, doc, "", " ")) indented.WriteByte('\n') want, err := os.ReadFile(filepath.Join("testdata", "openapi.json")) require.NoError(t, err) require.Equal(t, string(want), indented.String()) }) t.Run("valid against OpenAPI 3.2", func(t *testing.T) { require.NoError(t, validate(doc)) }) A handler is a plain function, so the business rules behind one can be unit-tested on their own too, with a store of the test’s own. A handler that reads parameters is tested through the API, since only the API decodes them: a Request the test builds itself has none, and ParamFrom panics on it.
The shoppingcart example/shoppingcart is humus’s reference service: an API for shopping carts, on Postgres, built on openapi/v3, jsoncodec and problem, and served by httpserver. It lives in the repository’s example module, so pgx, uuid and testcontainers stay out of the core module’s dependencies, and it is built and tested against the humus in the same commit. It has three packages:
endpoint, the API: six typed operations on carts and their items, their paths and parameters, the NotFound and Invalid answers, and the Store interface they are served on. database, the Store on a pgxpool.Pool, and the schema. app, the Init. It sources its settings with config.Struct, opens its pool through the Host and closes it with OnStop, builds the API with NewAPI, and serves it with httpserver.NewService. Its package doc lists every variable the service reads. Its tests run the whole service as Testing shows, its golden document is app/testdata/openapi.json, and a test behind the testcontainers build tag runs it once against Postgres in a container, on the OS Host, in a CI job of its own.
pgx’s ambient leaks pgx dials through the Host: the shoppingcart’s Init sets the pool’s DialFunc to the Host’s Dial, and its LookupFunc to one that returns the host unresolved, so the Host’s Dial resolves the name too. Everything else pgx reads, it reads from the real process, whatever Host the App runs on, as Ambient leaks lists:
pgxpool.ParseConfig, which parses DATABASE_URL, fills in whatever the URL leaves out from the real PG* variables, such as PGHOST, PGUSER, PGPASSWORD, PGSSLMODE and PGSERVICE, not from the Process’s environment. With no password in the URL or in PGPASSWORD, it reads the password from the real ~/.pgpass, or the file PGPASSFILE names. A PGSERVICE, or a service in the URL, is read from the real pg_service.conf. The files sslcert, sslkey and sslrootcert name, and ~/.postgresql’s defaults for them, are read from the real filesystem, not the Host’s. A URL with no host connects to a Unix socket, in /tmp or the like, through the Host’s Dial, which may not reach it. So the URL sets every field the service uses, host, port, user, password, database and sslmode, and nothing is left for pgx to find:
DATABASE_URL=postgres://carts:secret@db.internal:5432/carts?sslmode=verify-full The tests do the same, with a password generated for each test, so what a test runs doesn’t depend on the environment or the home directory of the machine it runs on.
Migration from rest.Run openapi/v3 replaces the REST half of rest.Run from before the reset, and bedrock’s REST DSL beneath it. Its server half is httpserver, as Serving HTTP describes.
Before the reset With openapi/v3 rest.Run(ctx, rest.Title(…), rest.Version(…), rest.Handle(route)) httpserver.Main(Init), with Init calling openapi.NewAPI(s, info, unmatched, requestErrors, catchAll, ops) and httpserver.NewService bedrockrest.Build(opts...), a bedrock.Builder[http.Handler] openapi.NewAPI, an *openapi.API and an error Title, Version, APIDescription; defaults "API" and "0.0.0" openapi.Info; Title and Version required SpecPath, default /openapi.json openapi.Document(path), an operation; no document unless the operations include one an OpenAPI 3.0.3 document an OpenAPI 3.2.0 document, from github.com/z5labs/humus/openapi/v3; following the latest 3.x rest.GET("/carts/{cartId}", h) … DELETE, a path template openapi.Get(cart, h, enc, parts...) … Delete, with cart := openapi.Root().Lit("carts").Param(cartID) cartID.Read(ep) for a path parameter nothing: the path declares it p.Read(ep) for a query or header parameter openapi.Query(p) or openapi.Header(p), a part Summary(s, ep), EndpointDescription, Tags, OperationID, MarkDeprecated openapi.Summary(s), Description, Tags, OperationID, Deprecated(), as parts PathParam[T any](name, opts...), an unsupported T failing every request with 400 openapi.PathParam[T ParamValue](name), a compile error, with constraints as methods Pattern(string), a bad expression failing every request .Pattern(*regexp.Regexp) ParamFrom returns the zero value for a parameter the endpoint didn’t read it panics, naming the parameter chi, chi.URLParam chi inside the API, read with openapi.ParamFrom; spans named after the route ReadJSON[T] jsoncodec.Decoder, given to the operation; plus 415, 413 and trailing data WriteJSON[Resp](status), written with the encoder’s error ignored jsoncodec.Encoder, and openapi.Status; encoded before the status is written ReadBinary(ct), WriteBinary(status, ct) a decoder or encoder of io.Reader in that media type, the end user’s own ReadFormFile, ReadFormField dropped a 204 with WriteBinary(204, "", …) and an empty reader an openapi.EmptyBody response, with openapi.EmptyEncoder: 204 by default ErrorJSON[E](status, ep) on every route openapi.Error[E](status, jsoncodec.Problem), or jsoncodec.Encoder for application/json, given to an operation or to NewAPI CatchAll[E](status, wrap, ep) on every route openapi.CatchAll(status, wrap, jsoncodec.Problem), given to NewAPI, and to an operation that overrides it a bad parameter or body: {"param", "error"} and a 400 outside the document a *openapi.RequestError, answered by RequestErrors, such as RequestErrors(problem.FromRequestError, jsoncodec.Problem), and a documented 400, 413 or 415 chi’s plain-text 404 and 405 the end user’s openapi.Unmatched handlers, such as problem.Handler, with Allow on the 405 the example’s own problem type problem.Details, embedded an error the catch-all answered: lost an ERROR record and a span event a panic: bedrock’s RecoverPanics around the runtime the catch-all, recorded otelhttp.NewHandler(h, "rest") on the globals, spans named rest httpserver’s instrumentation example/rest/shoppingcart in the root module; os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL") and pgxpool.New in main the example module; Init sources the URL, the pool dials through the Host, and OnStop closes it the example’s specs/ (a hand-written api.yaml, sequence diagrams) dropped; the served document is the golden file
description: How to serve an API with the openapi/v3 package: an Init that builds an *openapi.API with NewAPI and serves it with httpserver.NewService, typed paths and parameters, operations and the codecs every body names, jsoncodec and codecs of one's own, streaming ones included, the answers to errors, rejected requests, 404s and 405s, problem details, what happens on a panic or on a failure after the status, the OpenAPI 3.2 document, what the API records, how to test it, and what each piece of rest.Run became.
