body:
The queue/kafka package consumes Kafka topics as a humus.Service, with franz-go. The Service joins a consumer group, dials the brokers through the Setup’s Host, and hands each record to the end user’s queue.Processor, one record at a time per partition, in offset order. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with kafka.NewService, and returns it to humus.Main, whose defaults are a consumer’s.
The package produces records too. A kafka.Producer, which the end user’s Init builds with kafka.NewProducer, produces to one cluster for any Service of the process: a Processor that produces a dead letter or writes to another topic, an HTTP handler that publishes an event, a job. Producing describes it.
queue, in the core module, is the contract between the end user’s code and any broker: the Processor they write, and when a message is acknowledged. queue/kafka is in the nested module github.com/z5labs/humus/queue/kafka, so a service that doesn’t use Kafka doesn’t get franz-go in its module graph. The package has no App, no Main, no defaults of its own and no test package. The design behind the consumer is in Proposal: queue processing and the Kafka runtime, with its revision, and the design behind the producer in Proposal: producing to Kafka, with its revision 1.
The contract The end user writes one thing, whatever the broker: a queue.Processor, whose Process(ctx, msg) processes one message and returns an error when it couldn’t. queue.ProcessorFunc turns a function into one, and for Kafka the message is a kafka.Message: the record’s topic, partition, offset, key, value, headers and timestamp.
A queue.Delivery says when a message is acknowledged, relative to processing it:
queue.AtLeastOnce acknowledges a message once Process has returned nil for it. A message is never lost, and may be processed more than once. queue.AtMostOnce acknowledges a message before Process is called. A message is never processed twice, and is lost if processing fails or the process stops first. queue.CheckDelivery rejects any other value, the zero Delivery included, which is not a default. Every broker package’s Service keeps the rules of queue’s package doc:
A processing error under AtLeastOnce ends the Service. The message isn’t acknowledged, the Service stops as it would on a signal, and its Serve returns the error, so the App exits 1. The message is delivered again when the App restarts, to it or to another replica. A processing error under AtMostOnce is logged and counted, and processing goes on. The message was already acknowledged, so stopping wouldn’t bring it back. No panic is recovered. A panicking Processor crashes the process. Shutdown drains. On Serve’s context a Service stops taking messages, lets the ones in flight finish, acknowledges them, and returns. Process’s context is not cancelled when shutdown starts, only when the grace period runs out. Retries are the Processor’s. A Processor that wants to retry a transient failure does so itself, before it returns an error. Neither queue nor a broker package retries for it. So a Processor under AtLeastOnce must be idempotent. A message whose processing failed, or was cut short by a crash, a rebalance or the grace period running out, is delivered again, and processing it twice must leave the same result as processing it once. This Processor stores each order once, by the record’s key, and skips an order it has already stored:
// orders is the end user's Processor: it stores each order once, by the // record's key, so an order delivered again is skipped, and produces an // order it can't read to a dead-letter topic. type orders struct { mu sync.Mutex stored map[string]bool out io.Writer dlq *kafka.Producer } Its Handle method, the Processor’s function, hands each order it can read to store, and produces the others to a dead-letter topic with dlq, as Dead letters shows. store is the idempotent part:
// store stores the order m carries, unless it is stored already. It is // idempotent, as a Processor under queue.AtLeastOnce must be. func (o *orders) store(m kafka.Message) error { o.mu.Lock() defer o.mu.Unlock() id := string(m.Key) if o.stored[id] { return nil // delivered again: already stored } o.stored[id] = true _, err := fmt.Fprintf(o.out, "stored order %s: %s\n", id, m.Value) return err } A real Processor stores orders in a database, where the same idea is an upsert, or a unique key that turns a second insert into a no-op. The mutex is there because the Service processes its partitions concurrently, so Handle may be called from more than one goroutine at once.
A consumer The end user’s Init sources kafka.Settings with config.Struct, as Configuring a humus service describes, builds the Processor, and returns the Service that kafka.NewService builds. This one also sources kafka.ProducerSettings and builds the Producer its Processor produces dead letters with, as Building a Producer describes:
// Init is the end user's Init: it sources the Settings and the // ProducerSettings with config.Struct, builds the Producer and the // Processor, and returns the Service from NewService. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := kafka.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } list := func(v string) []string { return strings.Split(v, ",") } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) kafka.Settings { k := d // No .Default: Brokers, GroupID and Topics are required, so an unset variable fails as not found. k.Brokers = r.Get(env("KAFKA_BROKERS").Map(list).Validate(kafka.CheckBrokers)) k.GroupID = r.Get(env("KAFKA_GROUP_ID").Validate(kafka.CheckGroupID)) k.Topics = r.Get(env("KAFKA_TOPICS").Map(list).Validate(kafka.CheckTopics)) k.SessionTimeout = r.Get(env("KAFKA_SESSION_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.SessionTimeout).Validate(kafka.CheckSessionTimeout)) return k }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } dp := kafka.DefaultProducerSettings() producer, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) kafka.ProducerSettings { p := dp // The dead letters go to the orders' own cluster, so Brokers reads the consumer's variable. p.Brokers = r.Get(env("KAFKA_BROKERS").Map(list).Validate(kafka.CheckBrokers)) p.DeliveryTimeout = r.Get(env("KAFKA_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(dp.DeliveryTimeout).Validate(kafka.CheckDeliveryTimeout)) p.Breaker.OpenFor = r.Get(env("KAFKA_BREAKER_OPEN_FOR").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(dp.Breaker.OpenFor).Validate(kafka.CheckBreakerOpenFor)) return p }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } dlq, err := kafka.NewProducer(s, producer) // opens no connection: the first Produce does if err != nil { return nil, err } h := &orders{stored: map[string]bool{}, out: s.Process.Stdout, dlq: dlq} svc, err := kafka.NewService(s, settings, queue.ProcessorFunc[kafka.Message](h.Handle)) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc}, nil } env and list are the end user’s own helpers: env names a variable, and list splits a comma-separated value. The variable names are the service’s own: humus defines none of them.
The consumer’s main is one call to humus.Main, here with a telemetry Builder that names the service, as Telemetry describes:
humus.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) NewService opens no connection. It runs every check on the Settings again, rejects a nil Processor, and builds the Service’s instruments. It builds no client and registers no OnStop function, so an Init that fails after it leaks nothing. Serve builds the franz-go client, dials every broker through s.Host.Dial, joins the group and starts processing. Dialling through the Host is what puts the Service on a test’s network, with no test-only seam.
Init returns the consumer along with any other Service the process runs, such as a second consumer or the health Service. Any Service returning ends the App.
Settings kafka.Settings follows the settings convention: plain Go values, a check for each field, and kafka.DefaultSettings() for the defaults. Every field’s zero value means zero, never “use the default”, so an Init starts from DefaultSettings() and changes the fields it sources. The package reads no environment variable and no file, and defines no variable name.
Field Default Valid Check Brokers none: required at least one; each host:port, with a host and a port from 1 to 65535 CheckBrokers GroupID none: required not empty CheckGroupID Topics none: required at least one; none empty; no topic twice CheckTopics Delivery queue.AtLeastOnce queue.AtLeastOnce or queue.AtMostOnce queue.CheckDelivery TLS nil, which means plaintext any none SASL nil, which means no authentication any none SessionTimeout 45s positive CheckSessionTimeout RebalanceTimeout 60s positive CheckRebalanceTimeout FetchMaxBytes 50 MiB positive CheckFetchMaxBytes MaxPollRecords 500 positive CheckMaxPollRecords SessionTimeout and FetchMaxBytes keep franz-go’s defaults. RebalanceTimeout is franz-go’s 60s too, because a revoked partition’s record in flight has to finish within it before the partition moves to another member, as Revocation describes. MaxPollRecords bounds how many records one poll hands out, which bounds how many records an at-most-once crash can lose, and how long a revoke waits for the records in flight.
Other franz-go options become fields when end users ask for them, each with a default and a check. A new field breaks no one, because DefaultSettings supplies it.
Required fields Brokers, GroupID and Topics are required. None has a default: humus imposes no cluster, no group and no topic. DefaultSettings() leaves them nil and "", which their checks reject, and the end user’s chains for them have no .Default, as in Init above, so a variable that isn’t set fails as not found. The App exits 78, and config.Struct names every variable at fault in one error. With none of the three set:
init: config KAFKA_BROKERS: not found config KAFKA_GROUP_ID: not found config KAFKA_TOPICS: not found A value that fails its check fails the same way, naming the variable and the value. With KAFKA_BROKERS=kafka-0:9092,kafka-1:
init: config KAFKA_BROKERS: "kafka-1" is not host:port NewService runs the same checks itself, so a Settings built in code with a bad field fails Init too, naming the field, such as kafka: NewService: Settings.GroupID must not be empty. That error is no *config.Error, so the App exits 1: the fault is in the code, not in the configuration. How a bad value fails explains the exit codes.
The Delivery setting Delivery is set in code. Whether a record may be processed twice or lost is a property of the Processor, not of a deployment, so it is the end user’s design decision rather than an operator’s, and most Inits don’t source it. DefaultSettings() gives the safe one, queue.AtLeastOnce. An Init that wants at-most-once sets it on the Settings it builds:
clicks.Delivery = queue.AtMostOnce // a click lost to a crash is not worth a second count A Service has one Delivery and one Processor. A Message carries its topic, so one Processor can dispatch on it. Two topics that need different Delivery values are two Services.
TLS and mTLS Settings.TLS is the *tls.Config the Service dials the brokers with, and nil means plaintext. A client certificate in its Certificates makes it mTLS. The Service runs the TLS handshake itself over the connection s.Host.Dial returns, and sets ServerName from the broker’s host when the config leaves it empty, without changing the end user’s config.
The end user decodes the certificates from files, read through s.Host.FS so that a test reads them from its own directory and production from the real disk, as Reading a file describes. How they are stored and encoded is the end user’s decision. This chain reads the brokers’ CA from the PEM file KAFKA_TLS_CA_FILE names, and the client’s certificate chain and private key from the one KAFKA_TLS_CERT_FILE names:
// The CA's file is read first, and the client's certificate only once it has been. k.TLS = r.Get(env("KAFKA_TLS_CA_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).FlatMap(func(ca []byte) config.Value[*tls.Config] { return env("KAFKA_TLS_CERT_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(clientTLS(ca)) })) A missing variable, a missing file and a file that holds no certificate each fail as a config error with exit 78, named after its variable. readFile and clientTLS are the end user’s own helpers:
// readFile returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that reads the whole // file a variable names, through fsys. func readFile(fsys humus.FS) func(name string) ([]byte, error) { return func(name string) ([]byte, error) { f, err := fsys.Open(name) if err != nil { return nil, err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() return io.ReadAll(f) } } // clientTLS returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that builds the TLS // config of a client that trusts the CA in caPEM, and presents the // certificate chain and private key in the PEM file it is given. func clientTLS(caPEM []byte) func(certPEM []byte) (*tls.Config, error) { return func(certPEM []byte) (*tls.Config, error) { cert, err := tls.X509KeyPair(certPEM, certPEM) if err != nil { return nil, err } roots := x509.NewCertPool() if !roots.AppendCertsFromPEM(caPEM) { return nil, errors.New("holds no PEM certificate") } return &tls.Config{ Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert}, RootCAs: roots, MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12, }, nil } } Brokers whose certificates a public CA signed need no RootCAs: a config with only Certificates trusts the system’s roots. Brokers that need TLS but no client certificate take a config with only RootCAs.
SASL Settings.SASL is the mechanism the Service authenticates with, and nil means no authentication. It is franz-go’s own sasl.Mechanism, so the end user picks one of franz-go’s mechanisms, plain, scram, oauth or aws, and supplies its credentials from wherever they keep them: humus decides nothing about secrets. They are in franz-go’s own module, so they add no dependency. This chain builds SCRAM-SHA-512 credentials from two variables, reading the password only once the user name has been read:
k.SASL = r.Get(env("KAFKA_SASL_USER").FlatMap(func(user string) config.Value[sasl.Mechanism] { return env("KAFKA_SASL_PASSWORD").Map(func(password string) sasl.Mechanism { return scram.Auth{User: user, Pass: password}.AsSha512Mechanism() }) })) Both chains are from one Init, whose test runs it against a cluster that requires TLS with a client certificate and SCRAM-SHA-512. SASL sends its credentials over the connection, so PLAIN in particular belongs over TLS. A broker that refuses the credentials ends the Service with exit 1, rather than franz-go retrying a password that will never be accepted, as Failures lists.
Delivery What each Delivery commits, and when:
AtLeastOnce: each partition processes a batch of records, and then commits the last record it processed, which commits every record before it. A record is committed only once it and every earlier record of its partition were processed. A record whose processing failed, or was cut short, is delivered again. AtMostOnce: each partition commits a batch before it processes any of it, and then processes every record of the batch. A record is never processed twice, and the records of a batch are lost if the process stops before it has processed them. MaxPollRecords bounds a batch, and so how many records one crash can lose. Kafka acknowledges a partition’s offset rather than one record, so a commit covers every earlier record of its partition. Committing once per batch, rather than once per record, saves a round trip per record, and a revoke and a shutdown commit too, so only the records in flight at a crash are processed again.
Which records are processed again, by Delivery:
AtLeastOnce AtMostOnce Process returns an error that record and every record after it, when the App restarts. The records before it are committed. none: the error is logged and counted, and processing goes on the process crashes, or panics every record after the partition’s last commit none: the records of the committed batch that weren’t processed are lost a rebalance revokes the partition none: the record in flight finishes and is committed before the partition moves none: the batch in flight finishes before the partition moves the member is fenced out, and gives up the partition the records processed since the last commit, by the partition’s new owner none SIGTERM none: the record in flight finishes and is committed none: the batch in flight finishes the grace period runs out during a record that record and every record after it that record and the rest of its batch are lost Order and concurrency Each assigned partition has one goroutine, which processes its records one at a time, in offset order. Partitions are processed concurrently, so the concurrency is the number of partitions assigned to the Service. Kafka orders a partition and not a topic, so records of different partitions are processed in no particular order. Most consumers depend on the order within a partition, for example to apply one customer’s events in order, and a producer that keys records by customer puts each customer’s records on one partition.
A replica that wants more concurrency gets more partitions: a topic with more partitions than replicas spreads them across the group, and a replica processes each of its own at once. Under AtMostOnce as under AtLeastOnce, a partition’s records are processed one at a time.
Failures No panic is recovered: a panicking Processor crashes the process. Every other failure follows this table:
AtLeastOnce AtMostOnce Process returns an error not committed; the Service stops as on shutdown, and Serve returns the error, naming the record; exit 1 already committed; logged at ERROR, with the record’s topic, partition and offset; processing goes on Process panics the process crashes; nothing after the last commit is committed the process crashes; the batch was committed a commit fails because the member was fenced out of the group, or the group is rebalancing not an error: franz-go rejoins the group. A later commit covers the records only while the partition stays with the member, and otherwise its new owner processes them again the same, and the batch whose commit failed is not processed. It is logged at WARN with its offsets, and if the partition stays with the member, the batch is lost any other commit fails the Service stops, and Serve returns the error; exit 1 the same a poll returns an error franz-go doesn’t retry, such as an authorization failure the Service stops, and Serve returns the error; exit 1 the same a broker refuses the SASL credentials the Service stops, and Serve returns the error; exit 1 the same the brokers are unreachable franz-go keeps retrying and logs each failed attempt at WARN, and kotel counts it; the Service keeps serving the same A commit is refused for a fenced-out member with UNKNOWN_MEMBER_ID, ILLEGAL_GENERATION or FENCED_INSTANCE_ID, and during a rebalance with REBALANCE_IN_PROGRESS. A commit the Service doesn’t send, because the partition isn’t held under the member ID franz-go would send it under, is handled the same way: see Loss. A poll’s error ends the Service when it is an error code from Kafka that franz-go doesn’t retry; an error code franz-go retries, or a failure to connect, is franz-go’s to recover from.
An at-least-once failure stops the whole Service, not just its partition. The other partitions finish their record in flight and commit, so only the failed record and those after it are processed again, when the App restarts. The cause names the record, such as serve: kafka: processing orders, partition 0, offset 3: cannot process. An error that ends the Service is returned rather than logged, and the lifecycle logs it.
Stopping is loud on purpose. Retrying in place would block the partition with no limit, skipping would lose the record, and pausing the partition would hide the failure while the lag grows. A record that always fails shows up as a crash loop with its error in the logs.
Dead letters Dead letters are the Processor’s. A Processor that would rather skip a record that always fails than stop on it stores the record wherever it keeps dead letters, such as a table or a topic of its own, and returns nil. The record is then committed like any other, and the partition moves on. queue/kafka has no dead-letter topic, retry topic or skip policy: which records are worth stopping for, and where the others go, is the end user’s decision.
A dead-letter topic is produced to with a Producer. The orders Processor’s Handle produces an order that isn’t JSON, which would fail on every delivery, to orders.dlq, with the consumed record’s key, value and headers:
// Handle stores the order m carries. An order that isn't JSON would fail // on every delivery, so rather than stop the Service on it, Handle produces // it to the dead-letter topic, and returns nil once it is stored there. func (o *orders) Handle(ctx context.Context, m kafka.Message) error { if !json.Valid(m.Value) { // A dead letter, stored before the record is committed. return o.dlq.Produce(ctx, kafka.Record{Topic: "orders.dlq", Key: m.Key, Value: m.Value, Headers: m.Headers}) } return o.store(m) } The dead letter is stored before the record is committed. Produce returns nil only once the cluster has acknowledged every record, and Handle returns what Produce returns, so under AtLeastOnce the consumed record is committed only after its dead letter is stored. A dead letter that fails, because DeliveryTimeout passed, the circuit breaker is open or a broker refused the credentials, is Handle’s error: the Service stops as on any processing error, and the record is delivered again when the App restarts, rather than lost. Under AtMostOnce the record was committed before Handle ran, so a dead letter that fails is logged at ERROR, and the record is lost.
A dead letter may be stored twice. A record delivered again, after a crash between the dead letter’s acknowledgement and the commit, is produced again, and so is one whose Produce failed after its dead letter was stored anyway. Whatever reads the dead-letter topic tells duplicates apart by the key, as any consumer under AtLeastOnce must.
Copying m.Headers is safe: the Producer replaces the consumed record’s trace context with the dead letter’s own, as The send span describes. A Processor that wants a dead letter to say where it came from adds headers of its own, such as the record’s topic, partition and offset.
Shutdown and rebalances A Service gets the lifecycle’s two signals, and the consumer stops on the first:
Serve’s context is done as soon as the App starts shutting down. The Service stops polling, lets each partition’s record in flight finish, commits, leaves the group, closes the client and returns nil. Under AtMostOnce, the record in flight is every record of the batch that was committed. Shutdown stops Serve the same way, and waits for it to return. Process’s context is not cancelled when shutdown starts. It keeps the values of Serve’s context and carries the record’s span, but not Serve’s cancellation. So a Processor that honours its context doesn’t fail the record in flight on every SIGTERM, which under AtLeastOnce would make every rollout end in exit 1.
It is cancelled when the grace period runs out. Shutdown’s context carries the grace period as its deadline. When it is done before the records in flight are, Shutdown cancels Process’s context and the leave, waits for Serve to return, and returns an error that wraps its context’s error, which the lifecycle reports as a *humus.GracePeriodError, with exit 1. The records cut short are not committed.
Leaving the group rebalances it at once, so the other replicas take the partitions without waiting for SessionTimeout. A leave that fails, or that the grace period cuts short, ends in the same place: the coordinator drops the member once its session times out.
Revocation When the group rebalances and a partition moves to another member, such as when a replica starts or leaves, franz-go revokes the partition first. franz-go’s default balancer is cooperative-sticky, so a rebalance revokes only the partitions that move. The Service stops each revoked partition, waits for its record in flight, commits, and only then lets the rebalance go on, so the partition’s new owner starts after the last record this member processed. All of that has to fit in RebalanceTimeout: a member whose revoke outlasts it is fenced out of the group.
The Service polls with franz-go’s BlockRebalanceOnPoll, and allows rebalancing again right after each poll has handed out its records. So records are handed out only to partitions the member owns, and a slow record never holds up a rebalance beyond the revoke, which waits only for the record in flight.
Loss When the member is fenced out of the group, another member may own its partitions already. franz-go may report them as lost or, when it learns of the fence from a refused commit and rejoins the group as a new member, as revoked. Either way, the Service stops them after their record in flight and commits nothing more for them, and the partitions’ new owner processes the uncommitted records again.
Kafka checks a commit’s member ID and generation, but not who owns the partition, so it would accept a commit from the rejoined member for a partition another member now owns. So the Service sends a partition’s commit only under the member ID the partition is held under: that of the rebalance that assigned it, or of a later one that kept it. A member that gets a partition back after a fence commits it under its new member ID.
The defaults The consumer runs on humus.Main’s defaults, which are a consumer’s, so queue/kafka has no Main and no defaults of its own:
A grace period of 20s. A Processor that can’t finish its record in flight within it is cut short, and under AtLeastOnce the record is processed again. No drain. Nothing load-balances a consumer. Its traffic stops when it leaves the group, which it does as soon as its records in flight are done. The drain would only keep a consumer that has already stopped waiting. terminationGracePeriodSeconds When Kubernetes stops a pod, it sends the container SIGTERM, and then SIGKILL once terminationGracePeriodSeconds have passed, 30 by default. On humus.Main’s defaults, the worst case from SIGTERM to the exit is the 20s grace period and the telemetry’s shutdown, telemetry.Settings.ShutdownTimeout, 5s: 25s, inside Kubernetes’ 30s, with a margin for the process to exit.
A consumer that raises its grace period raises terminationGracePeriodSeconds with it, to at least the grace period plus the telemetry’s shutdown plus that margin. Otherwise SIGKILL ends the process first: its container exits 137, nothing in flight is committed, the group waits SessionTimeout before it moves the partitions, and the telemetry not yet exported is lost.
Overriding them An operator changes the grace period with HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, such as HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD=45s, and adds a drain with HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY, without a rebuild, as for any App. A team that wants another default in code passes humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod to humus.Main; the variable still wins over it. The lifecycle’s settings describes both variables.
Two Delivery values, two Services A Service has one Delivery. Two topics that need different ones are two Services, each with a group ID of its own, returned together from one Init. A group ID is shared by every replica of one consumer, and Kafka commits a group’s offsets per topic and partition, so the two Services need two groups:
payments := kafka.DefaultSettings() payments.Brokers = brokers payments.GroupID = "payments-consumer" payments.Topics = []string{"payments"} clicks := kafka.DefaultSettings() clicks.Brokers = brokers clicks.GroupID = "clicks-consumer" clicks.Topics = []string{"clicks"} clicks.Delivery = queue.AtMostOnce // a click lost to a crash is not worth a second count paymentsSvc, err := kafka.NewService(s, payments, p) if err != nil { return nil, err } clicksSvc, err := kafka.NewService(s, clicks, p) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{paymentsSvc, clicksSvc}, nil Either Service returning ends the App, so an at-least-once failure in payments stops clicks too, after its batch in flight.
Which Main Which Main the process uses depends on what a load balancer routes to, as the lifecycle’s runtime packages explains for mixed processes:
On its own, or next to a probes or metrics server, a consumer stays on humus.Main. Nothing routes to that server, and a drain would only delay the exit. Next to a server a load balancer routes to, such as an API, the process uses that server’s package’s Main: httpserver.Main for an HTTP server, with a 5s drain and a 10s grace period, or grpcserver.Main for a gRPC server, with a 5s drain and a 15s grace period. The consumer still stops taking records as soon as shutdown starts, and its records in flight then have the drain and that package’s grace period to finish, rather than humus.Main’s 20s. Producing A kafka.Producer produces records to one Kafka cluster. The end user’s Init builds it with kafka.NewProducer, from kafka.ProducerSettings, and any Service uses it: a Processor that produces a dead letter or writes to another topic, an HTTP handler that publishes an event, a job. It is not a Service. Producing has no loop of its own to serve: it is called from the Services that do, so it lives as long as they do and closes after them, as Shutdown and the grace period describes. One Producer is safe for concurrent use and serves every Service of the process.
Building a Producer The end user’s Init sources ProducerSettings with config.Struct, as it does the consumer’s Settings, and builds the Producer before the Services that use it. In the consumer’s Init, the dead letters go to the cluster the orders come from, so the chain reads the consumer’s KAFKA_BROKERS again:
dp := kafka.DefaultProducerSettings() producer, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) kafka.ProducerSettings { p := dp // The dead letters go to the orders' own cluster, so Brokers reads the consumer's variable. p.Brokers = r.Get(env("KAFKA_BROKERS").Map(list).Validate(kafka.CheckBrokers)) p.DeliveryTimeout = r.Get(env("KAFKA_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(dp.DeliveryTimeout).Validate(kafka.CheckDeliveryTimeout)) p.Breaker.OpenFor = r.Get(env("KAFKA_BREAKER_OPEN_FOR").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(dp.Breaker.OpenFor).Validate(kafka.CheckBreakerOpenFor)) return p }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } dlq, err := kafka.NewProducer(s, producer) // opens no connection: the first Produce does if err != nil { return nil, err } Each config.Struct names every bad variable of its own, and the consumer’s is read first, so with nothing set, Init fails naming KAFKA_BROKERS, KAFKA_GROUP_ID and KAFKA_TOPICS once each, as Required fields shows. A bad value of the producer’s, such as KAFKA_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT=0s, fails the same way, with exit 78.
Brokers, TLS and SASL are the consumer’s fields, repeated. They mean what they mean in Settings, take the same check, and dial through the Setup’s Host the same way, with the same TLS handshake. They are repeated rather than shared because a Producer may produce to a cluster other than the one a Service consumes, so each set is sourced on its own:
The same cluster, from the same variables: the chain reads the consumer’s variables again, as above.
The same cluster, copied: an Init that has already built the consumer’s Settings copies the three. The secure Init produces its dead letters over the same TLS, with the same SCRAM credentials:
producer := kafka.DefaultProducerSettings() // The same cluster, over the same TLS and with the same credentials. producer.Brokers, producer.TLS, producer.SASL = settings.Brokers, settings.TLS, settings.SASL Another cluster: the chain reads variables of its own, such as KAFKA_DLQ_BROKERS, with its own TLS and SASL chains.
A process that produces to two clusters builds two Producers.
ProducerSettings follows the settings convention, like Settings: kafka.DefaultProducerSettings() gives the defaults, every field’s zero value means zero, and the package reads no variable of its own.
Field Default Valid Check Brokers none: required at least one; each host:port, with a host and a port from 1 to 65535 CheckBrokers TLS nil, which means plaintext any none SASL nil, which means no authentication any none DeliveryTimeout 10s positive CheckDeliveryTimeout Breaker.Window 20 1 to circuit.MaxCount CheckBreakerWindow Breaker.Probes 1 1 to circuit.MaxCount CheckBreakerProbes Breaker.OpenFor 10s positive CheckBreakerOpenFor Breaker.ProbeTimeout 10s positive CheckBreakerProbeTimeout BreakerPolicy see The circuit breaker Trip and Probe set none: NewProducer checks it NewProducer opens no connection. It runs every check again, and fails naming each field at fault, such as kafka: NewProducer: ProducerSettings.DeliveryTimeout must be positive, which exits 1, as a bad Settings given to NewService does. It builds the breaker, the instruments and one franz-go client, and registers the Producer’s flush and close with s.OnStop. The first Produce dials the brokers.
Not settings: acks from all in-sync replicas and idempotent writes, which are franz-go’s and Kafka’s defaults, and which turning off would trade durability for latency in a way that stays invisible until a broker fails; and franz-go’s partitioner, which hashes keyed records with murmur2 as Kafka’s Java producer does, its linger, compression, batch size and buffer size. Like the consumer’s, a franz-go option becomes a field, with a default and a check, when end users ask for it.
A call Producer.Produce(ctx, records...) is synchronous. It returns nil once the cluster has acknowledged every record, with acks from all in-sync replicas, or an error once one has failed. So a record is either stored or failed when Produce returns, which is what AtLeastOnce needs: a Processor that produces before it returns nil has the consumed record committed only after the produced one is stored, as Dead letters shows.
More throughput is more records per call, or more goroutines. There is no asynchronous Produce. At franz-go’s level a synchronous call costs no throughput: it takes the same path through franz-go’s buffers, batches and requests in flight as an asynchronous one, and it stops franz-go’s linger on the partitions it produced to, so they are sent at once. Under load, records pile up while requests are in flight, and the next request takes them all, so the records of many callers share a batch. A caller that wants not to wait at all calls Produce in a goroutine of its own. An asynchronous call was rejected: its callback would run on franz-go’s one goroutine for results, where blocking stalls every producer of the process; a Processor that used it could commit a record whose output is later lost; and it would tie the API to franz-go’s.
Order. Records to one partition are stored in the order they are given: within one call, in the order of its records, and between calls on different goroutines, in the order they reach the client. When a record of a partition fails, franz-go fails the records buffered after it on that partition too, so a later record is never stored after an earlier one failed.
Errors. When a record failed, Produce returns one error joining each failed record’s error, with its topic, and its partition when one was chosen, so errors.Is finds kgo.ErrRecordTimeout, context.DeadlineExceeded or a kerr code in it. A failed call doesn’t say which of its records were stored: the records that failed may have been stored anyway. Produce rejects a record with no Topic before it sends anything, and returns nil when given no records.
Records outlive a cancelled call Produce honours its context up to the moment it hands its records to franz-go. A call whose ctx is already done sends nothing, starts no span, doesn’t reach the breaker, and returns an error that wraps ctx’s error.
After the hand-off, a ctx that ends returns the call at once, with the same error, and its records stay in the client, with a context of the call’s own, until the cluster acknowledges them or DeliveryTimeout fails them. Their spans and measurements are recorded then. So a handler whose request is cancelled returns at once, and the grace period reaches a Process blocked in Produce, as the lifecycle requires.
The records don’t follow ctx after the hand-off, because franz-go can’t cancel one caller’s records on their own:
A sent record can’t be taken back. The broker stores a request it has read, whether the client still waits for it or not. Cancelling the request would change what the caller is told, not what is stored. Only a batch’s first record counts. franz-go decides whether to fail a batch from its first record’s context alone, so a cancelled record in the middle of a batch is sent anyway. One cancelled record fails its partition. franz-go fails every record buffered behind it on that partition, whoever produced them. A cancelled request cuts the connection. It closes the broker’s produce connection and fails every request in flight on it, for every partition that broker leads. They are sent again after a new dial, TLS handshake and SASL authentication. It bumps the producer epoch. The next produce, on any broker, waits for the cluster to hand out a new producer ID. One Producer serves the whole process. If a caller’s ctx reached franz-go, any caller could fail any other caller’s records: an HTTP client that disconnects could fail a dead letter that a Processor buffered behind that handler’s event on the same partition. The Processor would get a context.Canceled that isn’t its own, and under AtLeastOnce that error ends the consumer, and the App exits 1.
DeliveryTimeout, and no retry settings DeliveryTimeout, 10s by default, bounds how long the cluster has to acknowledge the records of one call, franz-go’s retries included. A record that isn’t acknowledged by then fails, even one already sent, and may still have been stored, so a caller that produces it again may store it twice, which is at-least-once and what a Processor under AtLeastOnce already handles. Without the bound, a hung broker would hold a call, and the App’s shutdown, until it answered.
DeliveryTimeout is the one retry setting: how long a call lets franz-go keep trying. There is no retry count, no backoff and no retry budget, and no bedrock retry.Retrier around Produce, because franz-go retries, and a retry around it would do harm:
Duplicates. franz-go’s idempotent producer retries a batch on the sequence numbers that let the broker drop a batch it has already stored. A retry around Produce would hand the records over again under new sequence numbers, and store twice a record whose first send landed. Order. franz-go retries a partition’s batches in order. A retry around Produce would send its records after whatever other calls produced in the meantime. Retries don’t multiply with callers. franz-go retries a partition’s batch, which holds every caller’s records for that partition, once per backoff. A thousand callers waiting on a dead partition cost one retry per backoff, not a thousand, so there is no retry storm for a budget to stop. The default fits the grace periods of the runtime packages: it is half of humus.Main’s 20s, which a consumer runs on, so a Process blocked in Produce at SIGTERM finishes inside the grace period, and it equals httpserver.Main’s 10s, where a handler’s Produce returns sooner anyway when the grace period cancels its request.
The circuit breaker A circuit breaker guards the cluster, so that while the cluster keeps failing, Produce fails at once rather than hold every caller for DeliveryTimeout. Without it, an HTTP handler that publishes an event would hold its request for 10s during an outage before it answered 503. With it, the first few calls wait, and the rest fail at once until a probe gets through. It is bedrock’s circuit.Breaker, one per Producer: one Producer is one client to one cluster.
While the breaker is open, Produce returns at once, with nothing sent, an error wrapping a *circuit.RejectedError, which matches circuit.ErrRejected and says how much longer the breaker stays open in its RetryAfter. Produce doesn’t retry a rejected call: whether to wait and try again is the caller’s, as queue’s contract leaves retries to the Processor.
Each call to Produce is one call through the breaker. It is admitted before any of its records reach franz-go, and counted once every record has its result, which may be after Produce returns. The breaker counts the cluster, not the records or the callers:
A success is a call whose every record was acknowledged. An ignored call counts as nothing: its records failed for their own reasons or their topics’, not the cluster’s, with a Kafka error code franz-go doesn’t retry, such as MESSAGE_TOO_LARGE, INVALID_RECORD or TOPIC_AUTHORIZATION_FAILED, or UNKNOWN_TOPIC_OR_PARTITION once franz-go has given up on the topic. One topic’s mistake doesn’t open the breaker for the others. A failure is anything else, the cluster not storing records in time: DeliveryTimeout passing, kgo.ErrRecordTimeout, a retriable error code franz-go stopped on, or a connection that failed. A caller giving up never counts: the breaker sees each call’s result with the call’s own context, which a caller’s ctx doesn’t cancel. A call whose ctx was already done, and a call after a broker refused the credentials, return before the breaker, so it counts neither.
The defaults: the breaker opens after 5 failures in a row, or once half of the last 20 calls, Breaker.Window, failed. It stays open for Breaker.OpenFor, 10s, and then turns half-open: it lets Breaker.Probes calls through at once, 1, as probes, each holding its slot for at most Breaker.ProbeTimeout, 10s, which matches DeliveryTimeout, so a probe holds its slot no longer than its call does. It opens again on a failed probe, and closes after 3 successful ones. Breaker is bedrock’s own circuit.Config, with a check for each field, so an operator’s bad KAFKA_BREAKER_OPEN_FOR fails startup naming the variable, with exit 78.
BreakerPolicy is set in code. It is a circuit.Policy, two functions, Trip and Probe, so it can’t come from a variable. bedrock ships no policy, so DefaultProducerSettings holds humus’s, and the end user replaces it in their Init. A policy whose Trip always returns false turns the breaker off:
ps.BreakerPolicy.Trip = func(circuit.Counts) bool { return false } One breaker covers every partition. When one broker of three is down, the calls to the partitions it leads fail and the rest succeed, which the default policy may or may not trip on. A breaker per broker or per partition would follow Kafka’s failures more closely, but franz-go picks a record’s partition inside the client, after the breaker has admitted the call. franz-go moves unkeyed records away from backed-up partitions, and a keyed record has only one partition.
Each change of the breaker’s state is a log record, as The logs lists. The Producer measures the breaker too, with three instruments of humus’s own: its state, its changes of state, and the calls it counted or rejected, as humus’s own instruments lists. A rejected call is also an error on its records’ spans.
Refused credentials When a broker refuses the Producer’s SASL credentials, with SASL_AUTHENTICATION_FAILED, UNSUPPORTED_SASL_MECHANISM or ILLEGAL_SASL_STATE, the Producer fails every call. franz-go would otherwise retry the connection, and each call would wait out its DeliveryTimeout with no sign of why. A Service stops the App on a refusal, as Failures lists, and a Producer can’t, so it fails loudly instead:
on the first refusal, it emits one ERROR record, a broker refused the credentials, naming the broker, as The logs lists, and the calls waiting on their records return the refusal; from then on, every Produce returns the refusal at once, with nothing sent, and before the breaker. The error names the broker as host:port, as the Service’s does, and errors.Is finds its kerr code in it, such as kerr.SaslAuthenticationFailed. Credentials don’t fix themselves while the process runs, so the Producer never tries them again: a Processor that produces fails its record, under AtLeastOnce the Service stops, and the App is restarted with whatever the secret holds then.
Shutdown and the grace period The Producer is not a Service, so the lifecycle doesn’t stop it. The Services that use it stop first: the App calls their Shutdown, waits for every Serve to return, and only then runs the OnStop functions, so no Service is producing when the Producer closes. On SIGTERM, a Process blocked in Produce keeps its context, as Shutdown and rebalances describes, so its dead letter is stored, and its record committed, as the Service drains.
NewProducer registers one function with s.OnStop. It flushes the client with the grace period’s context, which waits for the records still in it, such as those of a call that returned when its ctx was done, at most DeliveryTimeout old. Then it closes the client.
When the grace period runs out first, closing the client fails what is left with kgo.ErrClientClosed, those records are lost, and the function returns an error that wraps the context’s error, which the lifecycle reports as a *humus.GracePeriodError, with exit 1. A Produce after that, from a goroutine the end user left running, fails at once with an error that wraps kgo.ErrClientClosed.
If the end user’s Init fails after NewProducer, the lifecycle runs the OnStop functions registered so far, so the client is closed and none of franz-go’s goroutines outlive the App.
Telemetry The Service and the Producer report through the Setup’s telemetry, s.Telemetry, and never through OpenTelemetry’s globals: their tracers and meters come from the SDK’s TracerProvider and MeterProvider, under the scope github.com/z5labs/humus/queue/kafka, and their propagator is the SDK’s Propagator.
The process span Each record is processed under a span of its own, named process <topic>, such as process orders, of kind CONSUMER. Process is given a context that carries it, so every span the Processor starts from that context is its child, and every record it logs with that context carries its trace ID.
Its parent is the producer’s. The span’s parent is the trace context the propagator extracts from the record’s headers, so a producer’s trace continues through the consumer. The producer’s baggage, and only the producer’s, is on Process’s context too. A record whose headers carry no trace context starts a new trace: Serve’s span is never a record’s parent.
Its attributes follow OpenTelemetry’s messaging conventions: messaging.system (kafka), messaging.operation.type and messaging.operation.name (both process), messaging.destination.name, messaging.destination.partition.id, messaging.consumer.group.name and messaging.kafka.offset. The record’s key is not recorded, because it often holds a customer’s identifier. When Process returns an error, under either Delivery, the error is recorded on the span as an exception event, with error.type and an error status.
The send span The Producer sends each record under a span of its own, named send <topic>, such as send orders.dlq, of kind PRODUCER, a child of the span in Produce’s context. Its attributes are messaging.system (kafka), messaging.operation.type and messaging.operation.name (both send) and messaging.destination.name, and, once the record is acknowledged, messaging.destination.partition.id and messaging.kafka.offset. The record’s key is not recorded, as the consumer doesn’t record it. The span ends when the record is acknowledged or fails, as its result arrives, which may be after Produce returns. A failure, a rejection by the breaker included, is recorded on it as an exception event, with error.type and an error status.
The span’s context goes into the record’s headers. The Setup’s propagator injects it, with the baggage of Produce’s context: with the default propagator, those are traceparent, tracestate and baggage. Before injecting, the Producer removes every header of the record whose key is one of the propagator’s fields. A dead letter that copies the consumed record’s headers would otherwise carry two traceparent headers, and the consumer would read the first, the old one.
So the process span of a Service that consumes the record, on any topic, is a child of its send span, and inside a Process, the send span is a child of the process span: one trace runs from the first producer through every topic a record passes through, its dead letter included.
When a span starts. Produce first checks the call: a record with no topic, a ctx already done, a closed client or a broker’s earlier refusal of the credentials returns it at once, and starts no span. Only then does each record’s span start, and its headers get the trace context, before the call goes through the breaker. So a call the breaker rejects has a span for each record, which records the rejection, and a call that never got past the checks has none.
The instruments The Service records three instruments of the messaging conventions, as semconv v1.43.0 names them:
Instrument Kind What it records messaging.client.consumed.messages counter the records handed to the Processor, with messaging.operation.name set to process messaging.process.duration histogram, in seconds how long each Process took, with messaging.operation.name set to process, and error.type when it failed messaging.client.operation.duration histogram, in seconds how long each commit took, with messaging.operation.name set to commit and messaging.operation.type to settle, and error.type when it failed Each also has messaging.system, messaging.consumer.group.name, messaging.destination.name and messaging.destination.partition.id.
The Producer records two more:
Instrument Kind What it records messaging.client.sent.messages counter each record once its result is known, with messaging.operation.name set to send, and error.type when it failed messaging.client.operation.duration histogram, in seconds how long each record took, from Produce taking it to its result, with messaging.operation.name and messaging.operation.type set to send, and error.type when it failed Each also has messaging.system, messaging.destination.name and, once franz-go has chosen it, messaging.destination.partition.id. The Producer’s messaging.client.operation.duration is the same instrument as the Service’s commits, told apart by messaging.operation.name. A record the breaker rejected, a record with no topic, and the records of a call whose context was already done were never sent, so neither instrument counts them: the conventions say a sent-messages count must not count messages that were created but haven’t been sent. A rejected record’s span records the rejection, and humus.circuit.calls counts its call.
The messaging conventions are still in development, so humus pins the semconv version it uses, and a change to these names is a breaking change to queue/kafka.
humus’s own instruments The Producer records three instruments of humus’s own for its breaker, with the Setup’s MeterProvider, in the scope github.com/z5labs/humus/queue/kafka, beside its messaging instruments:
Instrument Kind Unit Attributes Recorded humus.circuit.state asynchronous UpDownCounter {breaker} humus.circuit.state: closed, open or half-open at each collection: 1 for the breaker’s state, 0 for the other two humus.circuit.transitions Counter {transition} humus.circuit.state, the state it went to, and humus.circuit.previous_state, the one it left at each change of the breaker’s state, beside its log record humus.circuit.calls Counter {call} humus.circuit.outcome: success, failure, ignored or rejected once a call’s every record has its result, or as the breaker rejects it Every data point also carries the cluster’s attributes: messaging.system, set to kafka, and server.address and server.port of the first of ProducerSettings.Brokers, the seed the end user named first rather than the broker that answered. It carries nothing per call, such as messaging.destination.name: the messaging instruments break records down already. Each other attribute’s value is the String() of bedrock’s own type, circuit.State or circuit.Outcome.
humus.circuit.state is read, not tracked. At each collection it reads the breaker’s state once, so it shows half-open as soon as OpenFor has passed, with no call made. Two Producers for two clusters are two series, told apart by their first brokers. The App’s last collection, after the OnStop functions, still reads it, so the final export has the state the App stopped in. humus.circuit.transitions catches the short opens. A breaker can open, go half-open and close between two collections, a minute apart by default, and humus.circuit.state never shows it open. humus.circuit.calls counts a call when the breaker does. One call is one Produce, whatever its number of records, counted once every record has its result, which may be after Produce returns. A call whose records failed for their own reasons or their topics’ is ignored. A call the breaker rejects is rejected, once: it sent nothing, so it is in neither messaging instrument. A call whose ctx was already done, or one after a broker refused the credentials, never reached the breaker and counts nothing. There is no humus.retry.decisions, as humus’s HTTP and gRPC clients record: franz-go retries inside a produce request, and exposes no decision to count.
In Prometheus, they are humus_circuit_state, humus_circuit_transitions_total and humus_circuit_calls_total, and each attribute is a label such as humus_circuit_state. An alert on an open breaker reads the state, and one on breakers that open and close between scrapes reads the transitions:
# A breaker is open now. humus_circuit_state{humus_circuit_state="open"} > 0 # A breaker opened in the last 5 minutes, however briefly. increase(humus_circuit_transitions_total{humus_circuit_state="open"}[5m]) > 0 A View in the end user’s telemetry Builder drops or renames any of them. humus has no setting to turn them off. A test reads them as it reads any metric, with humustest.Telemetry’s Metrics, filtered to the scope.
franz-go’s broker metrics franz-go’s broker metrics come from the Meter of franz-go’s kotel plugin, which the Service and the Producer each build with the Setup’s MeterProvider and nothing else, and hand their client as hooks. kotel’s tracer is not used: the spans, the propagation through headers and the instruments above are humus’s own.
By broker, with a node_id attribute, kotel counts the connections opened, the connection errors and the connections closed, the bytes read and written, and the read and write errors. By broker and topic, with node_id and topic, it counts the records and the uncompressed bytes the Service fetched, and the records and the bytes the Producer produced, in messaging.kafka.produce_records.count and messaging.kafka.produce_bytes.count. The instruments are kotel’s, under its own scope, github.com/twmb/franz-go/plugin/kotel, with names such as messaging.kafka.connects.count, messaging.kafka.connect_errors.count, messaging.kafka.fetch_records.count, messaging.kafka.read_errors.count and messaging.kafka.write_bytes. They aren’t conventions, because the messaging conventions define none for a client’s connections or bytes. humus renames none of them, and pins the kotel version it uses, so a kotel release that renames one is a breaking change to queue/kafka.
A clean shutdown counts one read error. Against kfake, franz-go’s fake cluster, a clean shutdown counts one read error for the broker, during the shutdown and never before it. An alert on messaging.kafka.read_errors.count should allow for it.
The logs The Service logs through the Setup’s LoggerProvider, under its scope:
Record Severity When partitions assigned INFO the group assigns the Service partitions partitions revoked INFO a rebalance revokes them, after their records in flight are committed; after a fence, nothing more is committed for them partitions lost INFO the member was fenced out of the group processing a record failed ERROR Process returned an error under AtMostOnce. It carries the record’s span’s context, its topic, partition and offset, and the error as exception.message and error.type. batch skipped: its commit was refused WARN under AtMostOnce, a batch’s commit was refused for a member no longer in the group, or not sent for a partition the member no longer holds, so the batch wasn’t processed The partition records carry messaging.system, messaging.consumer.group.name, messaging.destination.name and messaging.destination.partition.ids. An error that ends the Service is returned, not logged here: the lifecycle logs it.
The Producer logs under the same scope:
Record Severity When circuit breaker open WARN the breaker opened, from closed or from half-open circuit breaker half-open INFO the breaker’s OpenFor passed, and it lets probes through circuit breaker closed INFO enough probes succeeded a broker refused the credentials ERROR the first time a broker refused the credentials. It carries messaging.system, server.address and server.port naming the broker, and the refusal as exception.message and error.type. A breaker record is emitted in the context of the call that changed the state, so it carries that call’s trace ID. Its attributes are the cluster’s, messaging.system, set to kafka, and server.address and server.port of the first of ProducerSettings.Brokers, then the state the breaker left as humus.circuit.previous_state, and the counts of that state: humus.circuit.successes, humus.circuit.failures, humus.circuit.consecutive_successes, humus.circuit.consecutive_failures and humus.circuit.timed_out. The bodies and the attributes are those of humus’s other clients’ breaker records, so one query finds every breaker. So an alert on circuit breaker open says the cluster kept failing, and the counts say how; an alert on a metric, humus.circuit.state, is in humus’s own instruments.
franz-go’s own logs go through the same LoggerProvider, under the scope github.com/twmb/franz-go/pkg/kgo, and never to standard error or the log package’s default logger. The Producer’s client logs there too, as the Service’s does. They include a broker it can’t reach, which it logs on every attempt while it retries, a rebalance, and a retried request. Each of franz-go’s messages is one record: the message is its body, and franz-go’s key-value pairs are its attributes, where a string, a number or a bool keeps its type, an error is its text, and any other value is its fmt text. franz-go’s levels are its severities: error is ERROR, warn is WARN, info is INFO and debug is DEBUG.
The Service and the Producer ask the Logger of that scope which severities it is enabled for, and franz-go builds no message below the lowest of them. So the end user’s Builder quiets franz-go as it does any scope:
On humus.Main’s default telemetry, whose LoggerProvider exports from INFO, franz-go writes its INFO records, such as joining group and leaving group, to standard output with the rest of the App’s, and builds no DEBUG message. A LoggerProvider with no severity filter is enabled for every severity, so with one franz-go logs at DEBUG: a record for every request it writes and every response it reads. A LoggerProvider whose Logger for github.com/twmb/franz-go/pkg/kgo is enabled only from WARN has franz-go log nothing at INFO or DEBUG, and one enabled for nothing has it log nothing at all. Unreachable brokers While the brokers are unreachable, the Service keeps serving. franz-go retries each connection with backoff, and the Service processes records once the brokers are back. Failing Serve after a bound would turn a broker outage into a crash loop of every consumer. A consumer that can’t connect shows up in three places:
kotel’s messaging.kafka.connect_errors.count counts each failed attempt, by broker, so a consumer that never connects shows up in its metrics. franz-go’s logs record each attempt at WARN, as unable to open connection to broker, with the broker’s address and the error. Its readiness, through Joined: a consumer that has never joined its group is not ready, so a rollout whose new pods can’t reach the brokers stalls. Readiness A consumer is ready once it has joined its group. Joined returns a health.Monitor that is unhealthy until franz-go first hands the member an assignment, empty or not, and healthy from then until Serve returns. It goes in the readiness of whatever exposes the probes: a probes server, such as httphealth.NewService in a pod with no server of its own, or a health Service:
probes := health.NewService(health.Readiness(consumer.Joined())) httphealth.NewService takes the same health.Readiness(consumer.Joined()) option, and is how a consumer’s pod, which has no server of its own, serves its probes: Health shows the Init and the manifest. A rollout whose new pods can’t reach the brokers then stalls, and is reported failed at its progress deadline, rather than replacing every old pod with pods that never consume. A member assigned no partition, because the group has more members than the topics have partitions, has joined, and is ready. Joined may be called in Init, before Serve, and its monitor never returns an error.
A broker outage after the first join doesn’t make a consumer unready. The outage hits every pod at once, so taking them all out of service would gain nothing, and franz-go rejoins the group on its own once the brokers are back. Neither does a rebalance, nor a fenced-out member rejoining.
Joined is for readiness only. A liveness monitor would restart every pod in a broker outage, and the kubelet’s restart backoff, up to five minutes by default, would then hold them down after the brokers return, while franz-go rejoins on its own. The errors a restart would fix, an error code franz-go doesn’t retry and credentials a broker refuses, already end Serve, so the pod exits and is restarted without a probe.
A Producer whose brokers are unreachable fails its calls. Each call waits out its DeliveryTimeout while franz-go retries the connection, and fails with an error matching context.DeadlineExceeded. Once enough have failed, the circuit breaker opens, and calls fail at once until a probe gets through. A Processor that produces fails its record, so under AtLeastOnce the Service stops, and the record is processed again once the App restarts.
Retries and panics Retries are the Processor’s. A transient failure, such as a database that is briefly unavailable, is the Processor’s to retry, before it returns an error, with whatever it likes, such as bedrock’s retry module, which retries with a budget and backoff. Neither queue nor queue/kafka retries, because a retry policy is the end user’s decision, and a retry inside the Service would block the partition just the same. A Processor that retries honours its context, so a retry loop still stops when the grace period runs out.
Panics crash the process. No panic is recovered, here or anywhere in the lifecycle. Under AtLeastOnce, a crash loses nothing that a recovered panic would have saved: every record after the last commit is processed again. Under AtMostOnce, a recovered panic would carry on in a process whose state the panic may have broken. The process exits with Go’s exit status 2 and the stack trace on stderr, and Kubernetes restarts the pod. A Processor that wants a panic handled differently recovers it itself.
Testing A consumer is tested whole, with humustest.Start, inside testing/synctest, as Testing a humus App describes for any App, against a fake cluster on the test’s Host.
The package ships no test package. It has no defaults of its own, so humustest.Start already runs a consumer on the ones production uses, humus.Main’s, and putting a fake cluster on its Host takes one option. The helpers below are a few lines each, which no API would save.
A fake cluster on the test Host franz-go’s kfake is a Kafka cluster in memory, built for synctest. kfake.ListenFn(h.Listen) makes it listen on humustest’s network rather than the real one, and a test builds it inside the bubble, with the bubble’s t, and closes it before the bubble ends:
// cluster returns a kfake cluster listening on h, with topic seeded with // the given number of partitions. It is closed when the test ends, inside // the bubble that built it. func cluster(t *testing.T, h *humustest.Host, partitions int32, opts ...kfake.Opt) *kfake.Cluster { t.Helper() all := append([]kfake.Opt{ kfake.ListenFn(h.Listen), kfake.NumBrokers(1), kfake.SeedTopics(partitions, topic), }, opts...) c, err := kfake.NewCluster(all...) require.NoError(t, err) t.Cleanup(c.Close) return c } A test’s producer is a franz-go client that dials h.Dial, so it reaches the cluster over the same network:
// produceRecords writes records, each to its own partition, through a // client that dials h with opts. func produceRecords(t *testing.T, h *humustest.Host, c *kfake.Cluster, records []*kgo.Record, opts ...kgo.Opt) { t.Helper() all := append([]kgo.Opt{ kgo.SeedBrokers(c.ListenAddrs()...), kgo.Dialer(h.Dial), kgo.RecordPartitioner(kgo.ManualPartitioner()), }, opts...) cl, err := kgo.NewClient(all...) require.NoError(t, err) defer cl.Close() require.NoError(t, cl.ProduceSync(context.Background(), records...).FirstErr()) } kfake.TLS(cfg) serves TLS, so mTLS is tested with certificates from humustest.NewCA, and kfake.EnableSASL with kfake.Superuser requires SASL credentials. A test never needs fixed certificates or passwords.
Running the end user’s Init humustest.Start runs the end user’s own Init on humus.Main’s defaults. humus.WithHost(h.Host()) puts the App on the Host the cluster listens on, and humustest.WithEnv sets the variables Init reads. This test produces one record, lets the consumer process and commit it, and stops the App with SIGTERM, as Kubernetes would:
func TestInit_processes_and_commits_a_produced_record(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { h := humustest.NewHost(t) c := cluster(t, h, 1) produce(t, h, c, 1) // key-0, with the value 0 tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() // keeps the App's logs off p.Stdout() p, status := humustest.Start(t, Init, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), humustest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "KAFKA_BROKERS": strings.Join(c.ListenAddrs(), ","), "KAFKA_GROUP_ID": "orders-consumer", "KAFKA_TOPICS": "orders", }), ) synctest.Wait() // the record is processed and committed p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-status require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) require.Equal(t, "stored order key-0: 0\n", p.Stdout()) require.Equal(t, int64(1), committed(c)[0], "the record is committed") require.Len(t, spansNamed(tel, "process orders"), 1) }) } synctest.Wait returns once every goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked: the consumer has processed and committed every record and is polling for more. Fake time means the consumer’s timeouts cost the test nothing, so a test of a revoke, a slow record or a grace period that runs out runs in milliseconds.
The committed offsets c.GroupInfo returns the group’s state as the cluster sees it: its members, and the offsets it has committed. A test asserts on what was committed, which is what decides what is processed again:
// committed returns the group's committed offset of each partition of // topic. func committed(c *kfake.Cluster) map[int32]int64 { offsets := make(map[int32]int64) info := c.GroupInfo(group) if info == nil { return offsets } for p, commit := range info.Commits[topic] { offsets[p] = commit.Offset } return offsets } A committed offset is the offset of the next record to process, so after offsets 0 to 2 are processed and committed, it is 3. This test shows an at-least-once failure and the redelivery after it, by running the App twice on one cluster:
st, seen := run(true) require.Equal(t, humus.ExitFailure, st.Code()) require.ErrorIs(t, st.Cause(), bad) require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), "orders, partition 0, offset 3") require.Equal(t, []int64{0, 1, 2, 3}, seen) require.Equal(t, int64(3), committed(c)[0], "0 to 2 are committed, 3 is not") st, seen = run(false) require.Zero(t, st.Code(), st.Cause()) require.Equal(t, []int64{3, 4}, seen, "3 is delivered again") require.Equal(t, int64(5), committed(c)[0]) What a Producer stored A Producer is tested the same way, through the end user’s Init, against the cluster on the test Host. The cluster seeds the topic the Producer produces to, kfake.SeedTopics(1, dlqTopic) here for orders.dlq, and the test reads it back with a client of its own, after the App has exited:
// readAll returns every record of topic, in each partition's order, // through a client that dials h with opts. It polls until a poll finds // nothing new for a second, which inside a bubble takes no real time, and // fails the test on any error but the poll's own deadline, so a client that // can't read the topic isn't mistaken for an empty one. func readAll(t *testing.T, h *humustest.Host, c *kfake.Cluster, topic string, opts ...kgo.Opt) []*kgo.Record { t.Helper() cl, err := kgo.NewClient(append([]kgo.Opt{ kgo.SeedBrokers(c.ListenAddrs()...), kgo.Dialer(h.Dial), kgo.ConsumeTopics(topic), kgo.ConsumeResetOffset(kgo.NewOffset().AtStart()), }, opts...)...) require.NoError(t, err) defer cl.Close() var out []*kgo.Record for { ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), time.Second) fetches := cl.PollFetches(ctx) cancel() fetches.EachError(func(_ string, _ int32, err error) { if !errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) { require.NoError(t, err, "reading %s", topic) } }) n := 0 fetches.EachRecord(func(r *kgo.Record) { out = append(out, r) n++ }) if n == 0 { return out } } } This test produces an order that isn’t JSON and one that is, and checks that the first became a dead letter, and that both were committed:
st := <-status require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) require.Equal(t, "stored order key-1: 1\n", p.Stdout(), "the dead letter didn't stop the partition") require.Equal(t, int64(2), committed(c)[0], "the dead letter's record is committed too") dead := readAll(t, h, c, dlqTopic) require.Len(t, dead, 1) require.Equal(t, "key-0", string(dead[0].Key)) require.Equal(t, "{", string(dead[0].Value)) require.Len(t, spansNamed(tel, "send "+dlqTopic), 1) Wait for the commit, not only for synctest.Wait. Wait returns as soon as every other goroutine in the bubble is durably blocked, and a Produce waiting on one of franz-go’s timers is, while fake time passes only once the test’s goroutine blocks too. So Wait can return while the dead letter is still on its way, and a SIGTERM then finds the next record unprocessed. The test waits for the condition it needs instead, the offset it expects committed, letting fake time pass meanwhile, which costs it nothing:
// waitCommitted lets fake time pass until the group has committed offset on // partition 0 of topic, failing the test if a minute of it passes first. // synctest.Wait isn't enough once a Processor produces: Wait returns as // soon as every other goroutine is durably blocked, and a Produce waiting // on one of franz-go's timers is, while fake time passes only once the // test's goroutine blocks too. func waitCommitted(t *testing.T, c *kfake.Cluster, offset int64) { t.Helper() for start := time.Now(); committed(c)[0] < offset; time.Sleep(10 * time.Millisecond) { require.Less(t, time.Since(start), time.Minute, "offset %d is never committed", offset) } } A Producer that is the whole of an App, such as one called from a job, is tested the same way: queue/kafka’s own tests run each Produce inside a job whose Init builds the Producer.
The Service contract queue/kafka’s own tests hold kafka.Service to the Service contract with humustest.TestService, and a Service of your own that wraps a consumer is checked the same way. The constructor builds a cluster on s.Host.Listen and closes it with s.OnStop:
func TestService_contract(t *testing.T) { humustest.TestService(t, func(t *testing.T, s *humus.Setup) humus.Service { c, err := kfake.NewCluster( kfake.ListenFn(s.Host.Listen), kfake.NumBrokers(1), kfake.SeedTopics(1, topic), ) require.NoError(t, err) s.OnStop(func(context.Context) error { c.Close() return nil }) svc, err := kafka.NewService(s, settings(c.ListenAddrs()...), queue.ProcessorFunc[kafka.Message](func(context.Context, kafka.Message) error { return nil })) require.NoError(t, err) return svc }) } Against Kafka itself kfake is not Kafka. queue/kafka’s tests against a real broker in a container, behind the testcontainers build tag, cover what a fake can’t show, such as a real broker’s cooperative-sticky rebalances and its fencing. They are the only tests in the package that open a real socket, and they run in a CI job of their own. A consumer’s own tests rarely need them: the behaviour they pin down is queue/kafka’s, not the Processor’s.
Migration from the queue and queue/kafka packages before the reset queue and queue/kafka replace the packages of the same names from before the reset:
Before the reset After queue.Processor[T], queue.ProcessorFunc[T] unchanged queue.Consumer, queue.Acknowledger, their Func adapters, queue.Runtime, queue.RuntimeFunc removed queue.ErrEndOfQueue removed; a finite queue is a job queue.NewApp(runtime) humus.Main(Init), with the end user’s Init returning the Service from kafka.NewService kafka.NewRuntime(brokers, groupID, opts...) kafka.Settings{Brokers, GroupID, Topics} and kafka.NewService(s, settings, p) kafka.AtLeastOnce(topic, p), kafka.AtMostOnce(topic, p) Settings.Topics and Settings.Delivery; one Processor per Service kafka.SessionTimeout, RebalanceTimeout, FetchMaxBytes Settings fields with checks; RebalanceTimeout defaults to 60s kafka.MaxConcurrentFetches removed: its zero meant unlimited, and franz-go’s default is unlimited kafka.WithTLS(cfg) Settings.TLS, dialled through Host.Dial kafka.Message.Attrs removed kafka.GroupIDAttr, TopicAttr, PartitionAttr, OffsetAttr removed; humus has no slog in its API, and the span and metric attributes follow the conventions messaging.client.messages.processed, messaging.client.messages.committed messaging.client.consumed.messages, messaging.process.duration, messaging.client.operation.duration otel.Get*, humus.Logger, kotel, kslog s.Telemetry; kotel’s Meter alone, given s.Telemetry.MeterProvider, for franz-go’s broker metrics HUMUS_KAFKA_* variables, planned before the reset none; the end user names and sources every setting unit tests on testcontainers unit tests on kfake over humustest’s Host; containers only behind the build tag Two behaviours change for an existing processor:
Under at-least-once, a processing error now stops the App, and the record is processed again, where before it was committed and lost. Under at-most-once, a partition’s records are processed in order, one at a time, where before a batch was processed concurrently.
description: How to consume and produce Kafka with the queue and queue/kafka packages: the contract a Processor keeps, an Init that sources kafka.Settings and returns the Service from NewService, what each Delivery commits and does with an error, how the consumer shuts down and rebalances on humus.Main's defaults, how a Producer built with NewProducer produces dead letters and events, what a call to Produce promises, its delivery timeout, circuit breaker and shutdown, what both record, and how to test them on kfake.
