title: Consuming and producing Kafka

body:
The queue/rabbitmq package consumes a RabbitMQ queue as a humus.Service, with amqp091-go, RabbitMQ’s own Go client. The Service dials the broker through the Setup’s Host, consumes one queue with manual acks, and hands each delivery to the end user’s queue.Processor, in the order the queue delivered them. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with rabbitmq.NewService, and returns it to humus.Main, whose defaults are a consumer’s.
The package publishes too. A rabbitmq.Publisher, which the end user’s Init builds with rabbitmq.NewPublisher, publishes to the broker with publisher confirms for any Service of the process: a Processor that publishes an event, an HTTP handler, a job. Publishing describes it.
queue, in the core module, is the contract between the end user’s code and any broker. queue/rabbitmq is in the nested module github.com/z5labs/humus/queue/rabbitmq, so a service that doesn’t use RabbitMQ doesn’t get amqp091-go in its module graph. The package has no App, no Main, no defaults of its own, no test package and no fake broker. The design behind it is in Proposal: RabbitMQ, with its revision 1.
The contract The end user writes the same thing for RabbitMQ as for any broker: a queue.Processor, whose Process(ctx, msg) processes one message and returns an error when it couldn’t. queue.ProcessorFunc turns a function into one, and for RabbitMQ the message is a rabbitmq.Message: the queue it came from, the exchange and routing key it was published with, whether it was Redelivered, its headers, its properties, such as MessageID and CorrelationID, and its body.
A queue.Delivery says when a message is acknowledged, queue.AtLeastOnce after Process has returned nil for it, or queue.AtMostOnce before Process is called. The rules every broker package’s Service keeps, and why a Processor under AtLeastOnce must be idempotent, are on the Kafka page, under The contract; they hold here unchanged. What RabbitMQ adds is in Delivery.
So a Processor under AtLeastOnce must be idempotent. This one stores each order once, by the message’s ID, and publishes an order.accepted event for it:
// orders is the end user's Processor: it stores each order once, by the // message's ID, so an order delivered again is stored once, and publishes // an order.accepted event for it. type orders struct { mu sync.Mutex stored map[string][]byte events events } Its Handle method, the Processor’s function, stores the order and then publishes the event:
// Handle stores the order m carries, and publishes an order.accepted event // for it, with the order's ID as the event's message ID. It publishes on // every delivery, a redelivery included: an event whose publish failed is // published when the order comes again, and an event published twice is // told apart by its ID, as any consumer under queue.AtLeastOnce does. func (o *orders) Handle(ctx context.Context, m rabbitmq.Message) error { if m.MessageID == "" { return errors.New("an order has no ID") } o.store(m) // Returns once the broker has confirmed the event, so the order is acked only after. return o.events.Publish(ctx, rabbitmq.Publishing{ Exchange: "orders", RoutingKey: "order.accepted", MessageID: m.MessageID, ContentType: m.ContentType, Body: m.Body, }) } store is the idempotent part: an order already stored is skipped. A real Processor stores orders in a database, where the same idea is an upsert, or a unique key that turns a second insert into a no-op. events is an interface of the end user’s own over Publish, which *rabbitmq.Publisher satisfies and the Processor’s unit tests fake, as A Processor as a unit shows:
// events is what the orders Processor publishes with: the one method of // *rabbitmq.Publisher it calls, behind an interface of the end user's own, // so that its unit tests can fake it. type events interface { Publish(ctx context.Context, m rabbitmq.Publishing) error } An order with no ID fails on every delivery. Under AtLeastOnce that stops the Service each time, until the queue’s delivery limit dead-letters the message, as Dead letters describes.
A consumer The end user’s Init sources rabbitmq.Settings with config.Struct, as Configuring a humus service describes, builds the Publisher and the Processor, and returns the Service that rabbitmq.NewService builds:
// Init is the end user's Init: it sources the Settings with config.Struct, // builds the Publisher and the Processor, and returns the Service from // NewService. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := rabbitmq.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) rabbitmq.Settings { k := d // No .Default: the address, the login and the queue are required. k.Connection.Addr = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_ADDR").Validate(rabbitmq.CheckAddr)) k.Connection.SASL = &amqp.PlainAuth{ Username: r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_USERNAME")), Password: r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_PASSWORD")), } k.Queue = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_QUEUE").Validate(rabbitmq.CheckQueue)) k.Prefetch = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_PREFETCH").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(d.Prefetch).Validate(rabbitmq.CheckPrefetch)) return k }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } pub, err := rabbitmq.NewPublisher(s, publisherOn(settings.Connection)) // opens no connection: the first Publish does if err != nil { return nil, err } h := &orders{stored: map[string][]byte{}, events: pub} svc, err := rabbitmq.NewService(s, settings, queue.ProcessorFunc[rabbitmq.Message](h.Handle)) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc}, nil } env is the end user’s own helper, which names a variable, and amqp is github.com/rabbitmq/amqp091-go. The variable names are the service’s own: humus defines none of them. publisherOn is the end user’s helper too, as Building a Publisher shows.
The consumer’s main is one call to humus.Main, here with a telemetry Builder that names the service, as Telemetry describes:
humus.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) NewService opens no connection. It runs every check on the Settings again, rejects a Concurrency above Prefetch and a nil Processor, and builds the Service’s instruments. It registers no OnStop function, so an Init that fails after it leaks nothing. Serve connects, as Connecting describes, and consumes. Dialling through the Host is what lets a test put the App on a network of its own, with no test-only seam.
A Service consumes one queue, with one Delivery and one Processor, and its acks are on the one channel it consumes on, so a failure stops only its own queue. Init returns it along with any other Service the process runs, such as a second consumer or a probes server, as Readiness shows. Any Service returning ends the App.
Settings rabbitmq.Settings follows the settings convention: plain Go values, a check for each field, and rabbitmq.DefaultSettings() for the defaults. Every field’s zero value means zero, never “use the default”, so an Init starts from DefaultSettings() and changes the fields it sources. The package reads no environment variable and no file, and defines no variable name. How the broker is reached is a rabbitmq.Connection of its own, in Settings.Connection, which the Publisher’s settings take too.
Field Default Valid Check Connection.Addr none: required host:port, with a host and a port from 1 to 65535 CheckAddr Connection.Vhost / not empty CheckVhost Connection.TLS nil, which means plain text any none Connection.SASL none: required not nil CheckSASL Connection.Heartbeat 10s a whole number of seconds, from 1s to 65535s CheckHeartbeat Connection.ConnectTimeout 30s positive CheckConnectTimeout Queue none: required 1 to 255 bytes CheckQueue Delivery queue.AtLeastOnce queue.AtLeastOnce or queue.AtMostOnce queue.CheckDelivery Prefetch 10 1 to 65535 CheckPrefetch Concurrency 1 1 to Prefetch CheckConcurrency, and NewService for the bound of Prefetch Heartbeat and ConnectTimeout keep amqp091’s defaults. Heartbeats can’t be turned off: a dead connection would then go unnoticed until TCP gave up. The broker’s heartbeat, if shorter, wins, and a connection silent for 1.5 intervals is dead. ConnectTimeout bounds each dial, its TLS handshake and its AMQP handshake together.
Prefetch is 10 and Concurrency is 1, so by default a queue’s deliveries are processed in the order the broker sent them, the round trip of each ack is hidden behind nine more deliveries, and at most ten messages are held back from the queue’s other consumers. Concurrency above Prefetch would leave workers that never get a delivery, so NewService rejects it.
Required fields Connection.Addr, Connection.SASL and Queue are required. None has a default: humus imposes no broker, no port and no queue, and AMQP has no anonymous login, so there is no login to default to. DefaultSettings() leaves them "", nil and "", which their checks reject, and the end user’s chains for them have no .Default, as in Init above, so a variable that isn’t set fails as not found. The App exits 78, and config.Struct names every variable at fault in one error. With none of Init’s set:
init: config RABBITMQ_ADDR: not found config RABBITMQ_USERNAME: not found config RABBITMQ_PASSWORD: not found config RABBITMQ_QUEUE: not found A value that fails its check fails the same way, naming the variable. CheckAddr never quotes the value: the likeliest wrong value is an AMQP URI, whose login would otherwise reach the logs. With RABBITMQ_ADDR=amqp://orders:…@rabbit:5672/:
init: config RABBITMQ_ADDR: is a URI, not host:port NewService runs the same checks itself, so a Settings built in code with a bad field fails Init too, naming every field at fault, such as rabbitmq: NewService: Settings.Queue must not be empty. That error is no *config.Error, so the App exits 1: the fault is in the code, not in the configuration. How a bad value fails explains the exit codes.
The Delivery setting Delivery is set in code. Whether a message may be processed twice or lost is a property of the Processor, not of a deployment, so it is the end user’s design decision rather than an operator’s, and most Inits don’t source it. DefaultSettings() gives the safe one, queue.AtLeastOnce. An Init that wants at-most-once sets settings.Delivery = queue.AtMostOnce on the Settings it builds. A Service has one Delivery: two queues that need different ones are two Services.
TLS and plain text Connection.TLS is the *tls.Config the broker is dialled with, and nil means plain text: humus makes a service as secure as it can, but it can’t control what the service connects to. The Service runs the TLS handshake itself over the connection s.Host.Dial returns, and an empty ServerName defaults to Addr’s host, on a clone of the config, so the end user’s config is never changed. RabbitMQ serves AMQP over TLS on 5671 by default, and plain text on 5672.
The end user decodes the certificates from files, read through s.Host.FS so that a test reads them from its own directory and production from the real disk, as Reading a file describes. This chain reads the broker’s CA from the PEM file RABBITMQ_TLS_CA_FILE names, and the client’s certificate chain and private key from the one RABBITMQ_TLS_CERT_FILE names, and logs in with the client certificate:
// The CA's file is read first, and the client's certificate only once it has been. k.Connection.TLS = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_TLS_CA_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).FlatMap(func(ca []byte) config.Value[*tls.Config] { return env("RABBITMQ_TLS_CERT_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(clientTLS(ca)) })) // The client certificate is the login: RabbitMQ's rabbitmq_auth_mechanism_ssl plugin takes it. k.Connection.SASL = &amqp.ExternalAuth{} readFile and clientTLS are the end user’s own helpers, the same ones the Kafka page shows under TLS and mTLS: Connection.TLS is a plain *tls.Config, as Kafka’s Settings.TLS is. A missing variable, a missing file and a file that holds no certificate each fail as a config error with exit 78, named after its variable. A broker whose certificate a public CA signed needs no RootCAs, and a config with no RootCAs reads the system’s roots, which are an ambient leak. A broker that needs TLS but no client certificate takes a config with only RootCAs, and a login of the next section.
Logins Connection.SASL is how the connection authenticates. It is amqp091’s own amqp.Authentication, so the end user picks one of amqp091’s mechanisms and supplies its credentials from wherever they keep them: humus decides nothing about secrets.
&amqp.PlainAuth{Username, Password} is RabbitMQ’s usual login, as in Init. It sends the password over the connection, so it belongs over TLS outside a cluster’s own network. &amqp.AMQPlainAuth{Username, Password} is RabbitMQ’s older AMQPLAIN mechanism, for a broker that offers only it. &amqp.ExternalAuth{} logs in with the client certificate in Connection.TLS, as the chain above does, on a broker with the rabbitmq_auth_mechanism_ssl plugin enabled. An OAuth 2 token is a PlainAuth password, sent when the connection opens; refreshing one on an open connection, with connection.update-secret, is out of scope. A broker that refuses the login ends the Service with exit 1, rather than the Service retrying a password that will never be accepted, as Failures lists.
An AMQP URI humus takes no URL. It builds none, and never calls amqp091’s Dial, DialConfig or DialTLS, which take one, so the password in SASL can’t reach a log in one. An end user who keeps an AMQP URI, such as amqps://orders:…@rabbit.internal/shop, parses it with amqp.ParseURI in their Init and fills the Connection from it. This parser does that, for config.Value.Parse:
// fromURI is a parser for config.Value.Parse that fills DefaultSettings' // Connection from an AMQP URI, for an end user who keeps one. Its errors // never quote the URI, which holds the password. func fromURI(uri string) (rabbitmq.Connection, error) { u, err := amqp.ParseURI(uri) if err != nil { return rabbitmq.Connection{}, errors.New("is not an AMQP URI") } if u.Username == "guest" { // ParseURI fills in guest when the URI has no login, and guest is no login to deploy with. return rabbitmq.Connection{}, errors.New("has no login of its own") } c := rabbitmq.DefaultSettings().Connection c.Addr = net.JoinHostPort(u.Host, strconv.Itoa(u.Port)) // brackets an IPv6 host c.Vhost = u.Vhost c.SASL = u.PlainAuth() if u.Scheme == "amqps" { // A nil TLS would dial the TLS port, 5671 by default, in plain text. c.TLS = &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12} } return c, nil } and a chain sources the whole Connection from one variable with it:
// The address, the vhost, the login and whether to dial TLS, from one variable. k.Connection = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_URI").Parse(fromURI)) ParseURI fills in guest and guest when the URI carries no login, so a parser that requires one checks u.Username itself. An amqps URI’s port defaults to 5671, so it means TLS must be set: a nil TLS would dial a TLS port in plain text. ParseURI’s own errors quote the URI, and with it the password, so fromURI returns one of its own.
Topology The Service and the Publisher declare nothing. The queue, its exchange, bindings, type, dead-lettering and delivery limit are the end user’s infrastructure, set up before the App starts, by RabbitMQ’s definitions, an operator, or the team that owns the exchange, as queue/kafka creates no topics. The Service is purely a consumer: a queue that doesn’t exist stops it with 404 NOT_FOUND, and the App exits 1. The Publisher publishes only to exchanges that exist: a missing exchange fails a Publish with 404 NOT_FOUND.
Declaring them from Settings would grow into RabbitMQ’s whole topology API, queue types, arguments, exchanges and dead-lettering, and would put the App in charge of something a deployment already owns.
Delivery The Service never consumes with auto-ack, even under AtMostOnce. RabbitMQ ignores the prefetch count of an auto-ack consumer and sends as fast as TCP allows, and amqp091 buffers every delivery without a bound: a backlog would fill the process’s memory, and a crash or a rollout would lose everything buffered, already acked. So every delivery is acked by the Service, and Prefetch always bounds what it holds.
What each Delivery acks, and when:
AtLeastOnce: a delivery is acked once Process has returned nil for it. A delivery whose processing failed, or was cut short by a crash or by the grace period running out, is delivered again. AtMostOnce: the Service takes a delivery and every delivery already buffered behind it, up to Prefetch, acks them with one basic.ack with multiple set, and waits for the reply to a basic.qos on the same channel. RabbitMQ handles a channel’s methods in order, so the reply means it has the ack, which has no reply of its own. Only then does the Service hand the batch to its workers, and it processes all of it. A message is never processed twice: if the connection drops before the reply, the batch isn’t processed, and the broker has either dropped it or requeues it. A crash loses at most one batch, and a clean shutdown loses nothing. A processing error Under AtLeastOnce, a processing error stops the Service:
the delivery is rejected with requeue, with basic.reject; the Service stops as on shutdown: the other workers finish their deliveries and ack them, and every delivery received but not processed is nacked with requeue, in one basic.nack; Serve returns an error that wraps the Processor’s and names the queue, and the message’s ID when it has one, such as rabbitmq: processing message 3 from orders: cannot process, so the App exits 1, and the broker delivers the message again when it restarts. Under AtMostOnce, a processing error is logged at ERROR, with the queue and the message’s ID, and processing goes on. The message was already acked, so stopping wouldn’t bring it back.
The delivery limit A failure rejects the one delivery and nacks the rest because RabbitMQ counts a basic.reject, and a channel or connection that closes with a delivery unacked, toward a quorum queue’s delivery limit, and doesn’t count a basic.nack. So exactly the message that failed is counted, and a message that was merely prefetched when another failed never is. A quorum queue reports the count in each message’s x-delivery-count header.
Which deliveries count toward the limit:
What happened to the delivery Counts Process returned an error for it, under AtLeastOnce yes: it was rejected it was prefetched behind one that failed, or unprocessed at a clean shutdown no: it was nacked it was unacked when the grace period ran out, the process crashed, or the connection was lost yes: its connection closed with it unacked A message that always fails crash-loops the pod until the queue’s delivery limit dead-letters or drops it: 20 deliveries on a quorum queue, by default since RabbitMQ 4.0. A classic queue has no delivery limit, and the crash loop is what shows the failure.
Which messages are processed again, by Delivery:
AtLeastOnce AtMostOnce Process returns an error that message, when the App restarts. The other deliveries in flight finish and are acked. none: the error is logged, and processing goes on the process crashes, or panics the deliveries in flight none: the rest of the acked batch is lost the connection is lost the deliveries in flight, once the Service reconnects: they finish, but their acks fail none: the acked batch is processed whole SIGTERM none: the deliveries in flight finish and are acked none: the batch in flight finishes the grace period runs out during a delivery the deliveries in flight the rest of the batch is lost What was received but never handed to the Processor is never processed twice: the broker delivers it again, under either Delivery, and the Service processes it then for the first time.
Order and concurrency A queue delivers its messages to one consumer in order. The Service hands them, in that order, to Concurrency workers, each of which processes one at a time, on the one channel it consumes on, so the Service has one prefetch window and one stream of acks. With Concurrency 1, the default, messages are processed in the order the queue delivered them.
Three things break that order, as for any RabbitMQ consumer: a redelivery, more than one replica, and Concurrency above 1. A Processor that needs the messages of a key processed in order uses a single-active-consumer queue, which is topology the end user sets up, and Concurrency 1: the broker then delivers to one replica at a time, and fails over to another when it goes. A Processor that doesn’t care about order raises Concurrency, up to Prefetch, to process more at once.
Failures No panic is recovered: a panicking Processor crashes the process. Every other failure follows this table:
AtLeastOnce AtMostOnce Process returns an error rejected, which counts toward the delivery limit; the Service stops as on shutdown, and Serve returns the error, naming the queue and the message’s ID; exit 1 already acked; logged at ERROR, with the queue and the message’s ID; processing goes on Process panics the process crashes; the broker requeues every unacked delivery, and each counts the process crashes; the batch acked is lost the broker is unreachable the Service keeps trying to connect, logging each attempt at WARN the same the broker refuses the login, the vhost or the queue the Service stops, and Serve returns the error; exit 1 the same the connection is lost after consuming started the deliveries in flight finish, their acks fail, and the broker delivers them again; the Service logs it at WARN and reconnects the same; a batch whose ack was confirmed is processed the broker closes the channel with 406 PRECONDITION_FAILED the Service stops, and Serve returns the error; exit 1 the same The login or the vhost is refused with ACCESS_REFUSED, or amqp091’s ErrCredentials, ErrSASL or ErrVhost. The queue is refused with 404 NOT_FOUND, 403 ACCESS_REFUSED, or 405 RESOURCE_LOCKED for a queue another connection consumes exclusively. An error that ends the Service is returned rather than logged, and the lifecycle logs it.
Stopping is loud on purpose, as for Kafka. Retrying in place would hold the delivery with no limit, and skipping would lose it. A message that always fails shows up as a crash loop with its error in the logs, until the delivery limit takes it out of the queue.
Dead letters Dead letters are the queue’s or the Processor’s. humus has no dead-letter exchange, retry queue or skip policy of its own, and the contract has no way to dead-letter a message on purpose. There are two ways to get one:
The queue’s. A quorum queue with a delivery-limit and a dead-letter-exchange, set by a policy or by its arguments, dead-letters a message once it has failed that many times, as The delivery limit counts them. The App needs nothing for it: each failure stops the Service, the pod restarts, and the last failure moves the message aside. That costs a restart per failure. The Processor’s. A Processor that would rather skip a message that always fails than stop on it publishes it to a dead-letter exchange with a Publisher, or stores it wherever it keeps dead letters, and returns nil. The message is then acked like any other. Under AtLeastOnce it is acked only once Publish has returned nil, which is once the broker has confirmed the dead letter, so a dead letter that fails stops the Service rather than losing the message. Which messages are worth stopping for, and where the others go, is the end user’s decision.
Shutdown A Service gets the lifecycle’s two signals. When Serve’s context is done, or Shutdown is called, the Service:
cancels its consumer, with basic.cancel, so the broker sends nothing more; hands out no more deliveries, except the rest of an AtMostOnce batch it already acked; waits for the deliveries in flight to finish, and acks them; nacks with requeue, in one basic.nack with multiple set, every delivery it received but didn’t process, which counts nothing against them; closes the channel and the connection, and Serve returns nil. Process’s context is not cancelled when shutdown starts. It keeps the values of Serve’s context and carries the delivery’s span, but not Serve’s cancellation. So a Processor that honours its context doesn’t fail the delivery in flight on every SIGTERM, which under AtLeastOnce would make every rollout end in exit 1.
It is cancelled when the grace period runs out. Shutdown’s context carries the grace period as its deadline. When it is done before the deliveries in flight are, Shutdown cancels Process’s context, closes the connection at once, waits for Serve to return, and returns an error wrapping its context’s error, which the lifecycle reports as a *humus.GracePeriodError, with exit 1. The broker then requeues every delivery that wasn’t acked, and each counts toward a quorum queue’s delivery limit.
Connection loss A connection is lost when the network drops it, when it is silent for 1.5 heartbeat intervals, or when the broker closes it. A node that shuts down closes every connection with 320 CONNECTION_FORCED, so a rolling upgrade of RabbitMQ loses every consumer’s connection once per node. The broker cancelling the consumer, because its queue was deleted, is handled as a lost connection too. When the connection or the channel closes, the Service:
lets the deliveries in flight finish. Their acks fail in the client, and the Service drops those errors: the broker already requeued the deliveries, and delivers them again; hands out nothing more: what the consumer had buffered was requeued too, except the rest of an AtMostOnce batch whose ack was confirmed, which is processed; logs the lost connection at WARN, with the AMQP reply code and reason when the broker gave one; connects again, as Connecting describes, with the same backoff, logging each failed attempt at WARN, and consumes again. So the Service rides out a rolling upgrade. It connects to a node that is up, or waits for one, and its pod neither restarts nor lands in Kubernetes’ crash-loop backoff, of up to five minutes once restarts repeat. What a lost connection costs is redeliveries: every delivery that was unacked is delivered again, with Redelivered set, and RabbitMQ counts each one toward a quorum queue’s delivery limit, as it does for any connection that closes with deliveries unacked. A delivery is never processed twice by one connection: the Service connects again only once the old one’s deliveries are done.
Some errors aren’t fixed by connecting again, and stop the Service instead, with Serve returning the error, so the App exits 1:
the refusals of Connecting: a login, a vhost, or a queue the broker refuses, such as the 404 NOT_FOUND the reconnect after a deleted queue meets; a channel the broker closes with 406 PRECONDITION_FAILED, as it does for a delivery held unacked past its consumer_timeout, 30 minutes by default. Connecting again would only hand the same Processor the same delivery. Shutdown while the Service connects again stops it at once, waiting for no backoff, and Serve returns nil.
Connecting The Service and the Publisher connect the same way, in three steps, and ConnectTimeout bounds all three together:
they dial Connection.Addr with the Setup’s Host, so the broker is reached only through the Host; with TLS set, they run the TLS handshake over that connection; they run the AMQP handshake with amqp.Open, logging in with SASL, opening Vhost and proposing Heartbeat. Serve makes its attempts to connect, and to consume on the connection, with bedrock’s retry: exponential backoff from 100ms up to 30s, with no budget and no limit on attempts, so only Serve’s context ends them. A broker that is down at startup is waited for. A wrong login fails with ErrCredentials, and a vhost the login can’t open with ErrVhost, and neither is retried.
amqp091’s experimental recovery, Config.Recovery since v1.15.0, isn’t used. It is experimental, it redials through DialConfig’s URL, which humus never builds, rather than through the Host, and it declares the topology again, which is the end user’s. The Service’s reconnect is a short loop of the same retry it connects with at startup, which humus tests.
Readiness Nothing routes traffic to a consumer, so its readiness only gates rollouts. A login, vhost or queue the broker refuses already ends the Service, and the pod’s crash loop stops the rollout. A wrong address doesn’t: the Service keeps retrying, as it does through a broker’s upgrade, and without a monitor its pod would turn ready and replace a pod that consumed.
A consumer is ready once it consumes. Consuming returns a health.Monitor that is unhealthy until the broker first answers the Service’s basic.consume, and healthy from then until Serve returns, through any number of lost connections and reconnects. It goes in the readiness of whatever serves the pod’s probes. A consumer’s pod has no server of its own, so that is a probes server made with httphealth.NewService, returned beside the consumer:
probes, err := httphealth.NewService(s, probeSettings, health.Readiness(consumer.Consuming())) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{consumer, probes}, nil Health shows the probes server and the manifest for a Kafka consumer, and a RabbitMQ consumer’s are the same but for the monitor. A new pod is then held not ready until it has consumed from its queue once, so a rollout whose new pods have a wrong broker address stalls, and is reported failed at its progress deadline, rather than replacing every pod that consumes with pods that don’t. Consuming may be called in Init, before Serve, and its monitor never returns an error.
A lost connection after that doesn’t make a consumer unready. A broker outage hits every pod at once, and taking them all out of service would change nothing but block the rollout that might fix it.
Consuming is for readiness only. A liveness monitor would restart every pod in a broker outage, and the kubelet’s restart backoff, up to five minutes by default, would then hold them down after the broker comes back. The Service reconnects on its own, and the errors a restart would fix already end Serve, as Connection loss lists, so the pod exits and is restarted without a probe.
Publishing A rabbitmq.Publisher publishes to the broker, and returns once the broker has confirmed the message. The end user’s Init builds it with rabbitmq.NewPublisher, from rabbitmq.PublisherSettings, and hands it to whatever publishes: a Processor that publishes an event, as orders does, an HTTP handler, a job. It is not a Service. It is called from the Services that do the work, so it lives as long as they do and closes after them. One Publisher is safe for concurrent use and serves every Service of the process.
Building a Publisher NewPublisher belongs in Init, on a connection of its own. NewPublisher opens no connection. The first Publish connects, as Connecting describes, on a connection of the Publisher’s own, separate from every Service’s. RabbitMQ applies TCP back-pressure to a connection that publishes faster than the broker can take, and a consumer’s acks on that connection would wait behind it, so RabbitMQ advises publishing and consuming on separate connections. Concurrent first calls connect once, and after the connection is lost, the next Publish connects again.
PublisherSettings.Connection is a Connection, as the Service’s is, so a Publisher on the consumer’s broker takes the consumer’s, as Init does with its helper:
// publisherOn is DefaultPublisherSettings with the consumer's // Connection: the same broker and the same login, on a connection of the // Publisher's own. func publisherOn(c rabbitmq.Connection) rabbitmq.PublisherSettings { p := rabbitmq.DefaultPublisherSettings() p.Connection = c return p } A Publisher to another broker sources a Connection of its own, from variables of its own. A process that publishes to two brokers builds two Publishers.
PublisherSettings follows the settings convention, like Settings: rabbitmq.DefaultPublisherSettings() gives the defaults, with DefaultSettings’ Connection, every field’s zero value means zero, and the package reads no variable of its own.
Field Default Valid Check Connection as in Settings; Addr and SASL required as in Settings as in Settings Channels 8 1 to 65535 CheckChannels Timeout 10s positive CheckTimeout MaxAttempts 3 1 or more CheckMaxAttempts BackoffBase 100ms positive CheckBackoffBase BackoffMax 5s positive, and at least BackoffBase CheckBackoffMax, and NewPublisher for the bound RetryBudget.MaxTokens 10 3 to retry.TokenLimit CheckRetryBudgetMaxTokens RetryBudget.TokenRatio 0.1 0.001 to retry.TokenLimit CheckRetryBudgetTokenRatio Breaker.Window 20 1 to circuit.MaxCount CheckBreakerWindow Breaker.Probes 1 1 to circuit.MaxCount CheckBreakerProbes Breaker.OpenFor 10s positive CheckBreakerOpenFor Breaker.ProbeTimeout 10s positive CheckBreakerProbeTimeout BreakerPolicy see The circuit breaker Trip and Probe set none: NewPublisher checks it NewPublisher runs every check again, and fails naming each field at fault, such as rabbitmq: NewPublisher: PublisherSettings.Timeout must be positive, which exits 1, as a bad Settings given to NewService does. It builds the breaker and the instruments, and registers the function that closes the Publisher’s connection with s.OnStop.
A call Publisher.Publish(ctx, m) publishes one rabbitmq.Publishing. It returns nil once the broker has confirmed the message, so a Processor that publishes before it returns nil has its delivery acked only after the published message is the broker’s, which is what AtLeastOnce needs:
// Returns once the broker has confirmed the event, so the order is acked only after. return o.events.Publish(ctx, rabbitmq.Publishing{ Exchange: "orders", RoutingKey: "order.accepted", MessageID: m.MessageID, ContentType: m.ContentType, Body: m.Body, }) A Publishing’s zero value is persistent, with delivery mode 2, so a message isn’t lost on a broker restart because a field was left out. Publishing.Transient makes it delivery mode 1. Every other field is passed to the broker as it is, and the caller’s Headers map is never changed.
Each channel the Publisher opens is in confirm mode and carries one publish at a time. Each attempt of a Publish takes a channel, connecting first if needed, publishes the message with mandatory set, so the broker returns a message no queue is bound to receive rather than dropping it, and waits for the broker’s answer:
confirmed: Publish returns nil; returned: Publish returns an error that matches rabbitmq.ErrUnroutable, with no retry, since another attempt would be routed the same way. A caller branches on it to fall back, for example to a dead-letter store; a channel error, such as 404 NOT_FOUND for an exchange that doesn’t exist, or 403 ACCESS_REFUSED: Publish returns the broker’s *amqp.Error, with no retry, since the broker refused the message, and the channel is replaced; nacked by the broker, a dropped connection, a failed dial or a failed handshake: the broker didn’t take the message, or its answer was lost, and another attempt, on a new channel or connection when the old one was lost, may well be confirmed. So another attempt follows, as Retries describes; the context’s deadline, or the caller cancelling it: no further attempt, and Publish returns an error wrapping the context’s error. There is no Classify. An HTTP client’s Classify exists because each API decides what its answers mean, but RabbitMQ’s protocol fixes what a confirm, a nack, a return and a channel error mean, so the table above is fixed, and the Publisher has no Classify setting, as Kafka’s Producer has none.
PublisherSettings.Channels bounds the publishes in flight at once: an attempt waits for a channel when every one is busy, and gives its channel back before any wait for the next. When the context is done during an attempt, the channel isn’t reused, since a confirm may still arrive on it.
Timeout, retries and the budget Timeout, 10s by default, bounds the whole Publish: every attempt, the waits between them and each confirm. A deadline the caller’s context already has wins when it is earlier. No attempt starts after it, and a wait that would end after it isn’t begun. Without the bound, a broker that has stopped answering would hold a call, and the App’s shutdown, until it answered.
A Publish makes up to MaxAttempts attempts, 3 by default. After a failure that may be retried, the next attempt waits for a time drawn from bedrock’s retry.Exponential(BackoffBase, BackoffMax), 100ms doubling up to 5s, and Publish returns the last attempt’s error. MaxAttempts 1 turns retries off.
The retries of every Publish of a Publisher share one budget, RetryBudget, as retry.Budget describes. Retries add load to a broker when it can least take it, so each failure that would be retried takes a token, each confirm adds back TokenRatio of one, and no attempt follows a failure while half the tokens or fewer are left. While the broker keeps failing, each Publish makes one attempt rather than MaxAttempts. A first attempt is never refused.
Publishing is at least once. When a connection is lost after the broker took the message but before its confirm arrived, the attempt that follows publishes it again. So a consumer of the message is idempotent anyway, under queue’s contract, and tells a duplicate apart by its ID, as the orders Processor publishes its events with the order’s ID as their MessageID.
The circuit breaker A circuit breaker guards the broker, so that while the broker keeps failing, Publish fails at once rather than hold every caller for Timeout. Without it, an HTTP handler that publishes an event would hold its request for 10s during an outage before it answered 503. With it, the first few attempts wait, and the rest fail at once until a probe gets through. It is bedrock’s circuit.Breaker, one per Publisher: one Publisher is one connection to one broker.
The breaker sits inside the retries: each attempt of a Publish is one call through it. While it is open, an attempt sends nothing and fails at once with an error wrapping a *circuit.RejectedError, which matches circuit.ErrRejected and says how much longer the breaker stays open in its RetryAfter, and no attempt follows it, since the breaker would reject that one too. Whether to wait and try again is the caller’s.
The breaker counts the broker, not the messages or the callers, so what an attempt’s result counts as is fixed too:
a success: confirmed; or returned, ErrUnroutable, or a channel error, such as 404 NOT_FOUND or 403 ACCESS_REFUSED, since the broker answered. A mistake in one exchange’s bindings doesn’t open the breaker for the others; a failure: nacked by the broker, a dropped connection, a failed dial or a failed handshake; or the context’s deadline, Timeout’s or the caller’s, since a broker that has stopped answering ends every attempt this way; not counted: the caller cancelling the context, which says nothing about the broker. The defaults: the breaker opens after 5 failed attempts in a row, or once half of the last 20 or more, Breaker.Window, failed. It stays open for Breaker.OpenFor, 10s, and then turns half-open: it lets Breaker.Probes attempts through at once, 1, as probes, each holding its slot for at most Breaker.ProbeTimeout, 10s, which matches Timeout. It opens again on a failed probe, and closes after 3 confirmed ones. Breaker is bedrock’s own circuit.Config, with a check for each field, so an operator’s bad value fails startup naming its variable, with exit 78.
BreakerPolicy is set in code. It is a circuit.Policy, two functions, Trip and Probe, so it can’t come from a variable. bedrock ships no policy, so DefaultPublisherSettings holds humus’s, and the end user replaces it in their Init. A policy whose Trip always returns false turns the breaker off, as on the Kafka page’s circuit breaker.
Each change of the breaker’s state is a log record, as The logs lists. There are no instruments of humus’s own for the breaker: its transitions are in the logs, and a rejected Publish is an error on its span. Whether humus records instruments of its own, such as gauges of the breaker’s state and the budget’s tokens, is Proposal: humus’s own metrics, in wave 5.
Shutdown and the grace period The Publisher outlives every Service that uses it. Its connection is closed by the function NewPublisher registers with s.OnStop, which runs once every Service has stopped, so a Processor finishing its delivery during the drain can still publish. On SIGTERM, a Process blocked in Publish keeps its context, as Shutdown describes, so its event is confirmed, and its delivery acked, as the Service drains. The closing function closes the connection within the grace period, and an error that the grace period cut it short is reported as a *humus.GracePeriodError. A Publish after it has run, from a goroutine the end user left running, fails at once.
If the end user’s Init fails after NewPublisher, the lifecycle runs the OnStop functions registered so far, so no connection outlives the App.
The defaults The consumer runs on humus.Main’s defaults, which are a consumer’s, so queue/rabbitmq has no Main and no defaults of its own:
A grace period of 20s. A Processor that can’t finish its delivery in flight within it is cut short, and under AtLeastOnce the delivery is processed again. A Publish in flight at SIGTERM fits in it: its Timeout is 10s. No drain. Nothing load-balances a consumer. Its traffic stops when it cancels its consumer, which it does as soon as shutdown starts. The drain would only keep a consumer that has already stopped waiting. terminationGracePeriodSeconds When Kubernetes stops a pod, it sends the container SIGTERM, and then SIGKILL once terminationGracePeriodSeconds have passed, 30 by default. On humus.Main’s defaults, the worst case from SIGTERM to the exit is the 20s grace period and the telemetry’s shutdown, telemetry.Settings.ShutdownTimeout, 5s: 25s, inside Kubernetes’ 30s, with a margin for the process to exit.
A consumer that raises its grace period raises terminationGracePeriodSeconds with it, to at least the grace period plus the telemetry’s shutdown plus that margin. Otherwise SIGKILL ends the process first: its container exits 137, nothing in flight is acked, the broker requeues it all, counting each delivery toward the delivery limit, and the telemetry not yet exported is lost.
An operator changes the grace period with HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD, and adds a drain with HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY, without a rebuild, as for any App. The lifecycle’s settings describes both variables.
Two queues, two Services A Service consumes one queue, with one Delivery. Two queues, or two Delivery values, are two Services, each built by rabbitmq.NewService from Settings of its own, returned together from one Init. Each has its own channel and its own acks, so an at-least-once failure stops only its own consumer, but either Service returning ends the App, so the other stops too, after its deliveries in flight. One Publisher serves both.
Which Main Which Main the process uses depends on what a load balancer routes to, as the lifecycle’s runtime packages explains for mixed processes:
On its own, or next to a probes or metrics server, a consumer stays on humus.Main. Nothing routes to that server, and a drain would only delay the exit. Next to a server a load balancer routes to, such as an API, the process uses that server’s package’s Main: httpserver.Main for an HTTP server, with a 5s drain and a 10s grace period, or grpcserver.Main for a gRPC server, with a 5s drain and a 15s grace period. The consumer still cancels its consumer as soon as shutdown starts, and its deliveries in flight then have the drain and that package’s grace period to finish, rather than humus.Main’s 20s. Telemetry The Service and the Publisher report through the Setup’s telemetry, s.Telemetry, and never through OpenTelemetry’s globals: their tracers and meters come from the SDK’s TracerProvider and MeterProvider, under the scope github.com/z5labs/humus/queue/rabbitmq, and their propagator is the SDK’s Propagator. Their names and attributes are OpenTelemetry’s semantic conventions for RabbitMQ, as semconv v1.43.0 has them. The messaging conventions are still in development, so humus pins the version it uses, and a change to these names is a breaking change to queue/rabbitmq.
The process span Each delivery is processed under a span of its own, named process <queue>, such as process orders, of kind CONSUMER. Process is given a context that carries it, so every span the Processor starts from that context is its child, and every record it logs with that context carries its trace ID.
Its parent is the publisher’s. The span’s parent is the trace context the propagator extracts from the message’s headers, so a publisher’s trace continues through the consumer, and the publisher’s baggage, and only the publisher’s, is on Process’s context too. Only a header whose value is a string is read: a traceparent header of any other type, such as bytes, is ignored. A message whose headers carry no trace context starts a new trace.
Its attributes are:
messaging.system (rabbitmq), and messaging.operation.type and messaging.operation.name, both process; messaging.destination.name, as semconv defines it for RabbitMQ: {exchange}:{routing key}:{queue}, leaving out what is empty, and the routing key when it equals the queue’s name. So a message published to the queue orders on the default exchange is orders, and one published to the exchange shop with the routing key order.created is shop:order.created:orders; messaging.rabbitmq.destination.routing_key, when the routing key isn’t empty, and messaging.rabbitmq.message.delivery_tag; messaging.message.id, and messaging.message.conversation_id, from the correlation ID, when they are set; server.address and server.port, from Connection.Addr. The message’s body is never recorded. When Process returns an error, under either Delivery, the error is recorded on the span as an exception event, with error.type and an error status.
The send span Each Publish has a span of its own, a child of the span on the caller’s context, named send <exchange>, or send amq.default for the default exchange, of kind PRODUCER. A Publish has one span, whatever its attempts. Its attributes are messaging.system (rabbitmq), messaging.operation.type and messaging.operation.name (both send), messaging.destination.name, as semconv defines it for a publish, {exchange}:{routing key}, leaving out what is empty, so orders:order.accepted for the orders Processor’s events, messaging.rabbitmq.destination.routing_key when the routing key isn’t empty, messaging.message.id and messaging.message.conversation_id when they are set, and server.address and server.port. The body is never recorded. A failed Publish is recorded on its span as an exception event, with error.type and an error status, a Publish the breaker rejected included.
The span’s context goes into the message’s headers. The span is started before the headers are written, and the Setup’s propagator injects its trace context, and the caller’s baggage, into a copy of the headers: with the default propagator, traceparent, tracestate and baggage. A nil Headers map gets a new one. So the process span of the Service that consumes the message is a child of its send span, and inside a Process, the send span is a child of the process span: one trace runs from the first publisher through every queue a message passes through, without the end user’s code touching the headers.
The instruments The Service records two instruments of OpenTelemetry’s messaging conventions:
Instrument Kind What it records messaging.client.consumed.messages counter the deliveries handed to the Processor messaging.process.duration histogram, in seconds how long each Process took, with error.type when it failed Each has messaging.system, messaging.operation.name (process), messaging.destination.name, server.address and server.port. The broker sends no reply to an ack, so settling a delivery has no duration, and the Service records no messaging.client.operation.duration.
The Publisher records two more, for each attempt that publishes:
Instrument Kind What it records messaging.client.sent.messages counter the messages published, with error.type when the attempt failed messaging.client.operation.duration histogram, in seconds how long the broker took to answer each, from the publish to its confirm, with error.type when the attempt failed Each has messaging.system, messaging.operation.name (send), messaging.destination.name, server.address and server.port. A return and a channel error have the broker’s AMQP reply code as error.type, such as 312 for a return and 404 for an exchange that doesn’t exist, and a nack has nacked. A nack followed by a confirm counts two messages sent, one with error.type nacked. An attempt that fails before it publishes, waiting for a channel or connecting, publishes nothing, so neither instrument records it, and neither does an attempt the breaker rejected.
A routing key that carries identifiers makes a series per key. semconv’s destination name includes the routing key, so each routing key a message arrives or leaves with is a series of its own in the instruments. A publisher that puts identifiers, such as an order’s ID, in its routing keys gives every consumer a series per key, which a metrics backend may struggle with; such identifiers belong in headers, or in the body, instead.
The logs The Service logs through the Setup’s LoggerProvider, under its scope:
Record Severity When consuming INFO the broker answered the basic.consume, on each connection. It carries the queue as messaging.destination.name. connecting failed WARN an attempt to connect, or to consume on the connection, failed, and the Service will try again. It carries the error. lost the connection WARN the connection or the channel closed after consuming started. It carries the AMQP reply code as error.type and its reason as exception.message when the broker gave one. processing a message failed ERROR Process returned an error under AtMostOnce. It carries the delivery’s span’s context, the queue, the message’s ID, and the error as exception.message and error.type. Every record carries messaging.system, server.address and server.port. An error that ends the Service is returned, not logged here: the lifecycle logs it.
The Publisher logs under the same scope, one record for each change of its breaker’s state, in the context of the Publish that made it, so it carries that call’s trace ID:
Record Severity When circuit breaker open WARN the breaker opened, from closed or from half-open circuit breaker half-open INFO the breaker’s OpenFor passed, and it lets probes through circuit breaker closed INFO enough probes were confirmed Their attributes are server.address and server.port, circuit.previous_state, and the counts of the state the breaker left: circuit.successes, circuit.failures, circuit.consecutive_successes, circuit.consecutive_failures and circuit.timed_out. So an alert on circuit breaker open says the broker kept failing, and the counts say how.
amqp091’s logger amqp091 logs through a package-level variable, amqp.Logger, which amqp.SetLogger replaces, and which logs nothing by default. humus never sets it: replacing it is process-wide state, which every App and every test in the process would share, so it is on the lifecycle’s ambient leaks, and humus’s lint forbids SetLogger in its own code. Left alone, amqp091’s few messages, such as a failure to answer the broker’s close of a channel, are dropped, and most of what it would log comes from its experimental recovery, which humus doesn’t use. What the Service and the Publisher need to say is in their own records, above. An end user who wants amqp091’s messages anyway sets the logger in main, once, knowing it reaches past the Setup’s LoggerProvider to whatever the logger writes to.
Testing humus ships no fake RabbitMQ broker, and no test package. humus is neither RabbitMQ’s client nor its server, so it doesn’t write or keep a broker of its own: a fake’s fidelity would be humus’s to maintain against every RabbitMQ release, and a test on it would show what the fake does rather than what RabbitMQ does. No in-memory RabbitMQ exists for Go either. So an App that uses RabbitMQ is tested in two ways:
its Processor, as a unit, inside testing/synctest, with no broker; the whole App, against RabbitMQ itself in a container, in real time. That second way departs from the charter’s principle 6, which runs every App whole inside synctest on a test Host: an App that uses RabbitMQ can’t, and the charter’s revision 10 records the exception. Testing a humus App says the same for every runtime package.
A Processor as a unit A queue.Processor[rabbitmq.Message] is a function of a plain struct, so service code is tested by calling it with rabbitmq.Message values, inside synctest, with its other dependencies, such as HTTP, gRPC or Kafka, on humustest’s Host. Service code that publishes takes an interface of its own over Publish, as orders takes events, which its unit tests fake:
// fakeEvents is the orders Processor's events in its unit tests: it records // what is published, and fails each Publish with err while err is set. type fakeEvents struct { mu sync.Mutex published []rabbitmq.Publishing err error } func (f *fakeEvents) Publish(_ context.Context, m rabbitmq.Publishing) error { f.mu.Lock() defer f.mu.Unlock() if f.err != nil { return f.err } f.published = append(f.published, m) return nil } This test delivers an order twice, the second time as a redelivery, and checks that it was stored once and that each delivery published its event:
func TestOrders_stores_an_order_once_and_publishes_its_event_on_each_delivery(t *testing.T) { synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ev := &fakeEvents{} h := &orders{stored: map[string][]byte{}, events: ev} m := rabbitmq.Message{Queue: "orders", MessageID: "order-1", ContentType: "application/json", Body: []byte(`{"total":42}`)} require.NoError(t, h.Handle(t.Context(), m)) m.Redelivered = true require.NoError(t, h.Handle(t.Context(), m), "a redelivery is no error") require.Equal(t, map[string][]byte{"order-1": []byte(`{"total":42}`)}, h.stored, "stored once") require.Len(t, ev.published, 2, "an event on each delivery") for _, p := range ev.published { require.Equal(t, rabbitmq.Publishing{ Exchange: "orders", RoutingKey: "order.accepted", MessageID: "order-1", ContentType: "application/json", Body: []byte(`{"total":42}`), }, p) } }) } A Message is a plain struct, so a test builds whatever delivery it needs: Redelivered set, headers carrying a traceparent, a body that isn’t JSON. A fake that returns an error matching rabbitmq.ErrUnroutable shows what the Processor does when no queue is bound to receive its event, and one that returns a *circuit.RejectedError what it does while the broker is down.
Init runs inside synctest too, as far as it goes without a broker: with its variables unset it exits 78, naming each one, and with nothing listening at its address it waits for the broker and exits 0 on SIGTERM.
The whole App, against a container The whole App runs against RabbitMQ in a container. Its test runs the App with humustest.Start and humus.WithHost(humus.OSHost()), so the Service dials the container through the real network, in real time, and the App still reads its environment from humustest’s process. This test runs an Init that sources its Settings as Init does, with a Processor that fails on one message, and shows the failure and the redelivery after it, with what a quorum queue counted:
func TestInit_at_least_once_stops_on_a_failure_and_redelivers(t *testing.T) { t.Parallel() // The queue is the end user's infrastructure, so the test declares it. q := quorumQueue(t) publish(t, q, ids(5)...) b := rabbit(t) // RabbitMQ in a container, with a login generated for this run bad := errors.New("cannot process") run := func(fail bool) (bedrock.ExitStatus, []rabbitmq.Message) { var got recorder p, status := humustest.Start(t, initWith(func(_ context.Context, m rabbitmq.Message) error { got.add(m) if fail && m.MessageID == "3" { return bad } return nil }), humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(humus.OSHost())), humustest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "RABBITMQ_ADDR": net.JoinHostPort(b.host, b.amqp), "RABBITMQ_USERNAME": b.username, "RABBITMQ_PASSWORD": b.password, "RABBITMQ_QUEUE": q, }), ) if !fail { eventually(t, func() bool { return len(got.ids()) == 2 }, "the redelivered messages were never processed") p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) // the drain acks what is in flight } return exit(t, status), got.messages() } st, seen := run(true) require.Equal(t, humus.ExitFailure, st.Code()) require.ErrorIs(t, st.Cause(), bad) require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), q) require.ErrorContains(t, st.Cause(), "message 3") require.Equal(t, []string{"0", "1", "2", "3"}, idsOf(seen)) st, seen = run(false) require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) require.ElementsMatch(t, []string{"3", "4"}, idsOf(seen)) for _, m := range seen { switch m.MessageID { case "3": require.Equal(t, int64(1), deliveryCount(t, m.Headers), "3 was rejected, which counts once") require.True(t, m.Redelivered) case "4": require.Zero(t, deliveryCount(t, m.Headers), "4 was nacked, which counts nothing") } } } initWith, recorder, eventually, exit, idsOf and deliveryCount are the test’s own helpers, a few lines each: initWith is the end user’s Init with the given Processor, and deliveryCount reads a message’s x-delivery-count header. The first run fails on message 3, so the App exits 1 naming the queue and the message, and the broker has 3 and 4 ready again. The second run processes them, and the counts show that 3, which was rejected, counted once toward the delivery limit, and 4, which was nacked behind it, didn’t.
Declaring the test’s queues The test declares its own queues, since the Service declares none, over an amqp091 connection of its own, as the end user’s infrastructure would in production. A queue of its own, under a name no other test uses, lets the tests run in parallel against one broker, and is deleted when the test ends:
// declare declares a durable queue with args, under a name of the test's // own, and returns the name. The queue is deleted when the test ends. func declare(t *testing.T, args amqp.Table) string { t.Helper() ch := adminChannel(t) name := unique("orders") // RabbitMQ 4 refuses transient queues that aren't exclusive. _, err := ch.QueueDeclare(name, true, false, false, false, args) require.NoError(t, err) t.Cleanup(func() { // On a connection of its own: a test may have closed every // connection. del := adminChannel(t) _, _ = del.QueueDelete(name, false, false, false) }) return name } A test of the delivery limit declares a quorum queue, with amqp.Table{amqp.QueueTypeArg: amqp.QueueTypeQuorum}, and one of a dead-letter exchange declares the exchange and the queue’s x-dead-letter-exchange and x-delivery-limit arguments too. A test of the Publisher declares the exchange it publishes to and binds a queue to it, which the test then reads.
A login generated per test The broker’s login is generated for each run, never the image’s guest. The test starts the official rabbitmq image, pinned to an exact release, with testcontainers’ RabbitMQ module, and gives it a login made with crypto/rand.Text:
broker.username = "humus-" + strings.ToLower(rand.Text()) broker.password = rand.Text() guest is the login every deployed broker should refuse, so a test that passes with it says nothing about the login the App is given, and a fixed password in a repository is one more secret to scan for, even in a test. A test of TLS issues the broker’s certificate from humustest.NewCA, writes it to a temporary directory, and copies it into the container, so there are no fixed certificates either.
Behind a build tag, in a CI job of its own Tests that start a container sit behind a build tag, so go test ./... runs the unit tests alone, with no Docker, and they open real sockets nowhere else. queue/rabbitmq’s own run behind testcontainers, starting with:
//go:build testcontainers and run in a CI job of their own, “RabbitMQ (testcontainers)”:
go -C queue/rabbitmq test -race -tags testcontainers ./... The job isn’t a required check, and the coverage gate counts the unit tests alone: a container test is slower, and depends on Docker and on pulling an image, so it informs a review rather than blocking one. The build job vets the tagged tests without starting a container, so they keep compiling. An end user’s own container tests fit the same shape: a tag of their own, a job of their own, and every test that doesn’t need a broker outside the tag.
The Service contract queue/rabbitmq’s own tests hold rabbitmq.Service to the Service contract with humustest.TestService, with nothing listening at Addr, so it shuts down as the lifecycle expects while it waits for a broker:
func TestService_passes_the_Service_contract_with_no_broker(t *testing.T) { humustest.TestService(t, func(t *testing.T, s *humus.Setup) humus.Service { svc, err := rabbitmq.NewService(s, settings(), queue.ProcessorFunc[rabbitmq.Message](func(context.Context, rabbitmq.Message) error { return nil })) require.NoError(t, err) return svc }) } A Service of the end user’s own that wraps a consumer is checked the same way.
Migration from amqp091-go humus had no RabbitMQ package before the reset. A consumer written on amqp091-go directly moves over like this:
On amqp091-go With queue/rabbitmq amqp.Dial(os.Getenv("AMQP_URL")) Settings.Connection, sourced in Init, dialled through s.Host; a URI parsed with amqp.ParseURI, as An AMQP URI shows ch.Qos(n, 0, false) Settings.Prefetch ch.Consume(q, "", autoAck, ...) and a loop over the deliveries Settings.Queue, Settings.Delivery, and a queue.Processor[rabbitmq.Message] d.Ack(false), d.Nack(false, true) the Service, as Delivery says conn.NotifyClose and a reconnect loop the Service, as Connection loss describes ch.QueueDeclare, ch.ExchangeDeclare, ch.QueueBind at startup the end user’s infrastructure, set up before the App starts ch.PublishWithContext Publisher.Publish, with confirms, returns, retries and a breaker amqp.SetLogger, OpenTelemetry’s globals s.Telemetry Two behaviours change for such a consumer:
Under at-least-once, a processing error now stops the App, and the message is rejected and delivered again, where a hand-written consumer often nacked it and carried on, or acked it and lost it. Auto-ack is no longer how at-most-once is done. AtMostOnce acks a batch of up to Prefetch deliveries, and waits for the broker to have the ack, before it processes any of them, so a backlog no longer fills the process’s memory.
description: How to consume and publish with RabbitMQ through the queue and queue/rabbitmq packages: the contract a Processor keeps, an Init that sources rabbitmq.Settings and returns the Service from NewService, what each Delivery acks and does with an error, how the consumer shuts down, rides out a broker's rolling upgrade and turns ready with Consuming, how a Publisher built with NewPublisher publishes with confirms, retries and a circuit breaker, what both record, and how to test an App that uses RabbitMQ, which humus ships no fake broker for.
