title: gRPC services

body:
The grpcclient package calls another service over gRPC. grpcclient.NewClient builds a Client for one dependency in the end user’s Init, from Settings the end user sources. The Client is a grpc.ClientConnInterface, so generated code takes it as it takes a *grpc.ClientConn. Its calls go through the Setup’s Host, are traced and measured with the Setup’s telemetry, are retried as the end user’s Classify decides, and fail at once while a circuit breaker says the dependency keeps failing.
The package is in the nested module github.com/z5labs/humus/grpc, next to grpcserver: grpcserver is the server half, and grpcclient the client half. The Client dials only through the Setup’s Host, so a test runs the end user’s whole App, its outbound calls included, on humustest’s network, as Testing shows.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: outbound gRPC clients, with its revision 1.
A Client for each dependency The end user’s Init sources the dependency’s grpcclient.Settings, builds its Client with NewClient, and hands the Client to generated code. Here the end user’s service, served with grpcserver, calls carts:
// Init is the end user's Init: it sources the carts dependency's Settings, // builds its Client with NewClient, and hands the Client to generated code, // in the end user's service, which it serves with grpcserver. func Init(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := grpcclient.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } cartsSettings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) grpcclient.Settings { c := d // No .Default: Addr is required, and carts serves TLS, so // CARTS_CA_FILE is too. c.Addr = r.Get(env("CARTS_ADDR").Validate(grpcclient.CheckAddr)) c.TLS = r.Get(env("CARTS_CA_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(clientTLS).Validate(grpcclient.CheckTLS)) c.Timeout = r.Get(env("CARTS_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.Timeout).Validate(grpcclient.CheckTimeout)) return c }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78, naming every bad variable } serverSettings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) grpcserver.Settings { return grpcserver.Settings{ Addr: r.Get(env("GRPC_ADDR").Validate(grpcserver.CheckAddr)), TLS: r.Get(env("GRPC_TLS_PEM_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Parse(serverTLS).Validate(grpcserver.CheckTLS)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err } // One Client for the dependency, built once and shared by every RPC // the service serves. carts, err := grpcclient.NewClient(s, cartsSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } api := &api{carts: testpb.NewTestServiceClient(carts)} svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, serverSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } testpb.RegisterTestServiceServer(svc, api) return []humus.Service{svc}, nil } The samples on this page use grpc-go’s interop/grpc_testing service, as testpb, where a real service has its own generated code. The handler passes its RPC’s context to the call, so the call ends when the RPC it serves does:
// api is the end user's service: grpc-go's interop/grpc_testing // TestService, whose UnaryCall asks carts, the dependency, for its username, // and answers with it. type api struct { testpb.UnimplementedTestServiceServer carts testpb.TestServiceClient } func (a *api) UnaryCall(ctx context.Context, _ *testpb.SimpleRequest) (*testpb.SimpleResponse, error) { // The call to carts ends with the inbound RPC's context. resp, err := a.carts.UnaryCall(ctx, &testpb.SimpleRequest{FillUsername: true}) if err != nil { return nil, err } return &testpb.SimpleResponse{Username: "orders, via " + resp.GetUsername()}, nil } The service’s main is the server’s, as gRPC services describes:
grpcserver.Main(Init, humus.WithTelemetry(buildTelemetry)) A service that serves HTTP, or runs a job, builds its Client the same way, and runs on that package’s Main.
A Client is not a humus.Service. It has nothing to serve, and nothing to drain: an RPC in flight ends with its own context. NewClient dials nothing, as grpc.NewClient doesn’t: the first RPC dials, or the first check of Connected. So a dependency that is down when the service starts doesn’t fail Init, and the service doesn’t crash-loop over another service’s outage. Its RPCs fail with Unavailable until the dependency is reachable.
NewClient registers the connection’s Close with s.OnStop. OnStop functions run after every Service has stopped, so no Service is still calling, and within the grace period. They run when Init fails after NewClient too. An RPC made after the close fails with Canceled, and grpc: the client connection is closing. Client has no Close of its own, so the end user’s code can’t close a connection that other Services share, under them.
One Client per dependency A Client is one dependency at one Addr, over one connection, with one retry budget and one circuit breaker. Build each Client once, in Init, and share it between every Service that calls the dependency: the Client is safe for concurrent use, and its RPCs share its connection, its budget and its breaker. A Client built for each call would dial and handshake for each call, start each with a full budget and a closed breaker that never sees a second failure, and register one more function with s.OnStop each time. NewClient takes the *humus.Setup because it belongs in Init.
Two Clients of one address Every method of a Client, from every goroutine, goes through its one breaker. Two APIs served at one address, such as behind one gateway, whose outages the end user wants kept apart get two Clients of that address, each with its own Settings, and so each with its own breaker and retry budget:
// Two Clients of one address, each with its own Settings, and // so its own breaker, built once in Init and shared by // everything that calls them. payments, err := grpcclient.NewClient(s, paymentsSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } ledger, err := grpcclient.NewClient(s, ledgerSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } While payments fails, and its breaker rejects its calls at once, ledger’s calls still go through. Each Client opens a connection of its own.
Settings grpcclient.Settings follows the settings convention: plain Go values, a DefaultSettings(), and a check for each field with a valid range. The package reads no environment variable and defines no variable name: the end user’s Init sources each field with config.Struct, with whatever variable names the service uses, and passes the field’s check to Validate, as Init above does. An operator’s bad value then fails startup with exit 78, naming the variable.
Field Default Valid Check Addr none: required host:port, with a host and a port from 1 to 65535, and no scheme CheckAddr TLS nil: plain text nil, or a config that allows TLS 1.2 or later CheckTLS Timeout 10s positive CheckTimeout MaxAttempts 3 1 or more CheckMaxAttempts BackoffBase 100ms positive CheckBackoffBase BackoffMax 5s positive, and at least BackoffBase, which NewClient checks CheckBackoffMax RetryBudget {MaxTokens: 10, TokenRatio: 0.1} MaxTokens from 3 to retry.TokenLimit, TokenRatio from 0.001 to retry.TokenLimit CheckRetryBudgetMaxTokens, CheckRetryBudgetTokenRatio Classify the table under The default set none: set in code Breaker {Window: 20, Probes: 1, OpenFor: 10s, ProbeTimeout: 10s} Window and Probes from 1 to circuit.MaxCount, the durations positive CheckBreakerWindow, CheckBreakerProbes, CheckBreakerOpenFor, CheckBreakerProbeTimeout BreakerPolicy see The circuit breaker Trip and Probe set none: set in code Addr has no default, so its chain has no .Default, and a variable that isn’t set fails as not found. CheckAddr rejects an empty host, which grpcserver.CheckAddr accepts: a client dials a host, it doesn’t listen on every name. It rejects a scheme, such as dns:///carts:9090, since the Client never resolves names itself, a named port, such as :grpc, and ?, # and %, which grpc-go’s target would read as something other than the address.
Classify and BreakerPolicy are set in code, not sourced. What a dependency’s codes mean, and how it fails, are the end user’s knowledge, not an operator’s choice. NewClient runs every check again, rejects a nil Classify, Trip or Probe, and a BackoffMax below BackoffBase, which takes both fields to tell, and reports every bad field in one error that names each one. That fails Init with exit 1, since the fault is in the code, or in a pair of values no check given to Validate sees together. How a bad value fails explains the exit codes.
TLS and plain text Settings.TLS is the config the Client dials with: the roots it trusts in RootCAs, and for mTLS, a client certificate in Certificates. The Client dials with a clone of it, so the end user’s config is never changed. grpc-go adds h2 to its ALPN and enforces it, and CheckTLS rejects a config that allows nothing from TLS 1.2 on, which HTTP/2 requires. Init above reads the dependency’s CA from a file, through s.Host.FS, as Reading a file describes, and trusts only that CA:
// clientTLS returns a client's TLS config that trusts only the CA // certificates in pem. func clientTLS(pem []byte) (*tls.Config, error) { roots := x509.NewCertPool() if !roots.AppendCertsFromPEM(pem) { return nil, errors.New("holds no PEM certificate") } return &tls.Config{RootCAs: roots}, nil } readFile and serverTLS are the same helpers as under gRPC services.
A config with no RootCAs trusts the system’s roots, which crypto/x509 loads from the real host: the files SSL_CERT_FILE and SSL_CERT_DIR name in the real environment, and the OS’s certificate files. That is one of the ambient leaks. A service that calls only its own services sets RootCAs to its CA, as clientTLS does, and reads nothing ambient, and a test sets it to the pool of a CA from humustest.NewCA.
A nil TLS means plain text. Addr is host:port and names no scheme, so a nil TLS is the one way to ask for it. humus can’t control what a service connects to: a mesh’s sidecar, a vendor’s agent or a local emulator may well be plain text. Every humus server requires TLS, so a Client of one always sets it, and a Client that dials one in plain text fails its RPCs.
:authority and the certificate grpc-go takes the authority from the target, so every RPC’s :authority is Addr, and TLS verifies the server’s certificate for Addr’s host. A Client of carts:9090 sends :authority carts:9090, and requires a certificate for carts. Two settings replace both, as they would on any grpc-go client: a ServerName in Settings.TLS, and a grpc.WithAuthority in NewClient’s options. A Client of 10.0.0.7:9090 whose TLS has the ServerName carts sends :authority carts, and requires a certificate for carts.
Names, addresses and load NewClient targets passthrough:/// and Settings.Addr, and dials with the Setup’s Host.Dial. The passthrough resolver hands Addr to the dialler as it is, so grpc-go looks no name up: the Host resolves the name when it dials. In main, humus.OSHost’s Dial looks the name up as net.Dial does, each time it dials. grpc-go’s dns resolver, the default for a target with no scheme, is never used: it would look the name up around the Host, and inside a testing/synctest bubble it crashes the test binary, as The dns resolver and synctest describes. The Client uses no HTTP CONNECT proxy, and never reads HTTPS_PROXY or the other proxy variables.
One connection, picked first The passthrough resolver hands grpc-go one address, whatever its form, a name or an IP, so the Client has grpc-go’s default pick_first policy, and every RPC goes over one HTTP/2 connection, to whichever backend that dial reached. OSHost’s Dial tries a name’s addresses in the order the lookup returns them, and keeps the first connection that succeeds. So:
Behind a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service, the Service’s name resolves to its one virtual IP, and kube-proxy picks a pod for each connection. The Client stays on that pod. Behind a headless Service, the name resolves to every ready pod, and the Client connects to the first that accepts. Clients in different pods may reach different backends, but each Client keeps one. When the connection ends, grpc-go dials the same name again, with its own connection backoff, which starts at 1s and grows to 120s, and the Host looks the name up again, so a Client finds pods that weren’t there when it first dialled. A pod’s IP, given as Addr, never moves. This is what an end user who calls grpc.NewClient with nothing but an address already has: grpc-go’s dns resolver and pick_first keep one connection too, even to a name with several addresses. The Client changes who looks the name up, not how many connections there are. Client-side load balancing is out of humus’s scope: it wouldn’t help a ClusterIP Service, whose name has one address whichever resolver looks it up.
Spreading the load with MaxConnectionAge Two things move a Client to another pod. grpcserver’s Shutdown sends every client a GOAWAY, so a rollout of the dependency moves them. And a server whose end user sets keepalive.ServerParameters{MaxConnectionAge} in grpcserver.NewService’s options sends a GOAWAY when a connection reaches that age. The Client then dials again, through the Kubernetes Service, and reaches whichever pod kube-proxy picks, or, behind a headless Service, whichever pod accepts first. gRFC A9 added MaxConnectionAge for this kind of rebalancing. The dependency’s Init sets it:
// Every connection is closed with a GOAWAY once it is about a // minute old, so its clients dial again, through the // Kubernetes Service, and reach whichever pod it picks. grpc.KeepaliveParams(keepalive.ServerParameters{MaxConnectionAge: time.Minute}), as an option of grpcserver.NewService, after the Settings, as Server options describes. grpc-go adds a jitter of 10% either way, so a dependency’s clients don’t all dial again at once. A GOAWAY lets the RPCs in flight finish, and the next RPC goes over a new connection, so a Client sees no error. A server whose streams may stay open for longer than that also sets MaxConnectionAgeGrace, after which the connection is closed with them still open.
A dependency that wants its callers’ load spread across its pods sets MaxConnectionAge to a minute or a few: shorter reaches a scale-up’s new pods sooner, and costs each client a new connection and TLS handshake that often.
Which calls are retried Every unary RPC is retried with bedrock’s retry package, as Settings.Classify decides. NewClient builds one retry budget, one schedule and one retrier, shared by every method and every goroutine, so a Client is one dependency with one budget. Each attempt is one grpc-go RPC, and the call returns the last attempt’s error.
Retries are bounded three ways:
MaxAttempts bounds the attempts of each call, 3 by default, and 1 turns retries off. RetryBudget bounds every call to the dependency together, as gRPC’s retry throttling does, and as retry.Budget describes: each attempt classified Retry takes a token, each Success adds a tenth of one back, and retries stop while half the tokens or fewer are left. So while the dependency fails, every call makes one attempt, rather than three, and the retries don’t multiply its load. First attempts are never limited. Timeout bounds each unary call: every attempt, and the waits between them. The Client applies it to the call’s context before the first attempt, so a caller’s earlier deadline wins, but a later one doesn’t extend it: an end user whose calls need longer sets the field. A Timeout that has passed fails the call with DeadlineExceeded, and a wait that would end after the call’s deadline isn’t started: the call returns the last attempt’s error at once. The wait before each retry is drawn from retry.Exponential’s schedule, with BackoffBase and BackoffMax: after attempt n, from 0 up to the smaller of BackoffMax and BackoffBase·2ⁿ⁻¹.
An interceptor or other option in NewClient’s options runs inside the retries, once per attempt: an interceptor chained with grpc.WithChainUnaryInterceptor sees every attempt, as grpc-go’s stats handlers do.
grpc-go’s own configurable retries are off. grpc-go retries an RPC by itself when a service config gives its method a retryPolicy. The Client passes grpc.WithDisableRetry, so no service config, from grpc.WithDefaultServiceConfig in the options or any other source, turns them on: whether an RPC is tried again is decided by the Client, never by a service config that an operator can’t see in Settings. grpc-go’s transparent retries stay on. They retry an RPC when no data reached the wire, or when the server reports it never processed it, such as a stream refused by a server that sent a GOAWAY, so they never repeat anything a server saw.
How an attempt’s result counts Every attempt’s result is classified twice: for retry, whether another attempt follows, and for the dependency’s circuit breaker, whether the result counts against the dependency. Settings.Classify returns both, in a Classification. Some of that is about the call, and the Client decides it the same way for every dependency. The rest is about what the dependency’s codes mean, which differs from one API to another, and Classify decides it.
Classify gets the RPC’s full method name, such as /cart.v1.CartService/AddItem, the error the attempt ended with, nil for OK, and the attempt’s trailer. status.FromError gives the error’s code and its details.
What the client decides Classify isn’t asked about these, and the call ends, since another attempt can’t help:
a call the circuit breaker rejected. It reached nothing, and the breaker would reject the next attempt too; an error once the call’s context was cancelled: the caller gave up. The breaker ignores it; an error once the call’s deadline passed, Timeout or a deadline the caller set or inherited. The breaker counts it as a failure. And whatever Classify returns:
a RetryAfter longer than BackoffMax ends the call, with the attempt’s error, as The pushback describes; a stream that opened is never retried, as Streams describes. The default DefaultSettings().Classify decides, of every other result, by its code, which status.Code gives, so an error with no gRPC status, such as one an interceptor returns, is Unknown:
An attempt’s code Retry Breaker OK Success Success Unavailable Retry, after the pushback if there is one Failure ResourceExhausted with a pushback of 0 or more Retry, after the pushback Failure ResourceExhausted without a pushback Stop Failure DeadlineExceeded, Internal, Unknown, DataLoss Stop Failure Canceled Stop Ignored any other code, such as NotFound, InvalidArgument or Aborted Stop Success A grpc-retry-pushback-ms that is negative or not a number makes any of these Stop but OK, which has nothing to retry: the server asked not to be tried again.
Unavailable is gRPC’s code for “try again”. It is what grpc-go returns when it can’t reach the server, and what grpcserver ends streams with at shutdown. ResourceExhausted is retried only when the server says when. Without a pushback it is as likely to be a quota as an overload, and a quota isn’t fixed by trying again a few hundred milliseconds later. Either way it counts against the dependency, which is shedding load. DeadlineExceeded while the call’s own deadline is live is the server’s: it gave up on something of its own, such as its dependency. It counts, as the call’s own deadline does, and isn’t retried, because the server’s deadline is likely to end the next attempt the same way. Canceled while the call’s context is live comes from the server cancelling the RPC, or the connection closing at OnStop. It says nothing about the dependency. Any other code is the dependency working. It answered, and the request was wrong or conflicted with its state, so the breaker counts the dependency healthy, and the default doesn’t try again. The default reads only the code and the trailer, never a status’s details.
The default retries every method on Unavailable, whatever the method. A server that returns Unavailable after acting on a request breaks gRPC’s meaning of the code, so for most APIs that is safe. But grpc-go also returns Unavailable when the connection breaks after the request was sent, and then the server may have acted on it. So a method that must never be sent twice, such as one that charges a card, opts out in Classify, which gets the method: there is no per-method table in Settings.
Writing a Classify An end user whose API means something else by a code writes a Classify of their own, which usually handles what differs and hands the rest to the default. This API aborts a write that races another write to the same account, which is over by the next attempt, so its Classify retries Aborted, and counts it for the dependency rather than against it:
classify := s.Classify s.Classify = func(method string, err error, trailer metadata.MD) grpcclient.Classification { if status.Code(err) == codes.Aborted { return grpcclient.Classification{Retry: retry.Retry, Breaker: circuit.Success} } return classify(method, err, trailer) } s is the Settings here, whose Classify starts as the default. A method opts out of retries in a Classify that asks the default first, and turns its Retry into Stop for that method alone, so its result still counts in the breaker as the default says. Here EmptyCall stands in for a method such as Charge:
classify := s.Classify s.Classify = func(method string, err error, trailer metadata.MD) grpcclient.Classification { c := classify(method, err, trailer) // EmptyCall must never be sent twice: it makes one // attempt, and its result counts in the breaker as // the default says. if method == "/grpc.testing.TestService/EmptyCall" && c.Retry == retry.Retry { c.Retry, c.RetryAfter = retry.Stop, 0 } return c } One Classify serves every API that shares a convention, such as a company’s own services. The function is the end user’s own, so it is written once and set on the Client of each, here the two Clients of one address above:
// The APIs at gateway:9090 share a convention: Aborted says // another write to the account raced this one, which is over by // the next attempt. One Classify says so, and is set on the // Client of each. classify := grpcclient.DefaultSettings().Classify ourAPIs := func(method string, err error, trailer metadata.MD) grpcclient.Classification { if status.Code(err) == codes.Aborted { return grpcclient.Classification{Retry: retry.Retry, Breaker: circuit.Success} } return classify(method, err, trailer) } paymentsSettings.Classify = ourAPIs ledgerSettings.Classify = ourAPIs An API that sends google.rpc.RetryInfo in its statuses’ details, rather than a pushback, has a Classify that reads it with status.FromError and returns it as RetryAfter.
Classify is called on the goroutine that made the call, once for each attempt, so it must be safe for concurrent use. It is asked about OK, a nil error, too, so a Classify that returns retry.Retry for every result sends a call that succeeded again: it returns retry.Success for OK, as the default does. A Classification with a zero Outcome, or with retry.Retry and a negative RetryAfter, panics, as bedrock’s classifiers do. The Client recovers nothing: the panic passes to the goroutine that made the call. humus exports no classifier but the default, and no helpers to build one.
The pushback grpc-retry-pushback-ms is gRFC A6’s trailer, in which a server says how many milliseconds to wait before the next attempt. The default Classify reads it from the attempt’s trailer and returns it as the Classification’s RetryAfter, so the wait before the next attempt is the larger of it and the schedule’s. A pushback that is negative, not a number or given more than once means “don’t retry”. An end user’s Classify returns whatever its API says.
A RetryAfter longer than BackoffMax isn’t waited for, from any Classify: the call ends, and returns the attempt’s error. A server that asks for longer than that is not one a call in flight should wait on, and a wait past the call’s deadline would end it anyway.
The circuit breaker Each Client has one circuit breaker, bedrock’s circuit.Breaker, which guards the dependency at Addr: while the dependency keeps failing, the Client fails calls at once, rather than hold every caller for its timeouts and retries, and a probe now and then finds out when the dependency is back. The breaker sits inside the retries, so each attempt is a call it admits or rejects.
What counts is the Breaker of each attempt’s Classification: a Success counts toward the dependency being healthy, a Failure against it, and an Ignored result counts nothing. The caller giving up is ignored. Every deadline counts as a failure, whether it is Timeout or a deadline the caller set or inherited from the request it serves: a dependency that hangs ends every call that way, so a breaker that ignored deadlines would never open on the outage it exists for.
The default opens after 5 failures in a row, or once half of the last 20 or more results failed. It then rejects every call for Breaker.OpenFor, 10s, and then lets Breaker.Probes calls through at once, one by default: a failed probe reopens it, and 3 successful ones close it. Settings.Breaker configures, from configuration, the Window of results the policy sees, the Probes, and the durations OpenFor and ProbeTimeout. Settings.BreakerPolicy decides when it opens and closes, in code: its Trip decides the 5 and the half of 20, and its Probe the 3 successful probes. The ratio rule needs 20 results, so with a Breaker.Window below 20 only the rule of 5 failures in a row trips it. A policy whose Trip always returns false turns the breaker off:
s.BreakerPolicy.Trip = func(circuit.Counts) bool { return false } The policy’s functions run with the breaker locked, on the goroutine of the call whose result they decide on, so they must be fast and safe for concurrent use. A panic in one passes to that goroutine, and the breaker stays consistent, so the next call goes through it as before.
Rejections A call the breaker rejects reaches neither grpc-go nor the backend, and isn’t retried: the call ends at once. Classify isn’t asked about it. Its error matches circuit.ErrRejected with errors.Is, and *circuit.RejectedError with errors.As, whose RetryAfter says how much longer the breaker stays open. Its gRPC status is Unavailable, as for a server the Client can’t reach, with the rejection’s message, such as circuit: call rejected: open for another 4.2s. So code that handles Unavailable handles a rejection too, and code that needs to know nothing was sent asks errors.Is(err, circuit.ErrRejected).
Its log records The Client logs through the Setup’s LoggerProvider, under the scope github.com/z5labs/humus/grpc/grpcclient, one record for each change of the breaker’s state, in the context of the call that made it:
Record Severity When circuit breaker open WARN the breaker opens, from closed or from half-open circuit breaker half-open INFO OpenFor has passed, and the breaker lets a probe through circuit breaker closed INFO enough probes succeeded Each has the dependency’s server.address and server.port, from Addr, the state the breaker left as humus.circuit.previous_state, and the counts of that state: humus.circuit.successes, humus.circuit.failures, humus.circuit.consecutive_successes, humus.circuit.consecutive_failures and humus.circuit.timed_out. The bodies and the attributes are those of httpclient’s, so one query finds every breaker. The Client logs nothing else: an error is returned to the end user’s code, not logged.
Streams A stream runs the same loop as a unary call, with MaxAttempts and the backoff, but not Timeout: a stream may rightly live as long as its caller wants, so it ends with the context its caller opened it with. Each attempt opens the stream, through the breaker:
Opening is retried. Opening fails before anything reaches the server: no connection, or the channel in transient failure. A failed open is classified as a unary attempt is, and Classify gets it with no trailer, since nothing came back. An open stream is never retried. The end user’s code sends and receives on it directly, and a retry would replay what it already saw. A stream that fails after it opened ends with that error. A stream that opens is counted in the breaker once, when it ends, with the Breaker of Classify’s answer: when RecvMsg returns an error, which Classify gets with the stream’s trailer, and io.EOF given as nil; or, for a client-streaming RPC, when RecvMsg returns its one response, given as nil. A stream whose caller cancelled its context is ignored. One whose context reached its deadline counts as a failure, as a unary call’s does.
A stream its caller abandons, without reading it to its end or cancelling its context, is never counted. While the breaker is closed that costs nothing. While it is half-open, the abandoned stream holds a probe’s slot, but for at most Breaker.ProbeTimeout, after which another probe may go, and the probe counts as timed out, which the default policy reads as neither a success nor a failure. So one leaked stream can’t keep the breaker from closing.
Telemetry The Client takes everything from the Setup’s telemetry. NewClient’s first dial option is a stats handler, OpenTelemetry’s gRPC instrumentation, otelgrpc, given the TracerProvider, the MeterProvider and the Propagator of s.Telemetry. Nothing reaches OpenTelemetry’s globals: a process that sets them sees none of the Client’s spans or metrics.
Each attempt is one span of kind CLIENT, a child of the span in the call’s context, such as the server span of the RPC the end user’s handler serves, or a job’s run span. A call the Client retries is a span for each attempt, siblings under the caller’s span, and so is a call that grpc-go retries transparently. A stream is one span, from its opening to its end.
The span is named after the full method without its leading slash, such as cart.v1.CartService/AddItem. It carries the attributes of OpenTelemetry’s RPC semantic conventions, among them rpc.system.name, which is grpc, rpc.method, and rpc.response.status_code, the name of the call’s code, such as UNAVAILABLE. Its status is Error for every code other than OK: otelgrpc counts every failed call as an error on the client’s side, NotFound included, unlike on a server’s. A call the breaker rejected still has a span. Nothing reached grpc-go, so otelgrpc makes none, and the Client starts one of its own, under the scope github.com/z5labs/humus/grpc/grpcclient, named and attributed as otelgrpc names an attempt’s span, with rpc.response.status_code UNAVAILABLE, and with server.address and server.port taken from Addr, since no connection was made. It ends at once, with status Error and the rejection’s message.
Each attempt carries the trace context of its span, and the baggage of the call’s context, in its metadata, written by the Setup’s propagator. So a dependency served with grpcserver joins the caller’s trace, its server span a child of the attempt’s client span, and its handler sees the caller’s baggage.
Each attempt records rpc.client.call.duration on the Setup’s MeterProvider, in otelgrpc’s instrumentation scope. The Client records four instruments of humus’s own as well, for its breaker and its retries, as humus’s own instruments lists. The breaker’s state changes are the Client’s only log records, as Its log records lists.
What is still read from the real environment is what gRPC services records: grpc-go’s logger, which reads GRPC_GO_LOG_SEVERITY_LEVEL and the other GRPC_GO_LOG_ variables and writes to the real standard error, grpc-go’s other GRPC_ variables, and OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN, which otelgrpc reads. The Client adds nothing to that list.
humus’s own instruments The Client records four instruments of humus’s own, for its breaker and its retries, with the Setup’s MeterProvider, in the scope github.com/z5labs/humus/grpc/grpcclient, the scope of its log records:
Instrument Kind Unit Attributes Recorded humus.circuit.state asynchronous UpDownCounter {breaker} humus.circuit.state: closed, open or half-open at each collection: 1 for the breaker’s state, 0 for the other two humus.circuit.transitions Counter {transition} humus.circuit.state, the state it went to, and humus.circuit.previous_state, the one it left at each change of the breaker’s state, beside its log record humus.circuit.calls Counter {call} humus.circuit.outcome: success, failure, ignored or rejected as each unary attempt or stream counts in the breaker, or as the breaker rejects it humus.retry.decisions Counter {decision} humus.retry.decision: again, succeeded, stopped, exhausted, throttled or expired after each unary attempt and each attempt to open a stream Every data point also carries the dependency’s server.address and server.port, from Addr, the same as the breaker’s log records, and nothing per call, such as rpc.method: otelgrpc’s instruments break calls down already. Each other attribute’s value is the String() of bedrock’s own type, circuit.State, circuit.Outcome or retry.Decision.
humus.circuit.state is read, not tracked. At each collection it reads the breaker’s state once, so it shows half-open as soon as OpenFor has passed, with no call made. It is a count of breakers in each state, so two Clients of one address add up, as closed 1 and open 1. The App’s last collection, after the OnStop functions, still reads it, so the final export has the state the App stopped in. humus.circuit.transitions catches the short opens. A breaker can open, go half-open and close between two collections, a minute apart by default, and humus.circuit.state never shows it open. humus.circuit.calls counts a call when the breaker does. One call is one unary attempt, or one stream’s open. A unary attempt counts once it has returned, and a stream once it has ended, as Streams describes, so a stream that is still open counts nothing yet. A stream whose caller cancelled it counts nothing at all. It is the only place the verdicts of the end user’s Classify show. A call the breaker rejects is rejected: it never reached grpc-go, so it is in no instrument of otelgrpc’s. humus.retry.decisions counts what retry decided, so throttled counts the retries the budget refused, exhausted the calls that used every attempt, and expired the calls whose deadline came before the next attempt could start. A rejected attempt is stopped, and a stream that opens is succeeded, however it later ends. In Prometheus, they are humus_circuit_state, humus_circuit_transitions_total, humus_circuit_calls_total and humus_retry_decisions_total, and each attribute is a label such as humus_circuit_state. An alert on an open breaker reads the state, and one on breakers that open and close between scrapes reads the transitions:
# A breaker is open now. humus_circuit_state{humus_circuit_state="open"} > 0 # A breaker opened in the last 5 minutes, however briefly. increase(humus_circuit_transitions_total{humus_circuit_state="open"}[5m]) > 0 A View in the end user’s telemetry Builder drops or renames any of them. humus has no setting to turn them off. A test reads them as it reads any metric, with humustest.Telemetry’s Metrics, filtered to the scope.
Readiness: Connected Client.Connected returns a health.Monitor for readiness. It is healthy once the Client has connected to Addr: unhealthy until its connection is first ready, its TLS handshake done, and healthy from then until the connection is closed. It never returns an error. It goes in the readiness of whatever exposes the probes, here a grpchealth probes port, as Health describes:
carts, err := grpcclient.NewClient(s, cartsSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, serverSettings) if err != nil { return nil, err } testpb.RegisterTestServiceServer(svc, &api{carts: testpb.NewTestServiceClient(carts)}) // The service turns ready once its Client has connected to // carts, and stays ready through an outage of carts after // that. probes, err := grpchealth.NewService(s, probeSettings, health.Readiness(carts.Connected())) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{svc, probes}, nil What it gates is a rollout. NewClient dials nothing, so without it a release with a wrong Addr, a CA that doesn’t trust the server, a missing TLS config, or a dependency it can’t reach turns ready, replaces the pods that worked, and fails every RPC. With Connected in its readiness, it never turns ready, and the rollout stops at its progress deadline with the old pods still serving.
It latches, as a Kafka consumer’s Joined does, for the same reason. After the first connection, an outage of the dependency hits every pod at once. Turning them all unready would take the service out of its load balancer, so its callers would get no answer instead of this service’s own error, and the parts of it that don’t need the dependency would stop too. It would also block a rollout that might be the fix. So once the connection has been ready, the monitor stays healthy whatever the connection’s state: after a GOAWAY, from a server’s MaxConnectionAge or a rollout of the dependency, after a lost connection, and after grpc-go closes a connection idle for 30 minutes. Every monitor Connected returns reads the same latch, kept on the Client, so an HTTP probe and a gRPC one agree.
Connected is for readiness only. A liveness monitor would restart every pod in an outage of the dependency, and restarting the pod doesn’t bring a dependency back.
Its first check dials. Until the connection is first ready, a check while it is idle starts it, so a service with Connected in its readiness dials at its first probe rather than its first RPC. The check then waits until the connection is ready, the connection is closed, or the check’s context is done. So a reachable dependency passes the first probe, and an unreachable one fails it when the probe’s own timeout ends the check. A check makes no RPC: the dependency sees no call, the trace has no span, and nothing is logged. After s.OnStop has closed the connection, the monitor is unhealthy; by then every Service has stopped, and the probes have already turned readiness false.
A monitor of the dependency’s grpc.health.v1 A monitor that asks the dependency’s own grpc.health.v1 service is the end user’s own, a few lines over the Client:
monitor := health.MonitorFunc(func(ctx context.Context) (bool, error) { resp, err := healthpb.NewHealthClient(carts).Check(ctx, &healthpb.HealthCheckRequest{Service: "grpc.testing.TestService"}) return err == nil && resp.GetStatus() == healthpb.HealthCheckResponse_SERVING, nil }) Such a monitor makes an RPC through the Client, so whatever fails the Client’s calls fails it too: an outage of the dependency, and an open circuit breaker. It then turns unhealthy, and with it every pod, in the outage Connected’s latch exists to ride out. Connected makes no RPC, so neither turns it unhealthy. humus ships no such monitor.
Testing A service that calls a dependency is tested whole, inside testing/synctest, as Testing a humus App describes for any App. The Client dials through the Setup’s Host, so the dependency is a second App on the same humustest Host: a grpcserver Service that answers as the dependency would, with a certificate from a CA that humustest.NewCA generates for the test. grpcclient’s own tests start one with a helper:
// startCarts runs the dependency on h, at carts:9090, over TLS with a // certificate for carts from ca. It returns a function that stops the // dependency and requires it to exit 0. func startCarts(t *testing.T, h *humustest.Host, ca *humustest.CA) (stop func()) { t.Helper() cert := ca.Issue(t, "carts") p, exit := humustest.Start(t, func(_ context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { svc, err := grpcserver.NewService(s, grpcserver.Settings{ Addr: "carts:9090", TLS: &tls.Config{Certificates: []tls.Certificate{cert.TLS()}}, }) if err != nil { return nil, err } testpb.RegisterTestServiceServer(svc, carts{}) return []humus.Service{svc}, nil }, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(telemetry.NoopBuilder))) <-h.Listening("carts:9090") return func() { <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-exit require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) } } Its certificate is for carts, the host the Client’s Addr names, so the Client’s verification passes. carts is the test’s implementation of the service, whose UnaryCall answers with the username carts.
The end user’s whole App then runs against it, with the end user’s own Init above, through grpcservertest.Start, and the environment production gives it. The test writes the App’s certificate and the dependency’s CA into the Host’s filesystem with humustest.WithFiles, and names them with humustest.WithEnv, as Giving the App its certificate describes. pemFile and caPEM are helpers of the test file that PEM-encode them: pemFile a certificate’s chain and private key, and caPEM the CA certificate that issued a certificate. orders and the dependency’s certificate are both issued by ca, so caPEM(orders) is the dependency’s CA too:
synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) { ca := humustest.NewCA(t) orders := ca.Issue(t, "orders") h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(map[string][]byte{ "tls.pem": pemFile(t, orders), "carts-ca.pem": caPEM(orders), })) stop := startCarts(t, h, ca) defer stop() p, exit := grpcservertest.Start(t, Init, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(telemetry.NoopBuilder)), humustest.WithEnv(map[string]string{ "GRPC_ADDR": ":8443", "GRPC_TLS_PEM_FILE": "tls.pem", "CARTS_ADDR": "carts:9090", "CARTS_CA_FILE": "carts-ca.pem", }), ) <-h.Listening("orders:8443") client := testpb.NewTestServiceClient(grpcservertest.NewClient(t, h, "orders:8443", ca.Pool())) for range 2 { resp, err := client.UnaryCall(t.Context(), &testpb.SimpleRequest{}) require.NoError(t, err) require.Equal(t, "orders, via carts", resp.GetUsername()) } <-p.Notified(syscall.SIGTERM) p.Signal(syscall.SIGTERM) st := <-exit require.Zero(t, st.Code(), "cause: %v", st.Cause()) }) The RPC reaches the App, the App’s handler calls the dependency through the Client, and the answer comes back, all on the Host’s in-memory network, in no real time. The Client trusts the CA through RootCAs, so the test reads no system root and skips no verification.
Fake time makes the Client’s waits free too. A dependency that answers Unavailable with a pushback of 2000 costs the test 2s of fake time and no real time, and a breaker’s OpenFor passes just as instantly, so a test of retries, timeouts or the breaker opening and closing runs as fast as one of a single call. A dependency stopped with the function startCarts returns tests an outage, and a test that asserts on the Client’s spans, metrics or breaker records gives the App humustest.NewTelemetry()’s Builder rather than telemetry.NoopBuilder.
description: How to call gRPC dependencies with the grpcclient package: one Client per dependency, built in Init from grpcclient.Settings sourced with config.Struct, TLS and plain text, names and addresses behind a ClusterIP or a headless Service and spreading load with the server's MaxConnectionAge, which calls are retried and how the end user's Classify decides what a code means, the pushback, the circuit breaker and its log records, streams, what it records, readiness with Connected, and how to test the end user's whole App next to a grpcserver backend.

body:
humus packages are configured with plain Go values. They read no environment variables for their settings, define no variable names and read no files on your behalf; the few variables humus does read are listed below. Every value is sourced in your own Init, with whatever names and formats your service already uses: an environment variable called READ_TIMEOUT or MYSVC_HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT, a duration written 5s, a file of PEM, a flag. The usual tool is bedrock’s config package, and this page uses it throughout.
A framework that defined variable names would have to teach them, keep them consistent and document them twice. With Go values, godoc is the only documentation of a package’s settings, and a service’s variables are whatever its team chooses.
The design behind everything on this page is in the configuration revision of Proposal: configuration for humus apps.
What a package with settings exports Every humus package with settings exports the same three things:
a Settings struct, whose fields are plain values; DefaultSettings(), which returns the package’s defaults; a check function, Check<Field>, for each field that has a valid range. A zero field means zero, never “use the default”. A package’s defaults are the values DefaultSettings returns, and nothing else: a field left at zero is checked, and used, as zero. This keeps zero meaningful, as it is for net/http’s timeouts, where a zero ReadTimeout means no timeout.
The godoc of each field gives its default, its valid range and its meaning, and names its check. A check is a func(T) error. Its error says what is wrong, such as must not be negative, and does not name the field: whatever reads the value adds the name.
The samples on this page use a stand-in, declared in the root package’s tests in the shape every package gives it. The telemetry package’s Settings has the same shape, and Telemetry sources it with the same pattern, in the App’s telemetry Builder rather than in Init:
// Settings configures a Greeter. Every field is a plain value, and a field's // zero value means zero, never "use the default". type Settings struct { // Greeting is what the Greeter says. Default "hello". Greeting string // ReadTimeout bounds reading a whole request. Default 5s. Zero means // no timeout. Must not be negative; checked by CheckReadTimeout. ReadTimeout time.Duration // MaxConns is how many connections the Greeter serves at once. // Default 100. Must be positive; checked by CheckMaxConns. MaxConns int } // DefaultSettings returns the defaults of a Greeter. func DefaultSettings() Settings { return Settings{ Greeting: "hello", ReadTimeout: 5 * time.Second, MaxConns: 100, } } // CheckReadTimeout reports why d is not a valid ReadTimeout, or nil if it // is. func CheckReadTimeout(d time.Duration) error { if d < 0 { return errors.New("must not be negative") } return nil } // CheckMaxConns reports why n is not a valid MaxConns, or nil if it is. func CheckMaxConns(n int) error { if n <= 0 { return errors.New("must be positive") } return nil } In a real service these come from the package, as httpserver.Settings, httpserver.DefaultSettings() and httpserver.CheckReadTimeout, and you never copy a range out of godoc. Serving HTTP sources httpserver.Settings this way.
Sourcing Settings in Init Init reads the package’s Settings with config.Struct. Each field is one config.Value chain: where the value comes from, how it is parsed, .Default with the field of DefaultSettings(), and then the package’s check, chained with .Validate:
func GreeterInit(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { d := DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) } settings, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) Settings { return Settings{ // The file is read as part of the setting, so a missing file // is a config error named after the variable. Greeting: r.Get(env("GREETING_FILE").Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)).Default(d.Greeting)), ReadTimeout: r.Get(env("READ_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(d.ReadTimeout).Validate(CheckReadTimeout)), MaxConns: r.Get(env("MAX_CONNS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(d.MaxConns).Validate(CheckMaxConns)), } }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return nil, err // exit 78: every bad variable, one line each } g, err := NewGreeter(settings, s.Process.Stdout) if err != nil { return nil, err } return []humus.Service{g}, nil } The check goes after .Default, and the order matters for two reasons:
The default is checked too. A value that is not set is never checked, so a check chained before .Default would let a bad default through. Chained after it, a bad default fails exactly as a bad variable does. The error names the variable. A check in a field’s chain fails under that value’s name, so the error says READ_TIMEOUT, which is what an operator sets. A check on the whole struct could only name the field, ReadTimeout, which no operator sets. config.Struct attempts every Get, even after one has failed, so a misconfigured service reports all of its problems in one error rather than one per restart. Read every value through the Process and the Host in Setup, never through package os, so that the whole App runs in a test.
Reading a file A setting that names a file reads the file inside the field’s chain. Here GREETING_FILE is parsed by readFile, which opens the file through s.Host.FS:
// readFile returns a parser for config.Value.Parse that reads the whole // file a variable names, through fsys. func readFile(fsys humus.FS) func(name string) (string, error) { return func(name string) (string, error) { f, err := fsys.Open(name) if err != nil { return "", err } defer func() { _ = f.Close() }() b, err := io.ReadAll(f) return string(b), err } } Because the file is read as part of the setting, a missing or unreadable file is a config error named after its variable, and it exits 78 with the rest. humus.FS has no ReadFile: a helper this small is your code, not humus’s API, and it stays unexported. The same goes for decoding: a package takes a decoded value, such as a *tls.Config, never a path or a file’s contents, so how a certificate is stored and encoded is yours to decide. A further .Parse in the chain does the decoding.
How a bad value fails A bad value renders as config <variable>: <cause>. With READ_TIMEOUT=-5s and MAX_CONNS=lots, the App above logs both at ERROR through its telemetry, in one record of two lines, and exits 78:
init: config READ_TIMEOUT: must not be negative config MAX_CONNS: strconv.Atoi: parsing "lots": invalid syntax The lifecycle wraps the error Init returns once, as init: <error>, and logs it as it renders. config.Struct joins its failures with errors.Join, which renders one line per failure, so only the first line carries the init: prefix. Every line that names a bad variable starts config , prefix or not, and that is the word to search for.
And with GREETING_FILE naming a file that does not exist:
init: config GREETING_FILE: openat etc/greeter/greeting.txt: no such file or directory The cause is whatever the Host’s FS returned. This output is from the example, on a humustest Host, whose FS opens files through an os.Root, hence openat. On humus.OSHost() the same file fails with open <path>: no such file or directory.
Every error a config.Value returns is a *config.Error. When one is in the chain of the error Init returns, the App exits 78 (humus.ExitConfig, EX_CONFIG from sysexits.h), which tells an operator “fix the configuration” apart from “the service failed”. errors.AsType[*config.Error] finds the first bad variable in the chain, which is READ_TIMEOUT in the run above. A test that checks every bad variable walks the joined error, whose Unwrap() []error returns one *config.Error per variable, or compares the whole of the record the App logged. The lifecycle’s exit codes list the rest.
Building Settings in code config is a convenience, not a requirement. Settings can come from flags, a YAML file, or plain code:
settings := DefaultSettings() settings.ReadTimeout = -time.Second settings.MaxConns = 0 _, err := NewGreeter(settings, io.Discard) fmt.Println(err) A Settings built this way never passes through a check in a config chain, so the package’s constructor runs every check itself. It reports every bad field in one error, naming each field rather than a variable:
ReadTimeout: must not be negative MaxConns: must be positive The constructor of the stand-in shows the shape:
func NewGreeter(s Settings, out io.Writer) (*Greeter, error) { var errs []error if err := CheckReadTimeout(s.ReadTimeout); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("ReadTimeout: %w", err)) } if err := CheckMaxConns(s.MaxConns); err != nil { errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("MaxConns: %w", err)) } if err := errors.Join(errs...); err != nil { return nil, err } return &Greeter{settings: s, out: out}, nil } Its error is not a *config.Error, so an Init that returns it exits 1. A service that sources its settings with config and chains each check never reaches it: the bad value has already exited 78, named after its variable.
The variables humus reads humus reads the environment in two places, and neither is a setting of a package:
The lifecycle reads its two variables, HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD and HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY. humus.App.Run reads them before it calls Init, with defaults from App’s own fields, and checks each after its default, as on this page:
HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD defaults to the App’s ShutdownGracePeriod field: humus.Main’s 20s, or whatever an option, such as a runtime package’s defaults or humus.WithShutdownGracePeriod, or an App literal set it to. HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY, when it is set, replaces the App’s Drain, whatever that is, with humus.DrainDelay of its value, and adds a drain to an App that has none. When it is not set, the App’s Drain is the drain. The lifecycle’s settings describes them.
job reads the variables its propagator’s keys name. A job’s run joins the trace of the process that started it: job.Service extracts a trace context from the Process’s environment with the telemetry’s propagator, reading each of the propagator’s keys under the name OpenTelemetry’s environment-variable carriers give it. With telemetry.New’s propagator, those are TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE; a Builder with a propagator of another kind, such as B3, changes them. When none is set, or the value is malformed, the run starts a new trace and nothing fails. Jobs describes them.
Apart from the lifecycle’s two, humus still defines no variable names. The names job reads are OpenTelemetry’s: its specification names them, from the propagator’s keys, so a process that starts a job sets the same variables whatever language the job is written in. The telemetry package reads no OTEL_* variable either: a Builder that wants them maps them onto telemetry.Settings itself, as Telemetry shows.
Logging and secrets humus logs no settings, and it does not redact any. Whether to log the values a service started with, which ones, and how to hide a secret among them are your decisions. Init is given the same Process and Host that humus has, so it can log anything it wants, environment variables included, to s.Process.Stderr or to a logger of its own.
What humus does log is the error Init returns, through the App’s telemetry, and a parse error often quotes the value it could not parse: parsing "lots" above. A malformed secret, such as a token in the wrong format or a key that does not decode, would be logged the same way. Keeping a secret out of that error is part of the same choice: give the secret’s chain a parser of your own whose error says what is wrong without quoting the input.
Testing it Settings are tested by running the whole App with humustest.Start: humustest.WithEnv sets the variables, and a humustest Host holds the files the settings name. One of the root package’s examples runs the App above this way:
h := humustest.NewHost(t, humustest.WithFiles(files)) tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() p, status := humustest.Start(t, GreeterInit, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithHost(h.Host()), humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), humustest.WithEnv(env), ) st := <-status humus.WithHost replaces the Host Start builds with one the example made with its files, and humus.WithTelemetry passes humustest.Telemetry’s Builder, so the example prints the errors the App logged from the recorder’s Logs(). Both are humus’s own options, passed with humustest.WithApp as main passes them to humus.Main.
The App runs with Main’s defaults, so its grace period is Main’s 20s, as in production, and a HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD or HUMUS_SHUTDOWN_DRAIN_DELAY the test passes in WithEnv overrides it, as an operator’s would. WithEnv given twice keeps only the last map, so a test that adds to a base environment merges the maps itself, as Testing a humus App shows.
A relative name given to the humustest Host’s FS is relative to the test’s temp directory, and an absolute one, from h.Path, must be inside it, so a setting naming a file never reaches the real disk. Testing a humus App covers the Host in full.
description: How a humus service's settings get their values: humus packages take plain Go values, and the service's Init sources each one, usually with bedrock's config package, so that a bad value fails startup with exit 78 and an error naming the variable.

title: Configuring a humus service

body:
A humus App builds its OpenTelemetry providers before Init, hands them to Init as one value, logs through them, and shuts them down last. The telemetry package builds them from a plain Settings value. humus.Main builds them from telemetry.DefaultSettings() unless the service passes a Builder of its own, which sources that value the same way Init sources any other package’s settings.
The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: OpenTelemetry without globals, Revision 2. The lifecycle describes when the App builds its telemetry and shuts it down.
Where the providers come from A Service gets its providers from s.Telemetry, the telemetry.SDK in the Setup that Init is given. An SDK is a plain struct: a TracerProvider, a MeterProvider, a LoggerProvider, a Propagator, and the Shutdown that the App calls once it has stopped. Neither Init nor a Service calls Shutdown.
humus never reads or sets OpenTelemetry’s global providers or its global propagator, and it never replaces slog.Default. Every humus package takes an SDK, and third-party instrumentation is handed its providers explicitly: otelhttp’s options, grpc’s stats/opentelemetry options, and otelslog.WithLoggerProvider. This Init takes its Service’s tracer and logger from s.Telemetry:
func CartsInit(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) ([]humus.Service, error) { tracer := s.Telemetry.TracerProvider.Tracer("carts") logger := otelslog.NewLogger("carts", otelslog.WithLoggerProvider(s.Telemetry.LoggerProvider)) return []humus.Service{&cartJob{tracer: tracer, logger: logger}}, nil } A library that reads only the global providers can be given them: set them in Init, from s.Telemetry. That is your decision and your global state, not humus’s. The one piece of global state humus does set is OpenTelemetry’s error handler.
Main’s default App.Telemetry is a telemetry.Builder. humus.Main defaults it to one that calls telemetry.New with telemetry.DefaultSettings(), the Host’s Dial and the Process’s stdout. So a service that passes no Builder:
writes its log records to standard output, as JSON lines in the console log format; gives its spans real trace and span IDs, which its log records carry, and exports none; builds no exporter that dials out, so it needs no collector, and a service that forgets its Builder doesn’t fail. The defaults below describe what DefaultSettings() does in full. humustest.Start keeps the same default, so a whole-App test that passes no Builder sees on p.Stdout() the JSON lines production would write. This example runs the App of this page that way:
p, status := humustest.Start(t, CartsInit) st := <-status printConsoleLogs(p.Stdout(), "carts") fmt.Println("exit code:", st.Code()) // Output: // INFO "cart created" map[cart.id:c-123], trace context: true // INFO "cart created, untraced" map[], trace context: false // exit code: 0 A service that exports anything passes its own Builder, with humus.WithTelemetry, and so does one that names itself, since DefaultSettings() names every service unknown_service:
humus.Main(CartsInit, humus.WithTelemetry(buildCartsTelemetry)) Writing the Builder The end user’s Builder is given the context a signal cancels, the bedrock.Process and the Host’s Dial, and it does three things:
sources telemetry.Settings from p.Environment with config.Struct, starting from telemetry.DefaultSettings(); chains each field’s check after its default, so a bad default fails as a bad variable does, and the error names the variable; calls telemetry.New with the Settings, dial and p.Stdout. Configuring a humus service explains the pattern. This Builder keeps the OpenTelemetry specification’s variable names, but the names are yours to choose:
func buildCartsTelemetry(ctx context.Context, p bedrock.Process, dial telemetry.Dialer) (telemetry.SDK, error) { d := telemetry.DefaultSettings() env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(p.Environment, name) } exporter := func(name string, def telemetry.Exporter) config.Value[telemetry.Exporter] { return env(name). Map(func(s string) telemetry.Exporter { return telemetry.Exporter(s) }). Default(def). Validate(telemetry.CheckExporter) } s, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) telemetry.Settings { s := d s.Disabled = r.Get(env("OTEL_SDK_DISABLED").Parse(strconv.ParseBool).Default(d.Disabled)) s.ServiceName = r.Get(env("OTEL_SERVICE_NAME").Default("carts").Validate(telemetry.CheckServiceName)) s.Traces = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER", d.Traces)) s.Metrics = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER", d.Metrics)) s.Logs = r.Get(exporter("OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER", d.Logs)) return s }).Read(ctx) if err != nil { return telemetry.SDK{}, err // exit 78: every bad variable, one line each } return telemetry.New(ctx, s, dial, p.Stdout) } s := d starts from every default, so a field the Builder does not source, such as LogLevel here, keeps its default. DefaultSettings cannot see the process, so it names the service unknown_service. The Builder names it.
With OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=zipkin, this App never calls Init. It writes the error to standard error, because it has no telemetry yet to log it through, and exits 78:
build telemetry: config OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER: "zipkin" is not one of none, console or otlp telemetry.New runs every check too, so a Settings built in code is checked as well. Its error names each bad field, such as telemetry: Settings.Traces: "zipkin" is not one of none, console or otlp, and an App whose Builder returns it exits 1, not 78: the bad value came from code, not from a variable.
A Builder that needs something Settings does not cover, such as a metric view or a Prometheus reader, builds the SDK value itself, Shutdown included. humustest’s recorder is built that way.
Settings telemetry.Settings follows the shape every humus package’s settings take: plain values, DefaultSettings(), and a check for each field with a valid range. A zero field means zero, never “use the default”.
Field Default Valid Check Spec variable Disabled false any OTEL_SDK_DISABLED ServiceName "unknown_service" not empty CheckServiceName OTEL_SERVICE_NAME ResourceOptions none, so no detector runs any OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES, as resource.WithAttributes Traces ExporterNone none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER Metrics ExporterNone none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER Logs ExporterConsole none, console, otlp CheckExporter OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER OTLP.Endpoint "localhost:4317" host:port, with a port from 1 to 65535 CheckOTLPEndpoint OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT, which is a URL in the spec OTLP.Protocol ProtocolGRPC grpc, http/protobuf CheckOTLPProtocol OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL OTLP.Headers none any OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_HEADERS OTLP.TLS nil, which means plaintext any OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_CERTIFICATE and the related variables OTLP.Timeout 10s positive CheckOTLPTimeout OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT Sampler sdktrace.ParentBased(sdktrace.AlwaysSample()) not nil CheckSampler OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER and OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG LogLevel log.SeverityInfo log.SeverityTrace1 to log.SeverityFatal4 CheckLogLevel none ShutdownTimeout 5s positive CheckShutdownTimeout none The godoc of each field is the reference; the table is its summary. The OTLP fields are checked even when no signal is exported over OTLP. The OTLP exporters dial the collector through the Dialer the Builder is given, which is the Host’s Dial, and over http/protobuf each signal is sent to its spec path: /v1/traces, /v1/metrics and /v1/logs.
humus reads none of these variables. The last column names the specification’s variable with the same meaning, for a Builder that wants to stay compatible with it, as the one above does. It is not a variable humus reads: there is no FromEnvironment and no parser for the specification’s formats. So a platform that injects OTEL_* variables, such as the OpenTelemetry Operator, has no effect on an App unless its Builder reads them.
telemetry.New gives the OpenTelemetry SDK every option explicitly, at the SDK’s own default where Settings has no field, so the SDK’s own reads of the real environment are overridden too. The few that still take effect, such as OTEL_GO_X_*, are listed under the lifecycle’s ambient leaks.
The defaults With DefaultSettings():
Logs are written to standard output, as one line of JSON per record, in the console log format. Traces are not exported, but spans still get IDs. At ExporterNone, the TracerProvider is still the SDK’s, built with the Sampler and the resource but with no span processor. Every span gets a real trace ID and span ID, and a record logged in it carries them, but nothing is exported. That is the usual local setup: the logs on standard output can be grouped by request without running a collector. Metrics are a no-op. Sampling is the same with or without an exporter: the TracerProvider keeps the configured Sampler, so the sampled flag passed on to downstream services does not change when Traces does.
Traces at none have a cost in the middle of a shared trace. A service at none in a traced call chain passes on span IDs that no backend ever receives. The trace ID is still the caller’s, so the trace holds together, but the downstream spans point to a parent that is missing. A service that takes part in a traced system sets Traces to otlp.
The console log format At ExporterConsole, each log record is written to standard output as one line of JSON, terminated by a newline:
{"timestamp":"2026-10-16T06:56:32.447829601Z","severity_text":"INFO","severity_number":9,"body":"cart created","trace_id":"e2f668b6c06f2de82e61e2517c2d7a07","span_id":"ff25eb972a5557d5","trace_flags":"01","scope":"carts","attributes":{"cart.id":"c-123"}} This format is part of humus’s API. Renaming, reordering, adding or removing a key, or encoding a value differently, is a breaking change. It is humus’s own, written by an exporter of the telemetry package, so upgrading OpenTelemetry does not change it. A golden test pins it byte for byte.
The keys are always written in this order, and each one only when the record has what it holds:
Key Value Present timestamp the record’s timestamp or, when that is unset, its observed timestamp, in UTC, as RFC 3339 with exactly nine fractional digits always severity_text the record’s severity text or, when that is empty, the short name of its severity number: TRACE, TRACE2, …, INFO, …, FATAL4 when the severity number is set, that is when it is one of OpenTelemetry’s severities 1 to 24 severity_number the record’s OpenTelemetry severity number, 1 to 24, for filtering by threshold under the same condition as severity_text event_name the record’s event name when it is not empty body the record’s body, encoded as below when the body is set trace_id, span_id, trace_flags the trace context of the span the record was logged in, as lowercase hex: 32, 16 and 2 digits only when the record has a valid span context, one whose trace ID and span ID are both non-zero scope the name of the record’s instrumentation scope, the name its logger was created with always, and empty when that name is attributes an object whose keys are the attribute keys, in the record’s order when the record has at least one attribute The keys are the OpenTelemetry log data model’s field names, in snake case. The trace context keys follow OpenTelemetry’s stable specification for trace context in non-OTLP log formats, so a log pipeline links a line to its trace by the names the specification gives. A record logged outside a span has none of the three, rather than zeros, because a zero ID would point to a trace that does not exist.
The record’s resource is never written: OTLP carries the resource, and on standard output whatever collects the logs, such as a Kubernetes log agent, adds its own metadata. Neither is its count of dropped attributes.
A body and an attribute value are encoded the same way:
a string as a JSON string, a bool as true or false, and an integer as a JSON number; a finite float as a JSON number, and NaN and the infinities as the strings "NaN", "+Inf" and "-Inf", so that every line is valid JSON; bytes as a string holding their standard, padded base64 encoding; a slice, typed slices included, as an array, and a map as an object with its keys sorted by their bytes, each element encoded by these rules; an empty value as null, as an attribute’s value or inside a slice or map. An empty body is not written at all. An attribute key a record holds more than once, which happens only when its logger provider allows duplicate keys, is written once for each value, and so is a key a map holds more than once. Strings are escaped as JSON requires and no further: <, > and & are written as they are. Invalid UTF-8 is replaced by U+FFFD.
The telemetry package doc is the specification of the format, and this section its summary.
Traces and metrics at ExporterConsole are written by OpenTelemetry’s stdouttrace and stdoutmetric. They are for debugging, and humus makes no promise about their format.
Trace context in logs telemetry.SDK exposes a LoggerProvider, not a logger: humus has no logging bridge of its own. Use the OpenTelemetry Logs API directly, or bridge the LoggerProvider to the logging library you already use, such as otelslog for log/slog, as CartsInit above does.
A record carries a trace context only when the log call is given the span’s context. With otelslog, that means InfoContext, not Info: Info logs with context.Background(), so its record has no trace fields, whatever exporter it goes to. In a handler, pass the request’s context, r.Context(). This Service logs both ways inside one span:
func (j *cartJob) Serve(ctx context.Context) error { ctx, span := j.tracer.Start(ctx, "create cart") defer span.End() // InfoContext, not Info: the record takes its trace context from ctx, // so it carries the span's trace_id and span_id. j.logger.InfoContext(ctx, "cart created", slog.String("cart.id", "c-123")) // Info logs with context.Background(), so this record has no trace // context, even though it is logged inside the span. j.logger.Info("cart created, untraced") return nil } With the defaults, the first line on standard output has trace_id, span_id and trace_flags, and the second has none of them.
A job’s parent trace A job’s run joins the trace of the process that started it. job.Service extracts a trace context from the Process’s environment through the SDK’s Propagator, the one s.Telemetry carries, and the run’s span is that context’s child. With telemetry.New’s propagator, W3C trace context and baggage, it reads TRACEPARENT, TRACESTATE and BAGGAGE, the names OpenTelemetry’s environment-variable carriers give its keys. A Builder whose SDK has a propagator of another kind changes the variables read along with it. When none is set, as under Kubernetes, the run starts a new trace.
These are trace context, not settings: the OTEL_* variables in the table above are still read only by a Builder that maps them. Jobs covers the run’s span in full.
Other settings LogLevel is the lowest severity the LoggerProvider exports, as an OpenTelemetry severity rather than a slog.Level. It is applied in the provider: its loggers’ Enabled reports false below it, so a bridge that asks Enabled before building a record, as otelslog’s handler does, skips a filtered record at no cost, and a record below it is dropped either way. A record with no severity, log.SeverityUndefined, is not on the scale and is kept. ShutdownTimeout bounds SDK.Shutdown: every provider is flushed and stopped within it. The App shuts telemetry down after the OnStop functions, separately from the grace period and with a context that a cancelled root context does not cancel, so ShutdownTimeout is what bounds it. Disabled is the counterpart of OTEL_SDK_DISABLED. telemetry.New ignores every other field and returns telemetry.Noop(), building and dialling nothing. The propagator stays W3C trace context plus baggage, because the specification disables signals, not propagation, so a request’s trace passes through. Unlike traces at none, a disabled SDK makes no IDs of its own: it passes on the span context a request brought. Resource detectors are opt-in. The resource is ServiceName plus whatever ResourceOptions adds, and by default no detector runs, so the resource is service.name alone. A detector, such as resource.WithHost() or a contrib cloud detector, reads the real host rather than the humus.Host: the host, process and container detectors read /etc, /proc and cgroups, and a cloud detector dials its metadata server. Opt in knowingly. ServiceName wins over a service.name any detector finds. telemetry.New fails if any option fails, even partly, and some detectors fail where their attribute cannot be found: resource.WithProcess includes the process owner, which cannot be looked up in an image without a passwd entry for its user. Opt in to the detectors whose attributes the environment has, such as resource.WithProcessPID, rather than to a group of them. Testing A test that asserts on what an App emits runs it with humustest.Start, and passes humustest.NewTelemetry()’s Builder with humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(…)), in place of the one production uses. The recorder uses the real OpenTelemetry SDK with in-memory exporters, records every severity, samples every span, starts no goroutine, so it works under synctest, and keeps what it recorded after the App has shut it down:
tel := humustest.NewTelemetry() _, status := humustest.Start(t, CartsInit, humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(tel.Builder())), ) st := <-status Once the App has exited, tel.Spans(), tel.Metrics(ctx) and tel.Logs() return what it emitted. Here they show the span create cart, and that the record logged with InfoContext is in it:
span := tel.Spans()[0] fmt.Println("span:", span.Name()) for _, r := range tel.Logs() { if r.InstrumentationScope().Name != "carts" { continue // the lifecycle's own records } inSpan := r.TraceID() == span.SpanContext().TraceID() && r.SpanID() == span.SpanContext().SpanID() fmt.Printf("logged %s: %s, in the span: %t\n", r.SeverityText(), r.Body().AsString(), inSpan) } The lifecycle’s own records, serving, shutting down, stopped and every failure after the telemetry is built, are in tel.Logs() too, under the scope github.com/z5labs/humus.
A test that does not assert on telemetry keeps Main’s default, or passes telemetry.NoopBuilder, whose SDK discards everything. A test of the Builder itself passes it with humustest.WithApp(humus.WithTelemetry(…)), sets the environment it reads with humustest.WithEnv, and reads standard output, where the console logs go, and standard error, where a bad variable goes. The root package’s examples run the Builder above that way.
Testing a humus App covers the rest of a whole-App test.
The error handler Telemetry cannot report its own failure: a failing OTLP log exporter would swallow the errors about itself, and each error would queue another record bound to fail. So once the SDK is built, Run sets OpenTelemetry’s process-wide error handler to one that writes each export error to the Process’s standard error, as one line starting with telemetry: . Export errors join the failures standard error already gets, those that come before there is any telemetry or that are about telemetry itself: a failure to build or shut it down, and a malformed lifecycle setting.
This is the one piece of OpenTelemetry’s global state humus sets, and its one call to otel.SetErrorHandler. Being process-wide, it has two consequences:
In a process that runs several Apps, the last App to start gets every App’s export errors. So a test that asserts on export errors does not run in parallel with another App. An end user who wants a different handler sets it in Init, which runs after Run has set its own. OpenTelemetry’s internal logger is separate from the handler, and writes its own errors to the real standard error. It is on the lifecycle’s list of ambient leaks.
